details.summary: Covers glycolysis, anaerobic respiration (fermentation), Respiratory Quotient (RQ), human breathing mechanics (inspiration/expiration), and the pathway of air in internal respiration.

subject: Biology
text:
Circulation of body fluids is also referred to as circulatory system or internal transport. In higher and multicellular organisms, there is no direct supply of the useful materials and the removal of wastes from the body cells, so they need a transport system called circulatory system.

Types of Circulatory System

1. Open Circulatory System: Blood may be present in blood vessels for sometime, but finally comes out from the blood vessels in open spaces called sinuses. Found in annelids, cockroach, prawns, insects, spiders, starfish, etc. Blood flows with very slow velocity and low pressure. In cockroach, blood circulation is completed in 5-6 minutes. Blood is in direct contact with the tissues.

2. Closed Circulatory System: Blood flow in closed vessels. Found in earthworm, Nereis, molluscs and all vertebrates. Blood flows with high speed and at high pressure. Exchange of materials occurs through the tissue fluids. Blood does not come in direct contact with tissue cells. Respiratory pigment is present in RBCs.

details.summary: Overview of the circulatory system, its function in transport, and the distinction between open and closed circulatory systems with examples.

subject: Biology
text:
Blood Vascular System consists of three components:

1. Blood Vessels

Elastic muscular tubes that carry blood:

  • Arteries: Thick-walled, carry blood away from the heart. Deep seated, no valves, carry oxygenated blood (except pulmonary artery), high pressure and speed.
  • Veins: Thin-walled, carry blood to the heart. Superficial, have valves to prevent backflow, low pressure and speed, carry deoxygenated blood (except pulmonary vein).
  • Capillaries: Thinnest vessels, connect arteries to veins. Single layer of flat cells, facilitate exchange of nutrients, gases, and waste.

2. Blood

Red vascular connective tissue. Average adult has 4-6L. Forms 6-10% of body weight and 30-35% of extracellular fluid. Specific gravity 1.06. Viscous. Saltish taste, mildly alkaline (pH = 7.4). Bright red when oxygenated, purple when deoxygenated. Study of blood is haematology.

Composition:

  • Plasma: Faint yellow, non-living fluid, 55-60% of blood volume. Slightly alkaline and viscous.
  • Blood Corpuscles: 40-45% of blood.
tables:
| Components of Plasma | Percentage |
|---|---|
| Water | 90-92% |
| Inorganic salt | 1-2% |
| Plasma protein in colloidal state | 6-7% |
| Other organic compounds | 1-2% |
image_descriptions: Diagram showing the structure of erythrocytes (red blood cells) as circular, biconcave discs.

details.summary: Overview of the blood vascular system, focusing on the structural differences between arteries, veins, and capillaries, and the general properties and composition of blood.

subject: Biology
text:
Functions of Plasma

  • Transports simple food components (glucose, amino acids) from intestine and liver to other body parts.
  • Transports metabolic wastes like urea, uric acid from tissues to kidneys.
  • Transports hormones from endocrine glands to target organs.
  • Keeps constant pH of blood.
  • Blood proteins and fibrinogen in plasma help in blood clotting.

Blood Corpuscles

Three types:

  • Red Blood Corpuscles (RBCs) / Erythrocytes: Oval, biconvex, nucleated in most vertebrates; circular, biconcave, non-nucleated in mammals (except camel/llama). Normal count determined by haemocytometer.
  • White Blood Corpuscles (WBCs) / Leucocytes
  • Blood platelets

RBC Facts:

  • Thrombocytes (spindle cells) help in clotting.
  • High altitude increases RBC count.
  • Low RBC count causes anaemia.
  • High RBC count is polycythemia.
  • Lifespan: 120 days (human), 100 days (frog), 50-70 days (rabbit).
  • Haemoglobin: Iron-containing pigment, ~280 molecules per RBC.
  • Structure: Bounded by elastic semipermeable membrane, lacks cell organelles to maximize space for haemoglobin.

details.summary: Detailed breakdown of plasma functions and the characteristics of blood corpuscles, specifically focusing on RBC physiology and pathology.

subject: Biology
text:
Red Blood Corpuscles (RBC)

  • Colour: Appears yellow when seen singly, but red in bulk due to haemoglobin.
  • Formation: In foetus, takes place in liver and spleen; after birth, mainly in bone marrow.
  • Maturation: Controlled by folic acid and vitamin-B12. Excess RBCs stored in spleen (blood bank of the body).
  • Functions: Maintains constant pH; transports CO2 from tissues to lungs and oxygen from lungs to tissues.

White Blood Corpuscles (WBCs)

Also called leucocytes or leukocytes. Involved in protecting the body against infectious disease and foreign invaders.

  • Shape: Rounded or amoeboid (irregular), nucleated, non-pigmented. Larger than RBCs.
  • Number: Much less than RBCs (ratio 1:6).
  • Leukemia: Pathological increase in WBCs.
  • Leucopenia: Fall in WBC count.
  • Colour: Colourless.
  • Formation: Red bone marrow.
  • Lifespan: 8-96 hours.

Classification of WBCs

Granulocytes (approx 65% of total leucocytes):

  • Neutrophils: 62% of total WBCs. Originate from bone marrow. Cytoplasm has fine granules. Nucleus is 3-5 lobed. Lifespan 10-12 hours. Help in sex differentiation and act as soldiers.
  • Basophils: Also called cyanophils. Nucleus is 2 or 3-lobed or S-shaped. Lifespan 8-12 hours. Secrete heparin and histamine (local anticoagulation).
  • Acidophils: Also called eosinophils. Lifespan 14 hours. Increase in allergic diseases. Help in healing of wounds.

Agranulocytes (approx 35% of total leucocytes):

  • Monocytes: Largest leucocytes (5.3%). Nucleus is oval, kidney or horse shoe-shaped and excentric. Formed in lymph nodes and spleen. Highly motile. Lifespan 3-4 days.
  • Lymphocytes: 30% of leucocytes. Nucleus is large and rounded. Formed in bone marrow, thymus, lymph nodes, spleen, tonsils. Lifespan 3-4 days. Produce antibodies and opsonin.

Blood Platelets

  • Shape: Oval-shaped, discoidal cytoplasmic fragments.
  • Number: 250,000-5,000,000.
  • Thrombocytopenia: Decrease in platelets.
  • Thrombocytosis: Increase in platelets.
  • Structure: Flat, non-nucleated large cells in bone marrow. Bounded by membrane, contain few organelles. Role in blood clotting.
  • Colour: Colourless.
  • Formation: Red bone marrow.
  • Lifespan: About one week.
image_descriptions: Microscopic structure of various WBCs showing Basophil, Eosinophil, Neutrophil, Lymphocyte, and Monocyte with visible granules and nuclei.
Flowchart showing classification of WBCs into Granulocytes (Neutrophils, Basophils, Acidophils) and Agranulocytes (Monocytes, Lymphocytes).

details.summary: Detailed overview of blood components including RBCs, WBCs (Granulocytes and Agranulocytes), and Platelets, covering their formation, structure, and functions.

subject: Biology
text:
Blood Groups: Landsteiner recognised three kinds of blood groups 'A', 'B' and 'O'. Fourth and most rare 'AB' blood group was discovered by Von Decastello and Sturle (1902). Landsteiner (1900) discovered two kinds of antigens called a and b. Antigens a and b are not proteins, but are mucopolysaccharides.

Rh-Factor: Rh-factor was first of all reported in RBCs of a monkey by Landsteiner and Wiener in 1940. Rh-factor is actually the Rh antigen present on the surface of red blood cells. Person having Rh-factor is called Rh+ and without Rh factor is Rh-. About 85% of world's people are Rh+. Percentage of Rh+ people in India is 97% of the population. Rh-factor is found in man and rhesus monkey, it has not been reported from other animals.
tables:
| Blood group | Antigens in RBCs | Antibodies in plasma | Can donate to groups | Can receive from groups |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | a | Anti-b | A, AB | O, A |
| B | b | Anti-a | B, AB | O, B |
| AB | a and b | None | AB | O, A, B, AB |
| O | None | Anti-a, Anti-b | O, A, B, AB | O |

details.summary: Overview of ABO blood grouping system, discovery history, and Rh-factor characteristics.

subject: Biology
text:
Heart: It is a muscular organ in both humans and other animals, which help in pumping blood via blood vessels of the circulatory system.

  • In amphibians, heart is three-chambered.
  • Reptilian heart is structurally three-chambered, but is functionally four-chambered (i.e. incompletely four-chambered) except in crocodile.
  • In crocodile, birds and mammals the heart is divided into four chambers (two auricles and two ventricles).
  • Every person's heart is of about the same size as that of person's first. The human heart is four-chambered, two auricles and two ventricles.
  • A thin, muscular wall called the interatrial septum separates the left and right atria, whereas thick-walled interventricular septum separates the right and left ventricles.
  • The atrium and ventricle of same side are separated by atrioventricular septum.
  • Opening between right atrium and right ventricle is tricuspid valve, formed of 3 cusps and opening between left atrium and left ventricle is called bicuspid or mitral valve.
  • Pulmonary artery and aorta are provided with semilunar valves to prevent backflow of blood.
  • Sino Atrial Node (SAN) is present in right upper corner of right atrium. Atrio Ventricular Node (AVN) is present in lower left corner of right atrium.

Cardiac Cycle: The sequence of events, which occur from the beginning of one heartbeat to the beginning of next is called cardiac cycle. Systole refers to contraction and diastole refers to relaxation. Single cardiac cycle involves four steps:

  1. Atrial Systole: Right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from superior and inferior vena cava. Left atrium receives oxygenated blood through pulmonary veins. The atria contract due to wave of contraction stimulated by SA node.
  2. Ventricular Systole: Action potential passes from SA node to AV node. The blood is then forced into ventricles leading to contraction of ventricles. At this time first heart sound is produced due to closure of valves. When the contraction is complete blood flows to pulmonary arteries carrying deoxygenated blood to lungs.
  3. Ventricular Diastole: Semilunar valves close to produce second heart sound. The ventricular relax. AV valve opens to allow blood to pass from atria to ventricles again. Left ventricles supply oxygenated blood to aorta, which in turn supplies blood to various body parts.
image_descriptions: Diagram of the internal structure of the human heart showing Vena cava, Right atrium, Right ventricle, Septum, Left ventricle, Left atrium, Pulmonary veins, Pulmonary arteries, and Aorta.

details.summary: Detailed anatomy of the heart across species and the physiological process of the cardiac cycle.

subject: Biology
text:
Blood Pressure (BP): The pressure exerted by the blood on the walls of the blood vessels due to the repeated pumping of heart is called blood pressure. The rate of pulsation increases during excitement.

  • Blood pressure is recorded as systolic/diastolic.
  • Blood pressure in a normal adult person = 120/80 mm Hg.
  • If a person has persistent high blood pressure then it is called hypertension. To avoid hypertension good cholesterol, i.e. high density lipoprotein should be consumed.
  • Hypotension is condition of low blood pressure.
  • ECG or Electrocardiogram is a graphic record of the electric current produced by the excitation of cardiac muscles.
  • The normal rate of heartbeat at rest is about 72-80 beats per minute.
  • In a newly born baby, heartbeat rate is about 140 beats per minute.
  • During heavy exercises, it may be high as 170-200 beats per minute.
  • Sphygmomanometer measures BP.

IMPORTANT POINTS TO REMEMBER

  • Haemoglobin can readily combine with carbon monoxide.
  • Blood does not coagulate inside the body due anti-coagulant heparin.
  • The crew and passanger of aircraft usually suffer from pulmonary problems because of the presence nitrogen oxide in the atmosphere.
  • Coronary arteries supply blood to the right atrium.
  • Hepatic portal system and renal portal system supply and take blood from liver and kidney respectively.
image_descriptions: Flowchart showing circulation of blood: Superior vena cava and Inferior vena cava lead to Right atrium, then to Right ventricle, then to Pulmonary artery, then to Lungs, then to Pulmonary veins, then to Left atrium, then to Left ventricle, then to Aorta, which branches to capillaries in head region and capillaries in body organs.

details.summary: Covers definition of blood pressure, normal values, hypertension, hypotension, ECG, heart rate variations, and key physiological facts regarding blood and circulation.

subject: Biology
topic: Excretory Organs and Types of Excretion
text:
Excretory Organs in Different Animals

  • Plasmalemma: Protozoans like Amoeba.
  • General body surface: Porifera (sponges), coelenterates (Hydra).
  • Flame cells: Platyhelminthes (Taenia and Fasciola).
  • Nephridia: Annelida.
  • Malpighian tubules: Arthropods (cockroach).
  • Coxal gland: Spiders.
  • Kidney: Main excretory organ in all vertebrates.
  • Antennal gland or green gland: Crustaceans crayfish.

Types of Excretion

Depending upon the form of nitrogenous waste excreted, there are three modes of excretion:

  1. Ammonotelism: Elimination of nitrogenous end product mainly as ammonia. Found in aquatic animals like protozoans (e.g. Amoeba, Paramecium), sponges (e.g. Sycon), coelenterates (e.g. Hydra), aquatic arthropods (e.g. Prawn), most aquatic molluscs (e.g. Pila), bony fishes (e.g. Labeo) and frog's tadpole.
  2. Ureotelism: Process in which main nitrogenous waste is urea. Common in man, whales, seals, camels, kangaroo, toads, frogs, sharks, etc.
  3. Uricotelism: Main nitrogenous waste is crystals of uric acid. Common in birds, land reptiles (snakes and lizards), insects, snails, etc.

Excretory System of Human

Consists of: (a) Kidneys (two), (b) Ureter (two), (c) Urinary bladder (one), (d) Urethra (one).

1. Kidneys: Bean-shaped, chocolate brown structure lying in the abdomen, one on each side of the vertebral column just below the diaphragm. These form the urine and control osmotic pressure. The left kidney is placed a little higher than the right kidney (but reverse in rabbit). Concavity of kidney called hilum or hilus, is always inward directed.

details.summary: Overview of excretory organs across animal phyla, classification of excretion modes (Ammonotelism, Ureotelism, Uricotelism), and anatomy of the human kidney.

subject: Biology
text:
Excretory System Components

  • Ureters: A pair of narrow tubes arising from the hilum, approx 30 cm in length, transporting urine to the urinary bladder.
  • Urinary Bladder: A medium pear-shaped sac in the lower pelvic region; stores urine temporarily. Absent in birds (they have a cloaca).
  • Urethra: Muscular tube extending from the bladder neck. In females, it is short and serves only for urine; in males, it is long and serves as a common passage for urine and spermatic fluids.

Nephron Structure

The structural and functional unit of the kidney, also called renal tubules or uriniferous tubules. It consists of:

  • Bowman's Capsule: Double-walled cup lined with podocytes, containing the glomerulus (capillary group) which acts as a dialysing bag.
  • Proximal Convoluted Tubule (PCT): Highly coiled, 12-24 mm long. Site of active reabsorption of vitamins, glucose, amino acids, sodium, and potassium.
  • Henle's Loop: U-shaped segment in renal medulla. Long in mammals/birds (secrete hypertonic urine), short in reptiles.
  • Distal Convoluted Tubule (DCT): Curved/twisted, connected to the collecting duct. Site of active Na+ reabsorption; impermeable to H2O.

Urine Characteristics

  • Pale-yellow transparent fluid due to urochrome pigment.
  • Acidic, heavier than water, faint aromatic odour.
  • Daily output: 1.5-1.8 L.
  • Composition: Water (95-96%), Urea (2%), others like uric acid/creatinine (2-3%).

Skeleton System

Composed of bones, muscles, cartilage, ligaments, and tendons (collagen fibres).

  • Axial Skeleton (80 Bones): Includes skull, vertebral column, and chest bones. Supports upright position.
  • Key Facts: Head (29 bones), Vertebral column (initially 33, 26 after development), Ribs (24 bones).
image_descriptions: Diagram of the human excretory system showing the Inferior vena cava, Aorta, Left kidney, Right kidney, Renal artery, Renal vein, Ureter, Urinary bladder, and Urethra.

details.summary: Detailed overview of the human excretory system components, nephron anatomy, urine composition, and the axial skeleton structure.

subject: Biology
text:
Appendicular Skeleton (126 Bones)

  • It consists of pelvic and pectoral girdles.
  • Girdles are the structures, which connect the limb bones with the vertebral column.
  • Their functions are to make locomotion possible and to protect the major organs of locomotion, digestion, excretion and reproduction.
  • Calcium and phosphorous are two minerals that helps in giving strength to bones. Deficiency of these may cause we opening of bones.

details.summary: Overview of the appendicular skeleton, its composition, and the role of minerals in bone health.

subject: Biology
text:
Nervous System

The nervous system provides the fastest means of communication within the body, so that suitable response to stimuli can be made at once. Nervous system is found only in animals and absent in plants. It is made up of nervous tissue. Nervous system controls the body by using a series of tissues throughout the body formed by a network of electrically conducting cells called neurons or nerve cells.

Neuron

It is the structural and functional unit of nervous system. Neurons are of three types:

  • (i) Motor: Conducts messages from central nervous system to effector organs.
  • (ii) Sensory: Conducts information from sensory organ to central nervous system.
  • (iii) Mixed: Works both as sensory and motor neuron.

Structure of Neuron

A neuron is a microscopic structure composed of three major parts, i.e. cell body, dendrites and axon.

  • Dendrites: Cytoplasmic processes from cell body. They carry impulses towards cell body.
  • Cell body: Also called cyton or soma. It contains cytoplasm and certain granular bodies called Nissl's granules.
  • Axon: Single long extension of cell body that protected by membrane neurolemma.
  • Synapse: It is the junction between the dendrites of one neuron with axon terminal knobs of other neuron.

Classification of Neuron/Nerve Cell

Neurons are of two types:

  1. Myelinated: Axon is composed of Schwann cell coated by myelin sheath. The gap between adjacent myelin sheath is called nodes of Ranvier.
  2. Non-myelinated: Axon is composed of Schwann cells not enclosed by myelin sheath.
image_descriptions: Flowchart showing classification of neurons based on axon and dendrites: Unipolar (one axon), Bipolar (one axon and one dendrite), Multipolar (one axon and two or more dendrites).

details.summary: Detailed breakdown of the nervous system, neuron structure, types, and classification.

subject: Biology
text:
Types of Nervous System

Main parts of nervous system are as follow: Central nervous system (Brain, Spinal cord) and Peripheral nervous system (Somatic nervous system, Autonomic nervous system (Parasympathetic, Sympathetic)).

Central Nervous System (CNS)

The CNS is the site of information processing and control. It consists of brain and spinal cord.

  • Grey matter is made up of cell bodies of neuron and white matter has only nerve fibres.
  • Brain lies in the cranial cavity of skull. Brain and spinal cord are covered by two meninges in frog and three meninges in mammals.
  • Cerebrospinal fluid is present in and around brain and spinal cord.

Human Brain

Brain is soft, whitish in colour and somewhat a flattened organ. It is the only thing in the universe, which is attempting to understand itself. It is mainly divided into three main parts: Forebrain, Midbrain, Hindbrain.

Forebrain

It forms the greatest part of brain. It consists of following types:

  • Cerebrum: It is the largest part of the brain covered by cerebral hemispheres. The roof of cerebrum is cerebral cortex. Cerebrum leads to consciousness, storage of memory of information.
  • Olfactory lobes: These are pair of small sized structure, completely covered by cerebrum. These are the centre of skull.
  • Thalamus: It is for integrity of sensory impulses sent from sense organs like eyes, ears and skin. It deals with pain, pressure and temperature.
image_descriptions: Flowchart of nervous system hierarchy: Nervous System -> Central (Brain, Spinal cord) and Peripheral (Somatic, Autonomic (Parasympathetic, Sympathetic)).
Flowchart of Brain: Forebrain (Cerebrum, Olfactory lobes, Thalamus/Hypothalamus), Midbrain (Corpora quadrigemina, Corpora diencephalon), Hindbrain (Cerebellum, Medulla oblongata, Pons).

details.summary: Overview of the Central Nervous System, its components, and the structure of the human brain.

subject: Biology
text:
• Broca's area: Present in brain and related with understanding speech.
  • Wernick's area: Related with understanding speech.
  • Hypothalamus: Deals with water balance in body, behavioural patterns of sex, sleep, stress, emotions, etc. It also regulates pituitary hormones and metabolism of fat, carbohydrate and water.

Midbrain

Located between hypothalamus and pons of the hindbrain.

  • Consists of two pairs of rounded swelling lobes called corpora quadrigemina (solid structures).
  • Deals with visual analysis, auditory, etc.
  • Midbrain of rabbit consists of four optic lobes.

Hindbrain

Consists of cerebellum, pons varolii and medulla oblongata.

  • Cerebellum: Bottom part of the head and back of it. Controls coordination of accurate movements and balancing. Considered as small brain.
  • Medulla oblongata: Lowermost part of brain, connected to spinal cord. Deals with control of heartbeats, blood vessels, breathing, salivary secretion and most of reflex and involuntary (uncontrolled) movements.
  • Pons Varolii: An oval mass that lies above medulla oblongata. It interconnects two cerebellar hemispheres and also joins the medulla with higher brain centres.

Spinal Cord

Long cord-like structure present at the back, centrally located and well-protected by bony vertebral column.

  • It gives out 31 pairs of spinal nerves in man.
  • It conducts impulses to and from the brain.
  • It is the centre for reflex actions and provides means of communication between spinal nerves and the brain.

Reflex Action

Unconditional, inborn and unlearned reflex to a stimulus.

Examples: Blinking of the eye when an object comes near to our eyes suddenly, rapid withdrawal of hand, while burned, sneezing, coughing, yawning, knee-jerk reflex, etc.

Acquired Reflex Action

Also called conditioned reflex and dependent on past experience, training and learning. These are under cerebral control during learning. First demonstrated by Ivan Petrovitch Pavlov in hungry dog.

Examples: Learning of dancing, cycling, swimming, singing and driving, etc.

details.summary: Overview of brain structures (Midbrain, Hindbrain), Spinal Cord, and types of Reflex Actions.

subject: Biology
text:
Peripheral Nervous System

Composed of 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves.

  • Cranial nerves emerge from brain, while spinal nerves arise from spinal cord. Different number of cranial nerves are present in different organism.
  • e.g. 10 pairs of cranial nerves are present in fishes and amphibians.
  • Number of cranial nerves found in rabbit is 12 (same as man) but 37 spinal nerves are present in rabbit.
  • The first 10 pairs are common for frog and rabbit.

Autonomous Nervous System

Discovered by Langley. It is entirely motor and operates without conscious control. Consists of two divisions:

  • (i) Sympathetic nervous system: Increases defence system of body against adverse conditions and active in stress conditions, e.g. pain, fear and anger.
  • (ii) Parasympathetic nervous system: Provides relaxation, comfort, pleasure at the time of rest and helps in the restoration and conservation of energy.

SENSE ORGANS

The sensory organs (receptors) enable us to detect all types of changes in the environment and send appropriate signals to the CNS, where all the inputs are processed and analysed signals are then sent to different centres of brain.

subject: Biology
text:
Ears are a pair of stato-acoustic organs meant for both sensory functions, i.e hearing and maintainance of body balance. The study of structure, function and disease of ear is called otology.

  • These are located on sides of head.
  • Hearing is controlled by auditory area of temporal lobe of cerebral cortex.
  • The measuring unit of sound frequency is decibel. Human ear can listen the sound of 60-80 decibel.
  • Human ear is sensitive to sound frequency 50-20000 cycles/sec and most sensitive to a frequency of 1000-3000 cycles/sec.
  • Human ear is divided into three parts as: External ear (pinna + external auditory meatus), middle ear (tympanic cavity), internal ear (membranous labyrinth).

(i) External Ear

  • The external organ consists of pinna and auditory canal.
  • Pinna is designed to collect sound waves.
  • Auditory canal contains few hairs and specialised sebaceous glands called ceruminous glands. These glands secrete cerumen (ear wax), it prevents foreign particles from entering the ear.

(ii) Middle Ear

  • Tympanic membrane (ear drum) separates middle ear from external ear.
  • The middle ear consist of three auditory ossicles. These are: (a) Malleus Outer and hammer-shaped. (b) Incus Middle and oval-shaped. (c) Stapes Inner and stirrup-shaped attached on the outer surface of fenestra ovalis membrane.
  • The smallest bone in human body is stapes.
  • The passage connecting the middle ear with pharynx is Eustachian tube.
  • Eustachian tube equalises pressure in both sides (external and middle ear) or tympanic membrane.

(iii) Internal Ear

  • The inner ear consists of a labyrinth of fluid-filled chambers within the temporal lobe of the skull. Labyrinth consists of two main divisions: (a) Bony labyrinth is filled with a fluid called perilymph, while membranous labyrinth contains endolymph. (b) Membranous labyrinth is concerned with both balancing and hearing.
  • Internal ear is formed of three parts: (a) Body proper (utricules and sacculus) (b) Semicircular canals (c) Cochlea
  • Cochlea is small snail-shaped structure.
  • It makes 2 1/2 turns in rabbit and 2 3/4 turns in man.
  • Three chambers in cochlea are scala vestibuli, scala media and scala tympani.
  • Scala media contains the organ of hearing named organ of Corti (discovered by Alfonso Corti).
  • Defects of ear are otalgia earache (pain in ear) acute infection of middle ear, labyrinthine disease (malfunction of ear).
image_descriptions: Anatomical diagram of the human ear showing the pinna, external auditory meatus, tympanic membrane, tympanic cavity, ossicles (Malleus, Incus, Stapes), semicircular canals, vestibular nerve, facial nerve, cochlea, and cochlear nerve.

details.summary: Overview of human ear anatomy, including external, middle, and internal ear structures, functions, and common ear defects.

subject: Biology
text:
The organ of sight is a pair of eyes in human. Eyes are situated in deep bony cavities called orbits or sockets of the skull. These are the sensitive detectors of light. It is most sensitive to yellow colour.

  • The study of structure, functions and diseases of eye is called ophthalmology.
  • Eyeball is made basically of three concentric layers:
  • Outermost fibrous layer composed of sclera and cornea.
  • Cornea is thin transparent front part of sclera, which locks blood vessels, but is rich in nerve endings.
  • Sclera outermost, tough and opaque part. It maintains the shape of eye.
  • Middle layer consists of choroid, ciliary body and iris.
  • Choroid chocolate coloured, pigmented (with melanin) present along innerside of sclera.
  • Iris consists of circular sphincter and radial dilators. It adjusts the size of pupil.
  • Pupil is the black hole in the centre of the iris, through it light enters the eyeball. It also controls the light entering into the eye.
  • Conjunctiva Cornea is covered by a thin transparent layer called conjunctiva. It refracts the incident light rays to focus on the retina.
  • Lens is a biconvex, transparent, circular, solid structure and is proteinaceous in nature.
  • Aqueous humor is filled between cornea and lens.
  • Vitreous humor is filled in space between the lens and the retina.

details.summary: Overview of human eye anatomy, including layers, components like cornea, iris, pupil, lens, and humors.

subject: Biology
text:
• Retina: Innermost and incomplete layer consisting of a nervous tissue layer and a pigmented layer. Image of object is formed on retina.
  • Retina is composed of two types of cells: rod cells and cone cells. The image formed on it is real and inverted.
  • Rods: Longer, slender and filamentous; highly sensitive to dim light, contain a reddish-purple pigment called rhodopsin.
  • Cones: Sensitive to bright light, hence differentiate colours (red, green, blue).
  • Yellow spot (macula lutea): Exact centre of the retina, area of sharpest vision due to high concentration of cones.
  • Blind spot (optic disc): Has no rods and no cones, hence no image forms in this region.
  • Tapetum lucidum: Increases the sensibility of vision; made up of zinc, cysteine and guanine. Causes eyes of carnivores (cat, dog, lion, seal) to glow at night.
  • Atropine: Chemical used by doctors to dilate the pupil.
  • Night blindness: Caused by deficiency of rhodopsin in rod cells.
  • Colour blindness: Caused by deficiency of cones. Visual pigments for colour: (a) Erythropsin (sensitive to red), (b) Chloropsin (sensitive to green), (c) Cyanopsin (sensitive to blue).

details.summary: Structure and function of the human eye, including photoreceptor cells and common visual pigments.

subject: Biology
text:
• Myopia (short-sightedness): Image of distant object formed in front of retina. Corrected by concave lens.
  • Hypermetropia (long or far-sightedness): Image formed behind the retina. Corrected by convex lens.
  • Astigmatism: Due to irregular cornea or lens, corrected by cylindrical lens.
  • Cataract: Eye disease in older people where lens becomes opaque; corrected by operation.
  • Conjunctivitis: Inflammation of conjunctiva by bacteria.

details.summary: Common eye disorders and their corrective measures.

subject: Biology
text:
Nose is a sense organ for smell or olfaction. The nose contains mucus coated olfactory (smell) receptors. The nasal cavity is lined by olfactory epithelium lines. Olfactory epithelium has three principal kinds of cells:

  • (i) Olfactory bipolar neurons
  • (ii) Columnar epithelial cells
  • (iii) Bowman’s gland

details.summary: Anatomy of the olfactory system.

subject: Biology
text:
Organs for gustation are taste buds, present in the mucosa of taste papillae on upper surface of tongue. Taste buds are numerous on the tongue, but also found on the soft palate, pharynx and epiglottis. A papilla may contain few to many hundreds of taste buds. Taste buds are more numerous in children than in adults.

Location of taste buds for basic tastes:

  • Sweet: On the tip of tongue.
  • Salty: On upper surface of anterior half.
  • Sour: Lateral side of tongue.
  • Bitter: Near the base of tongue.

Bitter taste is evolved by many organic substances, i.e. quinine, morphine, caffeine and urea.

details.summary: Gustatory organ anatomy and taste distribution.

subject: Biology
text:
In the vertebrate body, glands are classified based on the presence or absence of ducts.

  • (i) Endocrine Glands: Derived from Greek words 'endo' (within) and 'crines' (to secrete). Collection of glands that produce hormones regulating metabolism, growth, development, tissue function, sexual function, reproduction, etc. Science dealing with this is endocrinology. These glands do not have ducts (ductless glands). Secretion is called hormone or internal secretion. Examples: thyroid, pituitary, pancreas, hypothalamus, adrenal, etc.
  • (ii) Exocrine Glands: These glands have ducts. They secrete their secretions in ducts to carry them to sites of action, e.g., sweat and oil glands of skin, salivary gland, liver, etc.

details.summary: Classification of glands into endocrine and exocrine systems.

subject: Biology
text:
• Chemical messengers that regulate biological processes. They are steroids, proteins, peptides of amino acid derivatives.
  • They can act as coenzymes.
  • Organic compounds secreted in small amounts by endocrine glands.
  • Hormone was first discovered by Bayless and Ernst H Starling in 1903.
  • Secretin was the first hormone to be discovered.

details.summary: Definition and history of hormones.

subject: Biology
text:
There are total nine endocrine glands in human beings. Most of them are common to male and female.

  • (i) Pituitary (master gland)
  • (ii) Thyroid
  • (iii) Parathyroid
  • (iv) Thymus
  • (v) Adrenals (supra-adrenals)
  • (vi) Pancreas
  • (vii) Pineal gland
  • (viii) Gonads
  • (ix) Hypothalamus
image_descriptions: Anatomical diagram showing the location of human endocrine glands including Pineal body, Pituitary, Parathyroid, Thyroid, Thymus, Stomach, Adrenal, Pancreas, Kidneys, Intestine, Testes, and Ovaries.

details.summary: Introduction to the nine primary endocrine glands in the human body.

subject: Biology
text: It is the smallest gland, which is about the size of a pea, but plays a major role in endocrine system. It is also called as the master gland. It is slightly larger in woman than in man. It is located in region of forebrain.
tables:
| Parts of pituitary | Hormones | Target organs | Actions/Effects |
|---|---|---|---|
| Anterior pituitary | Growth Hormone (GH) | All tissues | Normal body growth. |
| Anterior pituitary | Adrenocorticotropin Hormone (ACTH) | Adrenal cortex | Glucocorticoid secretion. |
| Anterior pituitary | Thyrotropin Stimulating Hormone (TSH) | Thyroid gland | Thyroxine secretion. |
| Anterior pituitary | Prolactin | Alveolar cells of mammary glands | Milk secretion. |
| Anterior pituitary | Follicle Stimulating Hormone (FSH) | Ovarian follicles | Growth of ovarian follicle and oestrogen secretion in females and spermatogenesis in male. |
| Anterior pituitary | Leuteinising Hormone (LH) | Testes or ovaries | Development of corpus luteum and progesterone secretion in females, testosterone secretion in males. |
| Intermediate pituitary | Melanocyte Stimulating Hormone (MSH) | Skin | Synthesis of melanin in the skin. |
| Posterior pituitary | Oxytocin (protein) | Uterus, mammary glands | Milk ejection, uterine contraction, contraction of smooth muscles. |

details.summary: Details regarding the Pituitary gland, its location, size, and the hormones secreted by its anterior, intermediate, and posterior lobes.

subject: Biology
text:
Thyroid Gland: It is the largest endocrine gland. It is found on ventral and lateral sides of upper part of the trachea in the neck. It is brownish-red, shield-shaped, bilobed gland.

Parathyroid Glands: These are four in numbers and are embedded in thyroid glands. These are small glands, which are oval-shaped and yellow coloured and present in the human neck. Parathyroid gland produces parathyroid hormone.
tables:
| Hormones | Target organs | Actions/Effects |
|---|---|---|
| Calcitonin (CT) | Bones, kidney | Fall in blood calcium, excretion of Ca2+. |
| Thyroxine | Heart, liver, kidney, skeletal muscles, mast cells. | Tissue metabolism, growth, IQ, differentiation of gonads, metamorphism in amphibians. |

| Hormones | Target organs | Actions/Effects |
|---|---|---|
| Parathormone (PTH) | Bones, kidney | Rise in blood calcium level, phosphorus check of calcium secretion. |

details.summary: Characteristics and hormonal functions of the Thyroid and Parathyroid glands.

subject: Biology
text:
It is a mixed gland with both exocrine and endocrine function and located within the curve of duodenum. Three kinds of cells are found in islets of Langerhans namely alpha, beta and delta cells.

  • (i) α-cells Larger and peripheral cells, produce glucagon hormone.
  • (ii) β-cells Central and smaller cells, produce insulin that a peptide hormone.
  • (iii) δ-cells Middle cells produce somatostatin hormone.
tables:
| Hormones | Target organs | Actions/Effects |
|---|---|---|
| Insulin | All cells | Decreases blood sugar level, stimulates glycogenesis, increases stored protein in tissue. Hypersecretion results into diabetes mellitus. |
| Glucagon | Liver | Rise in blood sugar. |

details.summary: Structure and function of the Pancreas as a mixed gland, detailing cell types and hormonal output.

subject: Biology
text:
Our body has paired endocrine glands, located superior to kidneys. It is structurally and functionally divided into adrenal cortex and adrenal medulla.

It is also called as 4S gland because of its four functions including salt retention, sugar metabolism, as a source of energy and as a sex organ.
tables:
| Hormones | Target organs | Actions/Effects |
|---|---|---|
| Glucocorticoids | Tissues, mast cells | Carbohydrate, fat and protein metabolism. |
| Mineral corticoids | Kidney | Sodium and potassium metabolism, water absorption. |
| Sex corticoids | Body cells | External sex characters. |
| Adrenaline and noradrenaline | Mast cells | Heartbeat, blood pressure rise, contraction and relaxation of muscles. |

details.summary: Overview of Adrenal Glands, their structure, and hormonal functions.

subject: Biology
text:
It is a small gland in the brain derived from the embryonic ectoderm. It secretes hormones in duct response to nervous activity.

In man, it starts to degenerate at about age of 7 years.

In adult, it is largely a fibrous tissue.
tables:
| Hormone | Target organ | Action/Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Melatonin | Melanophores | Dispersion of melanin. |

details.summary: Overview of Pineal Gland characteristics and hormonal function.

subject: Biology
text:
It is a lymphoid gland that plays an important role in the development of immune system.

It is situated in front of the heart.

Thymus is active in young ones, but gradually becomes inconspicuous after sexual maturity.

It arises from the endoderm of the embryo and consists of peripheral cortex and central medulla.
tables:
| Hormone | Target organ | Action/Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Thymosin | — | Immune system of body produces lymphocytes. |

details.summary: Overview of Thymus Gland structure and function.

subject: Biology
text:
The complete endocrine system works more or less under the influence of hypothalamus.

It is located in the floor of forebrain.

Neurohormones were first discovered by Guillemin and Schally.
tables:
| Hormones | Target organs | Actions/Effects |
|---|---|---|
| Thyrotropin releasing hormone | Thyroid, adrenal gland | Thyrotropin secretion, Corticotropin secretion |
| Corticotropin releasing hormone | Pituitary | Secretion of pituitary gonadotropin |
| Somatostatin | Pituitary | Initiation of growth hormone secretion |

details.summary: Overview of Hypothalamus and its regulatory role in the endocrine system.

subject: Biology
text: The main function of gonads is to produce gametes. They also secrete sex hormones. Sex hormones are mostly steroids. The testes in male and ovaries in females are gonads.
tables:
| Endocrine gland | Hormones | Target organs | Actions/Effects |
|---|---|---|---|
| Testes | Testosterones | Male reproductive organ | Male secondary sex organs and external male characters. |
| Ovaries | Oestrogen | Female reproductive organ | Female secondary sex organ and external female characters. |
| Corpus luteum (ovaries) | Progesterone | Uterus, mammary glands | Pregnancy changes in female sex organs. |

details.summary: Overview of Gonads and their hormonal functions.

subject: Biology
text: Apart from these, hormones are also secreted from heart kidney and gastro-intestinal tract.

| Organ | Hormone | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Heart | Atrial natriuretic factor | Dilation of blood vessels |
| Kidney | Erythropoietin | Erythropoiesis |
| Gastro-intestinal tract | Gastrin, Secretin Cholecystokinin | Secretion of HCl, Action pancreas for the secretion of water acts on gall bladder and pancreas for bile secretion. |

details.summary: Hormones secreted by heart, kidney, and gastro-intestinal tract.

subject: Biology
text: The process by which new individuals are produced from their parents is called reproduction. Reproduction is of two kinds: Asexual and Sexual.
image_descriptions: Flowchart showing classification of Reproduction: Asexual (Binary fission, Multiple fission, Budding, Fragmentation) and Sexual (Syngamy, Conjugation, Endogamy, Exogamy).

details.summary: Introduction to reproduction and its classification.

subject: Biology
text:
Male reproductive system consists of following main parts:

  • Testes: These are the primary sex organ of males, which perform dual role, i.e. function as endocrine gland and also act as male sex organs. These are suspended in thin skin bag called scrotal sacs.
  • Epididymis: It is highly coiled, thin tube formed by union of seminiferous tubules.
  • Penis: It is muscular organ, richly supplied with the blood. Externally, the penis has a bulge called glans penis, which is covered by prepuce (a skin fold).
  • Male can produce spermatozoa (sperm) throughout their life starting from the age of 13-14 years.
  • The growth of hairs on body is due male sex hormones, i.e. androgen (testosterone).
tables:
| Reproductive organs of male | Number | Function performed |
|---|---|---|
| Testes | 2 | To produce sperms and testosterone. |
| Sperm duct | 2 | To conduct the sperms from the testes to urethra. |
| Seminal vesicles | 2 | To secrete seminal plasma. |
| Epididymis | 2 | To temporarily store sperms and provide mobility. |
| Urethra | 1 | To conduct urine, sperms. |
| Prostate gland | 2 | To secrete an alkaline fluid to neutralise the acidity of urethra. |
| Cowper's gland | 2 | To secrete an alkaline white fluid. |
| Penis | 1 | To pass urine and deposite sperms in female genital tract. |
image_descriptions: Diagram of the male reproductive system showing the urinary bladder, ureter, seminal vesicle, prostate gland, bulbourethral gland, erectile tissue of penis, urethra, scrotum, vas deferens, epididymis, testis, glans penis, and prepuce.

details.summary: Overview of male reproductive anatomy and functions.

subject: Biology
text:
The female reproductive system consists of the following parts:

  • Ovary: These are primary sex organs that produces females gametes (ovum) and several steroid hormone.
  • After maturity, the ovary releases an ovum (egg cell) after every 28 days.
  • Lactation: Child is delivered after its development and mother produces milk to nourish the child.
  • Placenta: It is the connection between developing embryo and mother. It supplies blood, nutrition, etc., to the foetus.
  • Gestation period: The embryo develops for nine months in uterus. This period is called gestation period.
  • Amniocentesis: A technique to detect chromosomal abnormalities, if any in the developing foetus by analysing the cells in the amniotic fluid. This technique is often misused to know the sex of the foetus. Ultrasound can also be used to detect sex of foetus.
tables:
| Reproductive organ of female | Number | Function performed |
|---|---|---|
| Ovaries | 2 | To produce ova and hormones. |
| Oviducts | 2 | To move the ovum towards uterus. |
| Uterus | 1 | To provide space for developing child. |
| Vagina | 1 | To receive the sperms. |
image_descriptions: Diagram of the female reproductive system showing fallopian tubes, ovaries, oviduct, fimbriae, follicles, corpus luteum, uterine wall, endometrium, uterus, cervix, and vagina.

details.summary: Overview of female reproductive anatomy, gestation, and diagnostic techniques.

subject: Biology
text:
• Reproductive period of a human female extends from puberty (9-13 years) to menopause (45-50 years).
  • Menopause: It is the stopping of ovulation and menses. It normally occurs between the ages of 45 and 50. In this stage, women lose the ability to reproduce. Menopause is characterised by hot flushes.
  • The periodic vaginal bleeding during menstrual cycle is called menstruation.
  • Menstrual cycle is controlled by FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone.
  • On an average, menstrual cycle is completed in 28 days.
  • It is absent during pregnancy, may be suppressed during lactation and permanently stops at menopause.
  • About 13 mature eggs are released from two ovaries of female in an year.

details.summary: Key facts regarding the female menstrual cycle and menopause.

subject: Biology
text:
Contraception is the prevention of union of sperm and ovum.

Some common contraceptive methods are as follow:

  • Natural contraception: Avoid copulation during ovulation.
  • Mechanical contraception: Use devices to avoid union of sperm and ovum, e.g. condoms, diaphragm, Intra Uterine Devices (IUDs).
  • Chemical contraception: Fertilisation is avoided by the use of drugs, spermicidal creams, tablets, foam, etc.
  • Vasectomy: It is the surgical removal of sperm ducts (vas deferens) in males.
  • Tubectomy: Cut and tied of Fallopian tubes in females.

details.summary: Overview of various contraceptive methods including natural, mechanical, chemical, and surgical procedures.

subject: Biology
text:
Human population is growing fast and its present rate is about 2% per annum. Malthus (1798) gave the concept of human population. Study of human population is called demography.

  • The physiological capacity of organisms is called biotic potential.
  • The maximum number of individuals, which an environment can support of sustain is called carrying capacity.
  • Population growth is determined by the number of organisms added to the population (through birth) minus the number of organisms lost (through death).
  • When the number of individuals lost is called zero population.

Growth curves are of following two types:

  • J-shaped curve: When there is no environmental resistance, a population grows exponentially and a J-shaped curve is obtained.
  • S-shaped curve: When environment resistance does not allow population growth to soar towards infinitely.

details.summary: Definitions and concepts related to human population growth, demography, and growth curves.

subject: Biology
text:
Health: It is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being. Any deviation from this state results in a disease.

  • According to World Health Organisation (WHO) (1948), 'health is a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely an absence of disease'.
  • Factors contributing to good health: balanced diet, personal hygiene and regular exercise.
  • Other factors: awareness about diseases, vaccination, proper disposal of waste, maintenance of hygienic food and water resources.

Human Diseases: A disease is an abnormal condition affecting the body of an organism or in other words, we can also say that 'any change from normal state causing discomfort is called disease'.

  • Intrinsic factors: The disease causing factors, which are within the human body are called intrinsic factors, e.g. malfunctioning of organs (like heart, kidney, etc.) genetic diseases, hormonal imbalance, etc.
  • Extrinsic factors: The disease causing factors, which come from outside the human body are called extrinsic factors, e.g. disease caused by microorganism, tobacco, alcohol, narcotics and inadequate diet.
  • The disease causing organisms are called pathogens.
  • Various microorganisms responsible for infectious diseases are bacteria, viruses, fungi, protozoans, worms, etc.

Classification of Diseases: Diseases may be broadly classified into two types: Acquired diseases and Congenital diseases.
image_descriptions: Flowchart showing classification of diseases: Diseases split into Acquired diseases and Congenital diseases. Acquired diseases further split into Communicable (spread from one person to another) and Non-communicable (do not spread). Communicable is further split into Contagious (by direct contact) and Non-contagious (by indirect contact).

details.summary: Definitions of health and disease, classification of factors affecting health, and the hierarchy of disease classification.

subject: Biology
text:
Communicable Diseases or Infectious Diseases are caused by pathogens and can spread from an affected person to a normal person.

(i) Bacterial Diseases

  • Pneumonia (Streptococcus), cholera (Vibrio cholerae), tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis), tetanus (Clostridium tetani), leprosy (Mycobacterium leprae), food poisoning (Salmonella), plague (Yersinia pestis).
  • Staphylococcus in nasal passage causes food poisoning via heat-resistant toxin.
  • Salmonella typhi causes typhoid fever (affects liver, pancreas, nervous system, GI tract, kidney).
  • Clostridium botulinum causes food poisoning in canned food.
  • Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae cause pneumonia.
  • Anthrax: Caused by Bacillus anthracis, spreads via spores.
  • Diphtheria: Caused by Cornebacterium diphtheriae, affects respiratory tract (sore throat, low fever, adherent membrane).
  • Pertussis (Whooping cough): Caused by Bordetella pertussis (Gram negative bacteria), incubation 1-3 weeks.
  • DPT: Vaccine for diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus.

(ii) Viral Diseases

  • Polio (polio virus), mumps (paramyxo virus), chickenpox (variola virus), measles (paramyxo virus), AIDS (HIV).
  • Dengue: RNA virus (Flaviviridae). Symptoms: headache, muscle/joint pain. Causes platelet count decrease by infecting bone marrow endothelial cells.
  • Conjunctivitis (pink eye/madras eye): Inflammation of conjunctiva (adenoviruses or bacterial).
  • Rabies: Viral disease (inflammation of brain). 97% human cases from dog bites, also bats.
  • Hepatitis: Inflammation of liver caused by hepatitis viruses.
  • Influenza (Flu): RNA virus (Orthomyxoviridae).
  • Measles (Rubeola/morbilli): Paramyxovirus. Symptoms: fever, cough, runny nose, red eyes.
  • Mumps: Mumps virus. Symptom: swelling of salivary glands (parotid gland).
  • AIDS: Weakens immunity. Spreads via sexual contact, blood transfusion, infected needles.

Antibiotics

Chemical substances produced by microorganisms to kill/inhibit others. Alexander Fleming discovered Penicillin. They inhibit metabolic activities like cell wall synthesis or nuclear membrane synthesis. Can be bacterial, fungal, or Actinomycetes origin.
tables:
| Antibiotics | Source |
|---|---|
| Penicillin | Penicillium notatum, P. chrysogenum |
| Streptomycin | Streptomyces griseus |
| Neomycin | Streptomyces fradiae |
| Tetracycline | Streptomyces erythraeus |

details.summary: Overview of common bacterial and viral communicable diseases, their causative agents, symptoms, and an introduction to antibiotics and their microbial sources.

subject: Biology
topic: Diseases Caused by Protozoans and Worms
text:
Diseases Caused by Protozoans and Worms

  • Malaria: Caused by Plasmodium sp. Transferred to the host by vectors. Anopheles serves as a vector for malaria, Culex for filaria, and Aedes for dengue and sandfly for kala-azar.
  • Kala-azar (dum-dum fever): Caused by protozoan Leishmania donovani.
  • Amoebiasis: Caused by Entamoeba histolytica in man. Parasitises large intestine; occurs due to poor sanitation and hygiene.
  • Sleeping sickness: Caused by a flagellate protozoan parasite (class-Mastigophora, genus-Trypanosoma). Also called trypanosomiasis. Transmitted by blood-sucking tse-tse fly.
  • Ascariasis: Helminthic infection (worm) caused by Ascaris lumbricoides. Characterised by internal bleeding, muscular pain, fever, anaemia, and blockage of intestinal passage.
  • Filariasis: Caused by filarial nematodes, Wuchereria bancrofti.

details.summary: Overview of diseases caused by protozoans and worms including causative agents and transmission vectors.

subject: Biology
topic: Diseases Caused by Fungi and Classification of Diseases
text:
Diseases Caused by Fungi

  • Ringworm (skin problems)
  • Food poisoning (Aspergillus)
  • Athlete's foot

Communicable diseases are of two sub-types:

  • (a) Contagious Diseases: Transferred through simple contacts (e.g., smallpox, ringworm, chickenpox, influenza, measles, leprosy).
  • (b) Non-contagious Diseases: Transferred through physical carriers like air, water, food (e.g., cholera, taeniasis, ascariasis, typhoid). Some are transmitted through disease carrier vectors (e.g., plague, AIDS, malaria, hepatitis).

Non-communicable Diseases or Non-Infectious Diseases:

These remain confined to the person who develops them. Four types:

  1. Organic (degenerative) diseases: Caused by organ malfunctioning.
  2. Deficiency diseases: Caused by deficiency of mineral, hormones, vitamins, and nutrients.
  3. Allergic diseases: Caused by hypersensitivity of body to foreign particle.
  4. Cancer: Caused by uncontrolled division of certain cells of body.

details.summary: Classification of diseases into communicable (contagious/non-contagious) and non-communicable types.

subject: Biology
text:
Diseases of Malfunctioning:

  • Heart: Cardiac failure.
  • Kidney: Kidney failure.
  • Bones: Osteoporosis.
  • Eyes: Myopia, hypermatropia, and cataract.

Deficiency Diseases:

  • Cretinism: Deficiency of thyroxine hormone (mentally retarded child).
  • Diabetes: Deficiency of insulin.
  • Dwarfism: Sluggish activity of pituitary gland (diminished growth).
  • Gigantism: Excessive activity of pituitary gland (excessive growth).
  • Goitre: Deficiency of iodine (swelling of thyroid gland).
  • Anaemia: Decrease in RBCs or haemoglobin (leads to hypoxia).

details.summary: List of diseases resulting from organ malfunction and hormonal/nutrient deficiencies.

subject: Biology
text:
Allergic Diseases: Unfavourable response to dust, serum, drugs, fabrics, pollen, etc. Symptoms include sneezing, irritation of throat, itching, and skin rashes. Asthma is caused by allergy.

Cancer: Uncontrolled growth of cells. Sometimes cells keep dividing and produce more cells than required, forming a tumour (benign or malignant).

Types of Cancers:

  • (a) Carcinomas: e.g., lung cancer, breast cancer, cancer of pancreas and stomach.
  • (b) Sarcomas: e.g., bone cancer.
  • (c) Leukemia: e.g., blood cancer.

Notes: Breast cancer is common among women; lung cancer is common among smokers. Radiations cause cancer, leukemia, and skin injuries by damaging genes/chromosomes and inducing uncontrolled cell division. Cancer is common in older people due to accumulated mutations.

details.summary: Explanation of allergic reactions and the nature, types, and causes of cancer.

subject: Biology
text:
Diseases Caused by Addictive Substances

Alcohol: Reduces alertness of mind and causes liver damage.

Narcotic drugs: Narcotic drugs are morphine, cocaine, heroin, hashish, ganja, opium, marijuana, barbiturates and LAD (Lysergic Acid Diethylamide).

Diseases Caused due to Pollution

Chemical pollution: Pneumoconiosis is caused by inhaling coal dust. Silicosis is caused by inhaling stone dust (silica). Asbestosis is caused by inhaling asbestos dust. Lung diseases and bronchitis are caused by smoke.

IMPORTANT POINTS TO REMEMBER: DOTS or directly observed treatment, short-course was launched by WHO as a strategy to control TB (Tuberculosis). It ensures a regular, uninterrupted supply of high quality anti-TB drug.

Congenital Diseases

These are anatomical or physiological abnormalities that come from birth. These diseases can be caused by genetic mutations or environmental factors. Diseases by genetic mutation can be transmitted to next generation, whereas diseases by environmental factors are non-transmissible. Some common congenital diseases are phenylketonuria, alkaptonuria, haemophillia, sickle-cell anaemia, etc.

Chromosomal Aberrations

These are any variation from the 46 chromosome number of humans. These includes Turner’s syndrom, klinfelter syndrom, etc.

VACCINATION

Louis Pasteur coined the term ‘Vaccine’ and vaccination for the first time.

  • The word ‘vaccination’ has been derived from a Latin word ‘vacca’ which means cow.
  • A vaccine is either a cell suspension or a byproduct excreted by the cell.
  • These vaccines, when introduced into the body, stimulate the production of antibodies.
  • Serum is used for obtaining antibodies.
  • This introduction of harmless antigenic material into healthy person for providing acquired immunity against the disease is known as immunisation and vaccination.

|---|---|---|---|

| Tuberculosis | Cattle, birds | Bacteria | Lungs, intestine |
| Rinderpest | Cattle, sheep, goat | Bacteria | Spleen |

subject: Biology
text:
FERTILISERS

Fertiliser is any material found naturally or formed synthetically and is applied to soil or plant tissues, to supply one or more plant nutrients essential to the growth of plants. They are of mainly two types:

1. Chemical Fertilisers

These are salt or an organic compound containing the necessary plant nutrients. They may be organic or inorganic, e.g. ammonium sulphate is an inorganic fertiliser, while urea is an organic fertiliser. If excess fertilisers are applied to a plant without water, crop will die due to the plasmolysis. Chemical fertilisers can be classified into following types:

(i) Nitrogenous fertilisers These are nitrogen containing fertilisers, e.g.

  • Ammonium nitrate [NH4NO3]
  • Ammonium sulphate [(NH4)2SO4]
  • Sodium nitrate [NaNO3]
  • Urea [NH2CONH2] (organic fertiliser)

(ii) Phosphatic fertilisers These are phosphorus containing fertilisers, e.g.

  • Ammonium phosphate [(NH4)3PO4]
  • Ammonium hydrogen phosphate [(NH4)H2PO4]
  • Superphosphate [Ca2(H2PO4)2]

(iii) Potassium fertilisers These are potassium containing fertilisers, e.g.

  • Potassium chloride [KCl]
  • Potassium nitrate [KNO3]

details.summary: Definition and classification of chemical fertilisers including nitrogenous, phosphatic, and potassium types.

subject: Biology
text:
Biofertilisers are biologically originated substances that enhance nutrient availability to crop plants. One important type is Manures.

Manures

  • Semi-decayed substances added to soil to enhance fertility.
  • Decomposed product of organic wastes.
  • Benefits: Improves fertility, aeration, water holding capacity, and crumb structure.
  • Types:
    • Farm Yard Manure (FYM): Mixture of cattle dung, crop residues, fallen leaves, twigs, etc.
    • Composite Manure (compost): Rotten vegetables, garbage, sewage sludge, animal refuse, etc.
    • Green Manure: Quick growing crops cultivated and ploughed into the soil, increasing yield by 30-50%.

Green Manuring

  • Technique of utilising green manure (e.g., Crotalaria juncea, Glycine max, Indigofera linifolia).
  • Anabaena azollae (cyanobacteria) is used as a biofertiliser in rice fields.
  • Sunnhemp plants are used for green manuring in India.

Advantages of Manuring

  • Improves soil fertility and structure.
  • Improves soil aeration capacity.
  • Helps in control of pests, insects, mites, and growth of weeds.

details.summary: Overview of biofertilisers, specifically focusing on manures, green manuring techniques, and their agricultural benefits.

subject: Biology
text:
Natural processes fix about 190 x 10^12 g per year of nitrogen through biological nitrogen-fixation. Sources include:

1. Free-living Nitrogen-fixing Bacteria

  • Found in rhizosphere; can be aerobic or anaerobic.
  • Aerobic: Azotobacter (maintains reduced oxygen conditions via high respiration), Gloeothece (photosynthetic during day, fixes nitrogen at night).
  • Anaerobic: Rhodospirillum (photosynthetic), Clostridium (non-photosynthetic).

2. Symbiotic Nitrogen-fixing Bacteria

  • Form symbiotic relationships with plants using nitrogenase enzyme.
  • Example: Rhizobium with leguminous plants, forming pink nodules containing leghaemoglobin.
  • Non-leguminous trees like Alder, Ceanothus, and Purshia associate with Frankia.

3. Free-living Nitrogen-fixing Cyanobacteria

  • Includes Anabaena, Nostoc, Aulosira, Cylindrospermum, Trichodesmium.
  • Add 20-30 kg of nitrogen per hectare.
  • Aulosira is active in rice fields; Cylindrospermum in sugarcane and maize fields.

4. Symbiotic Nitrogen-fixing Cyanobacteria

  • Anabaena and Nostoc are common symbionts in lichens, Anthoceros, Azolla, and Cycads roots.
  • Azolla (water fern) contains Anabaena azollae.

details.summary: Detailed classification of biological nitrogen-fixing agents including free-living and symbiotic bacteria and cyanobacteria.

subject: Biology
text:
Mycorrhizae (sing. mycorrhiza) are the mutualistic association of a fungus and the roots of higher plants. Mycorrhizae are found in most groups of vascular plants. There are two types of mycorrhizae listed as follow:

  • Ectomycorrhiza: The mycorrhizal fungi is present on the root surface only. The cortical cells are surrounded by a network of fungal hyphae called Hartig net. It is found in roots of oak, Pinus, peach, Eucalyptus, etc.
  • Endomycorrhiza: The mycorrhizal fungus enters the roots and spreads in the root cortex. It may be intercellular or intracellular.

The type of endomycorrhiza, which produce vesicles and arbuscules inside the cortical cells of roots are called VAM (Vesicular Arbuscular Mycorrhiza), e.g. orchids, common crop plants and grasses.

details.summary: Definition and classification of mycorrhiza (Ectomycorrhiza and Endomycorrhiza) and VAM.

subject: Biology
text:
Weed: Wild plants, which grow along with a cultivated crop are called weeds. Common weeds found in wheat and rice field are Phalaris minar (mandusi), Amaranthus (chaulai), Chenopodium (bathua). Exotic weeds are Parthenium hysterophorus, Eichhornia, etc. Most troublesome terrestrial weed is congress grass (Parthenium hysterophorus).

Weedicides: These are the chemical substances that are used to kill weeds. Some weedicides are butachlor 2,4-D (2,4-dichlorophenoxy acetic acid), MCPA (2-Methyl 4-Chloro, 1-Phenoxy Acetic acid).

details.summary: Definition of weeds, examples of common/exotic weeds, and chemical weedicides.

subject: Biology
text:
Pesticides are used to destroy pests (pathogens, insects, rodents, etc.) by spraying the crop.

  • Some microbes such as bacteria, fungi, viruses, protozoans, etc., and their products used for pest control are known as biopesticides.
  • These are inexpensive, cause no pollution, pick no risk to human health and have a long term capability to control pests.
  • Some common pesticides are warfarin sulphur, malathion, DDT (Dichloro Diphenyl Trichloroethane), BHC (Benzene Hexachloride), etc.
  • Some examples of pesticides are:
    • DDT and 2, 4-D were mainly used during the Second World War.
    • Endosulfan is an organochlorine pesticide and acaricide used on plants and insects.
    • Bordeaux mixture a fungicide, composed of CuSO4, Ca(OH)2 was discovered by Millardet.
    • Methyl isocyanate gas, which is responsible for Bhopal gas tragedy (3rd Dec, 1984), is used for synthesising carbaryl (selvin).
    • Rotenone is obtained from roots of Derris elliptica and Lonechocarpus.
    • Fumigation is another method of pest control used mainly to kill pests attacking stored grains. The substances used for fumigation are known as fumigants, e.g. methyl bromide, iodoform.

details.summary: Overview of pesticides, biopesticides, and specific chemical agents used in pest control.

subject: Biology
text:
ANIMAL HUSBANDRY: Animal husbandry is the science of rearing, caring, feeding, breeding, improvement and utilisation of domesticated animals. It is an agricultural practice of breeding and raising livestock.

  • The animals used for transport, milk, meat and agriculture are collectively called livestock.
  • On the basis of utility, the livestock can be categorised into the following categories: 1. Milk yielding animals (Cows, buffaloes and goats), 2. Meat and egg yielding animals (Sheeps, goats, pigs, chicken, ducks and fowls), 3. Animals utilised as motive power (Buffaloes, horses, donkeys, bullocks, camels and elephants), 4. Wool giving animals (Sheeps), 5. Miscellaneous uses (Hides of cattles).

Animal Breeding: It is an important aspect of animal husbandry. Breed is a group of animals related by descent and similar in most characters. Animal breeding can be classified as: (i) Inbreeding: Crossing of closely related animals within the same breed for 4-6 generation. (ii) Outbreeding: Breeding between unrelated animals (outcrossing) or different breeds (cross-breeding) or different species (interspecific hybridisation).

ARTIFICIAL INSEMINATION: It is the process in which the stored semen of a superior male animal is introduced into the genital tract of a selected female animal by using suitable instruments.
image_descriptions: A box containing the definition of Artificial Insemination.

details.summary: Introduction to animal husbandry, classification of livestock, animal breeding techniques, and artificial insemination.

subject: Biology
text:
The breeding, rearing and transplantation of fish by artificial means is called pisciculture. It involves raising fish commercially in tanks or enclosures usually for food.

Fishes are of two types:

  • Freshwater fishes: Rohu, Catla, carp, tirica, mali, singhara and calbasu.
  • Marine fishes: Bombay duck, conger eel, promphet, Salmon, Sardine, hilsa.

Fishes are the rich source of protein and vitamin (A and D).

text:
The term 'Poultry' means rearing of fowls, ducks, geese turkeys and some varieties of pigeons, but more often is used for fowl rearing.

Fowls are reared for food or for their eggs.

  • Broilers: Poultry birds reared for meat.
  • Layers: Female fowls raised for egg production.
  • Indigenous breeds: 'Desi' fowls exhibiting great variations in shape, size and colour (e.g., Assel, Ahagus).
  • Exotic breeds: 'Improved' breeds applied to exotic varieties (e.g., white leghorn, Rhode island red).

subject: Biology
text:
Biochemist Paul Berg is the father of genetic engineering. It involves the introduction of foreign DNA or synthetic genes into an organism.

Golden rice: A variety of Oryza sativa produced to biosynthesise β-carotene using:

  • (i) ψ (psy) (phytoene synthase) from daffodil.
  • (ii) crt I from soil bacterium Erwinia uredovora.

Key Terms:

  • Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR): Discovered by Kary Mullis (1985); technique of amplification of DNA segment using taq polymerase (isolated from Thermus aquaticus).
  • Restriction enzymes: Used to cut DNA at specific sites, also called molecular scissors.
  • Bioasphalt: Asphalt alternative from non-petroleum renewable resources.
  • Gene therapy: Insertion of genes into an individual's cell to treat disease.
  • Terminator technology: Technology to alter seeds so they fail to germinate after the first generation.
  • ELISA: Test for AIDS, based on Ag-Ab reaction.

Achievements:

  • Sweet bug: Bacterium Acetobacter oxylinum turns coconut water into confectionery.
  • Prof Anand Mohan Chakrabarty: Developed oil eating bacteria 'Superbug' using Pseudomonas.
  • Organic foods: Foods produced without synthetic pesticides/fertilisers.
  • Biodegradable plastic films (PSV): Made by blending polymers with additive.
  • Humulin: First human insulin produced by genetic engineering.

details.summary: Definitions and key achievements in genetic engineering.

subject: Biology
text:
DNA Fingerprinting is a technique employed by forensic scientists to assist in the identification of individuals by their respective DNA profiles. This technique is based upon the fact that the DNA constitution of an individual carries some specific sequences of nucleotides, which do not carry any information for protein synthesis. These are called VNTR regions, i.e., Variable Number Tandem Repeats or mini satellites.

Inventor: Dr Alec Jeffreys.

Process:

  • Collection of sample (most preferably buccal swab).
  • RFLP (Restriction Fragments Length Polymorphism) analysis.
  • Southern blotting DNA fingerprinting is a quite laborious method that requires large amount of undegraded sample so the method was replaced by what is used today based on STR (Short Tandem Repeats) and PCR.

details.summary: Overview of DNA fingerprinting technique, its basis in VNTR regions, and the evolution of the process from Southern blotting to STR/PCR.

subject: Biology
text:
Cloning in biology is the process of producing similar organism of genetically identical individuals that occur in nature when organisms such as bacteria, insects or plants reproduce asexually.

Types of cloning:

  • Reproductive cloning: Used for the production of offspring. A new individual is created from a single cell by replacing the nucleus in an egg cell with the nucleus (containing the genetic material) from another cell of the body. The cloned egg cell grows and develops into an embryo. The embryo is implanted inside a surrogate mother's womb to mature and produce a viable foetus.
  • Therapeutic cloning: Used for the development of embryonic stem cells. The inner cell mass of the blastocyst is then removed and used for the creation of an embryonic stem cell line that has the genetic make up of the donated nucleus.
image_descriptions: Box titled 'SUCCESSFULLY DEVELOPED CLONED' listing: Dolly (first mammal clone by Dr Wilmut, UK), Noori (first cloned Pashmina goat, India), world's first buffalo calf (Handguided Cloning Technique, 2009, NDRI, Karnal), and Garima-II (cloned buffalo, NDRI, Karnal).

details.summary: Definitions of reproductive and therapeutic cloning and notable examples of successful cloning.

subject: Biology
topic: Stem Cell Therapy and Transgenic Crops
text:
Stem Cell Therapy: The most promising use of stem cells is due to their ability to be modified into different functional adult cell types and serve as a potential source of replacement cells to treat numerous diseases. Stem cell research involves the use of several different types of cells besides embryonic stem cell, such as adult stem cells from humans or animals or stem cells from foetuses, umbilical cord or amniotic fluid.

Transgenic or GM Crops: A transgenic crop is a crop, which contains and expresses a transgene (a gene that is transferred into an organism by genetic engineering). It involves introduction of new DNA into a crop to confer a new superior trait. A popular term for the transgenic crop is genetically modified crops or GM crops.

  • Bt Crops: Produced by inserting toxic genes that code for a toxin directly into the genetic code of the crop to protect the crop from insects. Includes a promoter and a marker. Examples: Bt cotton, Bt brinjal, Golden rice.
  • Bt Cotton: Created by using a bacterium, Bacillus thuringiensis. It produces a protein that kills certain insects, e.g., beetles, flies, budworm.
  • Golden Rice: A transgenic rice biosynthesising β-carotene, vitamin-A, essential for eye sight precursor in the edible parts of rice.

Advantages of GM Crops:

  • Provides high nutrient containing varieties.
  • More tolerant to cold, insect, drought, salinity, etc.
  • Resistance to pest, herbicides and diseases.

details.summary: Explanation of stem cell therapy, transgenic crops, specific examples like Bt crops and Golden Rice, and advantages of GM technology.

subject: Biology
text:
Hybridisation is a technique, which involves cross breeding of different varieties of crop to get a new crop with desired characteristics. Such crops/varieties are called High Yielding Varieties (HYV) or hybrid.

  • Wheat: Lerma, Sharbati Sonara, Kalyan Sona, Roja 64, Pusa Lerma, Hera-Moti, Sonara-64, Sonalika and Arjun.
  • Paddy (rice): Jaya, Padma, Pusa 205, IR-6, T-141.
  • Maize: Ganga-101, Ranjit, Daccan hybrid.

Germ plasm: It is the living genetic resource such as seed or tissue maintained for the purpose of animal and plant breeding preservation and other research aspects.

subject: Biology
text:
• Genetic screening: An experimental technique used to identify genes that may produce damaging changes in the individuals. It involves collecting sequencing and comparison of DNA genomes.
  • Biochips: DNA chips single-stranded DNA chains or repetitive DNA segments fierily struck to silica glass chip.
  • Bioinformatics: An interdisciplinary field, which addresses biological problems using computational techniques and makes the rapid organisation and analysis of biological data possible.
  • Blue biotechnology: An application of biotechnology in the marine and aquatic, but rarely used.
  • Green biotechnology: It is an application of biotechnology in the agricultural processes.
  • Red biotechnology: It is an application of biotechnology in the medical processes.
  • White biotechnology: It is a branch of biotechnology applied to industrial processes.
  • Biomarkers (Biosignature): Are specific proteins used to diagnose disease.

details.summary: Definitions of various biotechnology-related terms and applications.

subject: Biology
text:
• Green Revolution (1940-70): Refers to a series of research, development and technology transfer initiatives that increased agricultural production around the world. Great increase in the production of food grain crops due to use of hybrid varieties, fertilisers and modern agricultural techniques took place. Father of green revolution in India is MS Swaminathan and in world is NE Borlaug.
  • Operation Flood (White Revolution): Great incereasement in the production of milk due to use of high milk yielding breads of cow and buffaloes. It resulted in making India the largest producer of milk and milk products and hence called white revolution. Operation flood was rural programme started by India's National Dairy Development Board (NDDB) in 1970.
  • Silver Revolution: Great increase in the production of eggs due to use of exotic breeds.

details.summary: Overview of major agricultural revolutions in India.

subject: Biology
text:
• Fermentation: The conversion of carbohydrates to alcohol and carbon dioxide or organic acids using yeasts, bacteria or a combination of there, under anaerobic conditions, e.g. Saccharomyces cerevisiae used in baking and alcohol industry. Cheese is formed by the process of coagulation of casein by enzyme rennin. Yoghurt is produced by fermentation using Lactobacillus and Streptococcus.
  • BIOGAS: Also called Landfill Gas (LFG) or digester gas. It is the gas produced by biological breakdown of organic matter in the absence of O2. It is methane rich and produced by anaerobic digestion of biomass with the help of methanogenic bacteria. It is mainly produced from animal wastes. Non-biodegradable waste cannot be broken down by microorganism, so cannot used for biogas production. Organic wastes such as dead plants or animal material, animal dung, and kitchen waste are also called biodegradable waste. It mainly comprises methane CH4 (50-70%) and carbon dioxide CO2 (25-50%) and hydrogen sulphide H2S (0-3%), moisture and siloxanes.
  • Advantages of Biogas: It is cheaper than other fuels and ideal for small scale application. It helps to clean environment because waste materials can be used as substrate. It is a renewable source of energy.

details.summary: Explanation of fermentation processes and biogas production.

subject: Biology
text:
• BIOREMEDIATION: It is the treatment of environmental problems by the use of biological methods. It may be defined as treatment, which include microorganisms or their enzymes to return the environment that has been to its original condition. It may be employed in order to attack specific contaminants, such as chlorinated pesticides that are degraded by bacteria.
  • PHYTOREMEDIATION: This is the treatment of environmental problems through the use of plants. The term phytoremediation is a combination of two words, i.e. phyto means plant and remediation means to remedy. It helps in depolluting contaminated soils, water and air with plants, able to degrade or eliminate metals, pesticides, solvents, explosives, crude oil and its derivatives.

details.summary: Definitions of bioremediation and phytoremediation techniques.
