subject: Mathematics
topic: Definitions of Sequence, Series, and Progression
text:
Sequence: A set of numbers arranged in a definite order according to some definite rule is called a sequence. e.g., 2, 4, 6, 8, ... is a sequence.

Series: If a1, a2, a3, ..., an is a sequence, then the expression a1 + a2 + a3 + ... + an is called the series. The series is said to be finite or infinite depending upon the last term is given or not.

  • (i) a1, a2, a3, ..., an is a finite sequence and is denoted by {ak}k=1n.
  • (ii) a1, a2, a3, a4, ... is an infinite sequence and is denoted by {an}n=1∞ or simply {an}.

Here, a1 is called the first term and in case of finite sequence an is called the last term. e.g., 2, 4, 6, 8, ..., 100 is a finite sequence. 1, 2, 3, 4, ... is an infinite sequence.

Progression: Sequence following certain patterns are called progressions. e.g., 2, 3, 4, 5, ... is a progression, here each term is increasing by 1.

Arithmetical Progression (AP): An arithmetic progression is a sequence in which the difference between any term and its preceding term is constant throughout. The constant 'd' is called the common difference. The first term of an AP is represented by 'a'.

details.summary: Introduction to fundamental concepts of sequences, series, and progressions, including the definition of Arithmetical Progression (AP).

subject: Mathematics
text:
If an AP has first term a and common difference d, then the general form of an AP is a, a+d, a+2d, a+3d, ..., a+(n-1)d.

  • nth term of an AP is T_n = a+(n-1)d.
  • Sum of the first n terms of an AP is S_n = n/2[2a+(n-1)d] or S_n = n/2[a+l], where l = last term.

details.summary: Definitions and formulas for Arithmetic Progression.

subject: Mathematics
text: When three terms are in AP, then the middle term is called arithmetic mean of the other two. If a, b and c are in AP, then b is AM of a and c. Let a and b be two numbers and M be the AM between them. Then, a, M, b are in AP, M = (a+b)/2.

details.summary: Definition and formula for Arithmetic Mean.

subject: Mathematics
text:
A geometric progression is a progression of numbers, whose first term is non-zero and each of the term is obtained by multiplying its preceding term by a constant quantity. This constant quantity is called the common ratio of the GP. Thus, if t_1, t_2 and t_3 are in GP, then common ratio r = t_2/t_1. If a is the first term and r is the common ratio, then GP can be written as a, ar, ar^2, ar^3, ..., ar^{n-1}. nth term of a GP is T_n = ar^{n-1} = l.

  • Sum of the n terms of a GP is S_n = a(r^n-1)/(r-1), if r > 1 and S_n = a(1-r^n)/(1-r), if r < 1.
  • Sum of infinite terms of a GP is S_n = a/(1-r).

details.summary: Definitions and formulas for Geometric Progression.

subject: Mathematics
text: If three terms are in GP, then the middle term is called the geometric mean of the other two. If a, b and c are in GP, then b is the GM of a and c. Let a and b be two numbers and G be the GM between them. Then, a, G, b are in GP, G = sqrt(ab), a > 0, b > 0.

details.summary: Definition and formula for Geometric Mean.

subject: Mathematics
text: A sequence is said to be harmonic progression (HP). If the reciprocals of its terms are in arithmetic progression (AP). e.g. The sequence 1, 1/3, 1/5, 1/7... is an HP because the sequence 1, 3, 5, 7... is an AP. If a_1, a_2, a_3, ..., a_n are in HP, then 1/a_1, 1/a_2, 1/a_3, ..., 1/a_n are in AP. nth term of an HP is T_n = 1 / (1/a_1 + (n-1)(1/a_2 - 1/a_1)).

details.summary: Definition and formula for Harmonic Progression.

subject: Mathematics
text: If three terms are in HP, then the middle term is called the harmonic mean of the other two. If a, b and c are in HM, then b is the HM of a and c.

details.summary: Definition of Harmonic Mean.

subject: Mathematics
topic: Harmonic Mean and Relation between Means
text:
Let a and b be two numbers and H be the Harmonic Mean (HM) between them. If a, b, c are in Harmonic Progression (HP), then H = 2ab / (a + b).

Relation between Arithmetic, Geometric and Harmonic Mean:

  • A ≥ G ≥ H
  • G^2 = AH

details.summary: Definitions of Harmonic Mean and the fundamental inequalities/relations between Arithmetic, Geometric, and Harmonic means.

mcq.question: If a,b,c are in AP, p,q,r are in HP and ap,bq,cr are in GP, then p/r + r/p is equal to
mcq.explanation: Since a,b,c are in AP, b = (a+c)/2. Since p,q,r are in HP, q = 2pr/(p+r). Since ap, bq, cr are in GP, (bq)^2 = (ap)(cr) => b^2q^2 = apcr. Substituting values leads to the result.

subject: Mathematics
topic: Sum to n Terms of Special Series
text:
The sum of first n terms of some special series is given below:

  • Sum of first n natural numbers: Σn = 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2
  • Sum of square of the first n natural numbers: Σn^2 = 1^2 + 2^2 + ... + n^2 = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6
  • Sum of cubes of the first n natural numbers: Σn^3 = 1^3 + 2^3 + ... + n^3 = [n(n+1)/2]^2

details.summary: Standard summation formulas for natural numbers, squares, and cubes.

subject: Mathematics
text:
This page contains solutions and derivations for problems related to sequences and series, including Arithmetic Progressions (AP), Geometric Progressions (GP), and Harmonic Progressions (HP).

  • Middle term of an AP: T_{(n+1)/2} = a + ((n+1)/2 - 1)d
  • Sum of infinite geometric series: S_infinity = a/(1-r) + dr/(1-r)^2
  • Harmonic Progression property: If a, b, c are in HP, then b = 2ac/(a+c).
  • Arithmetic and Harmonic Means: For two numbers a and b, A = (a+b)/2, G = sqrt(ab), H = 2ab/(a+b). The relationship AH = G^2 holds true.

details.summary: Mathematical derivations and solutions for problems involving AP, GP, and HP sequences, including properties of means and summation formulas.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Factors: If number 'a' divides the number 'b' without leaving a remainder, then 'a' is said to be the factor of 'b'.

Examples:

  • 4 is a factor of 16 as 16 = 4 x 4
  • 9 is a factor of 729 as 729 = 9 x 9 x 9

Prime Factors: The factors that cannot be again factorized i.e. the factors which are prime numbers are called prime factors.

Examples:

  • 9 is a factor of 729, but 3 is a prime factor of 729.
  • 8 and 9 are factors of 72, but 2 and 3 are prime factors of 72.

details.summary: Introduction to factors and prime factors with examples.

subject: Mathematics
text:
1. Common Multiple: A common multiple of two or more numbers is a number which is exactly divisible (without leaving remainder) by each of them.

e.g. 30 is a common multiple of 2, 3, 5, 6, 10 and 15 because 30 is exactly divisible by each number. Similarly, 72 is a common multiple of 2, 3, 4, 6, 12 and 18.

2. Least Common Multiple: The least common multiple of two or more given numbers is the least number which is exactly divisible by all the given numbers.

e.g. 84, 162, 252 are the common multiples of 2, 3, 4, 7. But, 84 is the LCM of 2, 3, 4, 7.

Methods of Finding LCM:

1. Prime Factorization Method: Write down the given numbers as the product of prime factors. Then, the LCM is the product of the highest powers of all the prime factors.

details.summary: Definitions of common multiples, LCM, and the prime factorization method for finding LCM.

subject: Mathematics
text: Division Method: Write the given numbers in a row and divide them with the common prime divisor. Write the quotient in each case below the number. If any number is not divisible by the respective divisor, then write it as such in the next row. Keep on dividing the quotients until you get 1. Multiply all the divisors to get the required LCM.
formulas: LCM(x, y, z) = product of all divisors
image_descriptions: A table showing the division method for finding the LCM of 120, 144, 160, and 180 using prime factors 2, 3, 5.

subject: Mathematics
text:
• The least number which when divided by x, y and z leaving the remainders a, b and c, respectively is given by [LCM of (x, y, z) - p], where p = (x - a) = (y - b) = (z - c).
  • The least number which when divided by x, y and z leaving the same remainder R in each case is given by [LCM of (x, y, z) + R].
formulas: Required number = LCM(x, y, z) - p
Required number = LCM(x, y, z) + R

subject: Mathematics
text:
Common Factor: A common factor of two or more numbers is a number which divides each of them exactly. e.g. 2 is common factor of 2, 10, 20.

Highest Common Factor (HCF): The Highest Common Factor (HCF) of two or more numbers is the largest number that divides all the given numbers exactly. It is also known as Greatest Common Divisor (GCD). HCF is always a factor of LCM. e.g. HCF of the numbers 18 and 24 is 6.

Methods of Finding HCF:

  1. HCF by Prime Factorization: Write the given number as product of prime factors and then find the product of least powers of common prime factors. This product is the required HCF of given numbers.
  2. HCF by Division Method: Suppose we have to find the HCF of two given numbers, divide the large number by the smaller one. Now, you will get the remainder. Divide the divisor by the remainder. Repeat this process until no remainder is left, the last divisor used in this process is the desired greatest common divisor i.e. HCF. In order to find the HCF of three numbers, then, HCF of [(HCF of any two) and (third number)] gives the HCF of given three numbers.
image_descriptions: A step-by-step division method calculation for finding the HCF of 204, 1190, and 1445.

details.summary: Definitions and methods for calculating the Highest Common Factor.

subject: Mathematics
text:
IMPORTANT POINTS

  • For integers x, y and z, if HCF (x, y) = 1 and HCF (x, z) = 1, then HCF of (x, y, z) is always 1.
  • The greatest number that will divide x, y and z leaving remainders a, b and c, respectively is given by HCF of (x - a), (y - b), (z - c).
  • The greatest number that will divide x, y and z leaving the same remainder in each case is given by [HCF of |x - y|, |y - z|, |z - x|].

details.summary: Properties of HCF for multiple integers and finding numbers with specific remainders.

subject: Mathematics
topic: How to Calculate LCM and HCF of Fractions
text:
The LCM and HCF of fractions can be obtained from the following formula:

  1. HCF of fractions = (HCF of numerators) / (LCM of denominators)
  2. LCM of fractions = (LCM of numerators) / (HCF of denominators)
formulas: HCF of fractions = (HCF of numerators) / (LCM of denominators)
LCM of fractions = (LCM of numerators) / (HCF of denominators)

details.summary: Formulas for calculating HCF and LCM of fractional numbers.

subject: Mathematics
topic: Relation between LCM and HCF of Two Numbers
text: Product of two numbers = (Their HCF) * (Their LCM)
formulas: Product of two numbers = (Their HCF) * (Their LCM)

subject: Mathematics
text:
Fraction: If any unit is divided into some parts, then each of these parts is called fraction of that unit. A fraction is represented as p/q, where q ≠ 0 and here q is called denominator and p is called numerator. e.g. 1/2, 3/4, 6/7 etc. are fractions.

Simple fraction: The fraction which has denominator other than power of 10, is called simple fraction. e.g. 6/5, 2/9 etc. Note: Simple fraction is also known as vulgar fraction.

Decimal Fraction: Fraction that has powers of 10 in the denominator are called decimal fraction. e.g. (i) 1/10 is the tenth part of 1 is written as 0.1. (ii) 1/100 is the hundredth part of 1 is written as 0.01.

Types of Decimals: 1. Recurring Decimals: A decimal number in which a digit or set of digits repeats regularly is called non-terminating repeating decimals or recurring decimals. To represent these fractions, a line is drawn on repeating digits.

details.summary: This section defines fractions, simple (vulgar) fractions, decimal fractions, and recurring decimals with examples.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Pure recurring decimal: A decimal fraction in which all the digits after the decimal points are repeated, is called a pure recurring decimal. e.g., 0.786786786... = 0.786 (bar over 786), 0.77777... = 0.7 (bar over 7).

Mixed recurring decimal: A decimal fraction in which some digits after the decimal point are not repeated while some are repeated, is called a mixed recurring decimal. e.g., 0.179999... = 0.179 (bar over 9), 0.053939... = 0.0539 (bar over 39).

Note: The decimal expansion of a rational number is either terminating or non-terminating recurring. In other words, a number whose decimal expansion is terminating or non-terminating recurring is a rational number.

details.summary: Definitions of pure and mixed recurring decimals with examples.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Addition and Subtraction: While making addition or subtraction of decimal fractions the numbers are placed in such a way that the decimal point lie in one column. Then, the numbers can be added or subtracted as usual.

Note: Adding/Annexing zeroes to the extreme right of a decimal fraction does not change its value.

Multiplication: While multiplying two or more decimal fractions, consider them without decimal point and multiply them as usual. In the product so obtained the decimal point is marked off as many places from the right as in the sum of the decimal places in the given numbers.

Division: While dividing the given decimal fraction by a natural number, divide it without the decimal point to get quotient. Here, in the quotient so obtained, place the decimal point after as many places from the right as are there in the dividend. For dividing a decimal fraction by a decimal fraction, multiply the dividend and the divisor by a suitable power of 10 to make the divisor a whole number and then proceed as in the previous rule.

details.summary: Rules for addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division of decimal fractions.

subject: Mathematics
topic: Conversion of Recurring Decimals to Fractions
text:
To Convert a Pure Recurring Decimal into a Simple Fraction: In order to convert a pure recurring decimal fraction into simple (vulgar) fraction, we write the repeated figures only once in the numerator without decimal point and write as many nines in the denominator as the number of repeating figure.

Example: 0.5 bar = 5/9 or 0.45 bar = 45/99

To Convert Mixed Recurring Decimal into a Simple Fraction: The numerator is obtained by taking the difference between the number formed by all the digits after decimal point (repeated digits taken only once) and the number formed by non-repeating digits. The denominator is obtained by placing as many nines as in repeating digits followed by as many zeroes as the number of non-repeating digits.

details.summary: Methods for converting pure and mixed recurring decimals into vulgar fractions.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Comparison of Fractions By Converting in Decimal Form: To compare the fraction using decimal, convert each one of the given fractions in decimal form and now arrange them in ascending or descending order as per the requirement.

By Equating Denominators: For comparison of fractions, take LCM of the denominator of all fractions. So, that their denominators are same. Now, the fractions having largest numerator is the largest fraction.

details.summary: Techniques for comparing fractions using decimal conversion or denominator equalization.

subject: Mathematics
topic: HCF and LCM of Decimal Fractions
text: For finding the HCF or LCM of decimal fractions, first make the given fractions to have same number of decimal places by annexing zeroes, if needed. Now, find the HCF or LCM of the numbers without considering decimal. Finally, in the result mark as many decimal places as there are in each of the given numbers.

details.summary: Procedure for calculating HCF and LCM of decimal numbers.

subject: Mathematics
text:
The square of a number is obtained by multiplying the number by itself.

e.g., Square of 5 = 5 × 5 = 25, square of 6 = 6 × 6 = 36

Perfect square: A natural number n is called a perfect square or a square number, if there exists a natural number m such that n = m^2.

e.g., The numbers 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, ... are perfect squares.

details.summary: Definition of square and perfect square.

subject: Mathematics
text:
The properties of perfect squares are discussed below:

  • (i) A number having 2, 3, 7 or 8 at unit's place is never a perfect square. e.g., 172, 2783
  • (ii) The squares of odd numbers are odd and the squares of even numbers are even.
  • (iii) The difference of squares of two consecutive natural numbers is equal to their sum. e.g., 7^2 - 6^2 = 7 + 6 = 13
  • (iv) The product of four consecutive natural numbers plus one is a always square.
  • (v) A number ending in an odd number of zeroes is never a perfect square.

details.summary: Five key properties of perfect squares.

subject: Mathematics
text:
The square root of a number x is that number which when multiplied by itself gives x as the product. It is denoted by √.

In general, y^2 = x => y = √x

Here, y is the square root of x, if and only if x is the square of y.

e.g., √4 = √2 × 2 = 2

Thus, 2 is the square root of 4.

details.summary: Definition and notation of square root.

subject: Mathematics
text:
The square root of a given number can be determined by using any of the following two methods:

  • Prime Factorization Method
  • General Method/Division Method

Prime Factorization: In this method, we express the given number as the product of prime factors. Now, for finding square root, we take the product of these prime factors choosing one out of every pair of same prime factors.

Division Method: To find the square root of a given number using this method, the following steps are to be followed:

  • Step I: In the given number, place bars over every pair of digits starting with the unit's digit. Each pair and the remaining one digit (if any) on the extreme left is called a period.
  • Step II: Think of the largest number whose square is less than or equal to the first period.
  • Step III: Put the quotient above the period and write the product of divisor and quotient just below the first period.
  • Step IV: Subtract the product of divisor and quotient from the first period and bring down the next period to the right of the remainder. This becomes the new dividend.
  • Step V: Double the quotient and enter it with a blank on its right.
  • Step VI: Guess a largest possible digit to fill the blank which will also become the next digit in the quotient, such that when the new divisor is multiplied to the new quotient the product is less than or equal to the dividend.
  • Step VII: Repeat the above steps till all the periods have been taken up. Now, the quotient so obtained is the required square root of the given number.
image_descriptions: Division method calculation table for square root of 1522756 resulting in 1234.
Division method calculation table for finding the largest three-digit perfect square (961).

details.summary: Covers Prime Factorization and Division methods for calculating square roots.

subject: Mathematics
text:
CUBE: If a number is multiplied three times with itself, then the result of this multiplication is called the cube of that number. e.g., 8 = 2 x 2 x 2 = 2^3.

Properties of Cube:

  • Cubes of all even natural numbers are even and all odd natural numbers are odd.
  • Cubes of the numbers ending in digit 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 and 9 are the numbers ending in the same digit.
  • Cubes of negative integers are negative.
  • Cubes of numbers ending in digits 3 and 7 ends in digit 7 and 3, respectively.

CUBE ROOT: The cube root of a given number is the number whose cube is the given number. In general, we can say that a^3 = b, then cube root of ‘b’ is ‘a’. Cube root of a number ‘a’ is denoted as cube_root(a). e.g., cube_root(64) = cube_root(4 x 4 x 4) = 4. Thus, 4 is the cube root of 64.

Method to Find Cube Root: Prime Factorization Method. In this method, we express the given number as the product of prime factors. Now, for finding cube root, we take the product of these prime factors choosing one out of every three, from the factors.

details.summary: Definitions and properties of cubes, cube roots, and the prime factorization method for finding cube roots.

subject: Mathematics
text:
POWERS OR EXPONENTS: An expression that represents repeated multiplication of the same factor is called a power. It is written as 'x^n' and is read as 'x' raised to the power n. Here, x is called the 'base' and n is called the 'exponent'. e.g., 6^5 = 6 x 6 x 6 x 6 x 6 = 7776.

Laws of Exponents: Let (x/y) be any rational number and m, n be any integers. Then: (i) (x/y)^m * (x/y)^n = (x/y)^(m+n), (ii) (x/y)^m / (x/y)^n = (x/y)^(m-n), (iii) [(x/y)^m]^n = (x/y)^(mn), (iv) (x/y)^(-n) = (y/x)^n, (v) (x/y)^0 = 1.

SURDS OR RADICALS: Let x be a rational number and n be a positive integer, such that n-th root of x is irrational, then n-th root of x is called a radical or surd of order n and here x is called the radicand.

  • A surd of order 2 is called a quadratic surd i.e., sqrt(2), sqrt(3).
  • A surd of order 3 is called a cubic surd. i.e., cube_root(2), cube_root(3).
  • A surd of order 4 is called a biquadratic surd i.e., 4th_root(5), 4th_root(7).

Laws of Radicals: (i) (n-th root of x)^n = x, (ii) n-th root of (xy) = (n-th root of x) * (n-th root of y), (iii) n-th root of (x/y) = (n-th root of x) / (n-th root of y), (iv) (n-th root of x)^m = n-th root of (x^m), (v) m-th root of (n-th root of x) = (mn)-th root of x = n-th root of (m-th root of x).

details.summary: Laws of exponents and radicals/surds.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Types of Surds:

  • Pure surds: A surd which has only 1 as a rational factor is called a pure surd. e.g., sqrt(2), cube_root(2), fourth_root(3) are all pure surds.
  • Mixed surds: A surd which is not a pure surd or has factor other than unity is called a mixed surd. e.g., 2*sqrt(3), 5*cube_root(12), fourth_root(35/3) are mixed surds.
  • Like and Unlike surds: When the radicands of two surds are same, then those are known as like surds. e.g., 6*sqrt(3) and 2^2*sqrt(3). When radicands of two surds are different, then they are called unlike surds. e.g., 4*sqrt(7) and 6*sqrt(5).

details.summary: Definitions and classification of pure, mixed, like, and unlike surds.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Comparison of Two Surds:

  • If two surds are of the same order, then the one whose radicand is larger, is the larger of the two. e.g., sqrt(17) > sqrt(13), cube_root(21) > cube_root(16).
  • If any two surds have different orders to be compared, then we will first reduce them to the same but smallest order and then compare them.

Note: Let n_root(x) be a surd of order n. Then, n_root(x) = x^(1/n) i.e., (x^(m/n))^(1/m) is a surd of order m.

details.summary: Rules for comparing surds based on order and radicand.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Addition and Subtraction of Surds: Addition or subtraction takes place only between like surds, using laws of numbers. e.g., (i) 2*sqrt(3) + 4*sqrt(3) + sqrt(5) = 6*sqrt(3) + sqrt(5); (ii) 6*sqrt(5) - 3*sqrt(2) + 7*sqrt(5) + 4*sqrt(2) = (6*sqrt(5) + 7*sqrt(5)) + (4*sqrt(2) - 3*sqrt(2)) = 13*sqrt(5) + sqrt(2).

Multiplication and Division of Surds: Suppose given surds are n_root(a), n_root(b) and n_root(c), then first find the LCM of p, q and r to make the radial powers of the surds same and then their multiplication and division can be done using following rules: (i) n_root(x) * n_root(y) = n_root(xy); (ii) n_root(x) / n_root(y) = n_root(x/y).

details.summary: Arithmetic operations on surds including addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Rationalisation of Surds: Process of converting surd into rational number is called as rationalisation of surds. When the product of two surds is a rational number, then each surd is called a rationalising factor of each other. e.g., cube_root(25) * cube_root(5) = cube_root(125) = 5. So, cube_root(25) and cube_root(5) are rationalising factor of each other.

Rationalising factors of a given surd:

  • Rationalising factor of 1/sqrt(a) = sqrt(a)
  • Rationalising factor of 1/(sqrt(a) + sqrt(b)) = sqrt(a) - sqrt(b)

details.summary: Explanation of rationalisation and identifying rationalising factors.

Properties of Numbers and Algebraic Expressions:

  • Consecutive Numbers: The product of four consecutive numbers plus one is always a square. Example: 3x4x5x6 + 1 = 361 = (19)^2.
  • Consecutive Cubes: The difference of two consecutive cubes is never divisible by 2. Example: 5^3 - 4^3 = 61.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Distance: The length of the path travelled by any object or a person between two places is known as distance. The unit of distance is m or km.

Time: The duration in hours, minutes or seconds spent to cover a certain distance is called time.

Speed: The distance travelled by any object or a person per unit time is known as speed of that object or a person. The unit of speed is m/s or km/h.

details.summary: Basic definitions of distance, time, and speed.

subject: Mathematics
text:
To convert speed of an object from km/h to m/s, multiply it by 5/18.

e.g. 36 km/h = 36 * (5/18) m/s = 10 m/s

subject: Mathematics
text:
Conversion: To convert speed of an object from m/s to km/h, multiply it by 18/5. Example: 5 m/s = 5 * 18/5 km/h = 18 km/h.

Average Speed: Defined as total distance travelled divided by total time taken.

Relative Speed: The speed of an object with respect to another. If two bodies move with speeds x km/h and y km/h:

  • If moving in opposite directions: (x + y) km/h
  • If moving in same direction: (x - y) km/h

Important Rules:

  • Rule 1: If A travels with speed x km/h for t1 h and with speed y km/h for t2 h, then average speed = (x*t1 + y*t2) / (t1 + t2)
  • Rule 2: If a man/vehicle covers two equal distances with speed x km/h and y km/h respectively, average speed = (2xy) / (x + y)
  • Rule 3: If a man changes his speed to (x/y) of his usual speed and gets late by t min, the usual time taken = (t * x) / (y - x). If he reaches early by t min, the usual time taken = (t * x) / (y - x)
formulas: Average speed = Total distance / Total time

topic: Distance between two points with varying speeds
text:
Rule 4: When a man travels from A to B with a speed x km/h and reaches t1 h later after the fixed time and when he travels with a speed y km/h from A to B, he reaches his destination t2 h before the fixed time, then distance between A and B = (xy(t1 + t2)) / (y - x) km.

Rule 5: A person travels from A to B with a speed x km/h and reaches t1 h late. Later he increases his speed by y km/h to cover the same distance and he still gets late by t2 h, then the distance between A and B = (t1 - t2)(x + y) * x / y.

text:
Problems based on trains are same as the problems related to speed, Time and Distance. The only difference is that the length of the moving object (train) is taken into consideration in these types of problems.

Rule 6: (i) Time taken by a train x m long in passing a single post or pole or standing man = Time taken by the train to cover x m. (ii) Time taken by a train x m long in passing an object of length y m = Time taken by the train to cover (x + y) m.

Rule 7: Time taken by a train of length l1 metre moving at a speed of s1 m/s to cross another train of length l2 moving at a speed of s2 m/s in same/opposite direction is (l1 + l2) / (s1 ± s2). Use '+' for opposite direction. Use '-' for same direction.

Rule 8: If two trains start at the same time from points A and B towards each other and after crossing each other, they take t1 and t2 time in reaching points B and A respectively, then ratio of their speed = sqrt(t2 / t1) or S1 / S2 = sqrt(t2 / t1).

subject: Mathematics
topic: Problems Based on Boat and Stream
text:
Boat and Stream Concepts:

  • Still water: If the speed of water is zero, then water is considered to be still water.
  • Stream water: If the water of a river is moving at a certain speed, then it is called stream water.
  • Downstream motion: In water, the direction along the stream is called downstream.
  • Upstream motion: In water, the direction against the stream is called upstream.

Rules:

  • Rule 9: If the speed of a boat in still water = x km/h and speed of stream = y km/h, then:
    • Speed of boat downstream = (x + y) km/h
    • Speed of boat upstream = (x - y) km/h
  • Rule 10: Let the speed of boat in downstream = u km/h and speed of boat in upstream = v km/h, then:
    • Speed of boat in still water = 1/2(u + v) km/h
    • Speed of stream (current) = 1/2(u - v) km/h
formulas: Speed of boat downstream = x + y
Speed of boat upstream = x - y
Speed of boat in still water = 1/2(u + v)

text:
Usually (2-4) questions have been asked from this chapter. Generally questions are asked on Man-hours formulae, total wages paid for a work, number of days to complete a certain work and pipes and cisterns.

In this chapter, we will study the relationship among the quantity of work given, wages given, stipulated time, number of persons etc.

IMPORTANT RULES AND FORMULAE

  • Rule 1: If a person can do a piece of work in 'n' days, then he will do 1/n of the work in one day and if a person can do 1/n th of work in one day, then he will complete the work in n days. e.g. If Raj can do a piece of work in 20 days, then he will do 1/20th of the work in one day.
  • Note: In the problems related to time and work it is always considered that a man/woman works at uniform rate.
  • Rule 2: A and B can do a piece of work in x days and y days, respectively. Then, time taken by (A + B) to complete the work is equal to reciprocal of (A + B)'s one day's work, i.e. xy / (x + y).
  • Rule 3: If A and B can complete a work in x days and A alone can finish that work in y days, then number of days required to complete the work by B = xy / (y - x) days.
  • Rule 4: If A and B can do a piece of work in x days, B and C can do same work in y days, C and A can do same work in z days. Then, they will complete the same work in 2xyz / (xy + yz + zx) days by working together.

details.summary: Introduction to Time and Work chapter covering basic definitions, uniform rate assumption, and four fundamental rules for calculating work completion time for individuals and groups.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Rule 5: If two groups, M1 persons of the first group can do W1 work in D1 days working T1 hours in a day earning a sum of R1 and M2 persons of the second group can do W2 work in D2 days working T2 hours in a day earning a sum of R2. If each person of both group has the same efficiency of work, then:

(M1 * D1 * T1) / (W1 * R1) = (M2 * D2 * T2) / (W2 * R2)

Rule 6: If 'm' men or 'n' women can do a piece of work in 'a' days, then x men and y women can do the same work in 1 / (x/(m*a) + y/(n*a)) days.

Rule 7: If A can do a work in x days and B can do y% faster than A, then B will complete the work in (100 * x) / (100 + y) days.

Rule 8: If A, B and C can do a piece of work in x, y and z days, respectively and they received ₹ k as wages by working together, then:

  • share of A = (yz / (xy + yz + zx)) * k
  • share of B = (xz / (xy + yz + zx)) * k
  • share of C = (xy / (xy + yz + zx)) * k
formulas: share of A = (yz / (xy + yz + zx)) * k
share of B = (xz / (xy + yz + zx)) * k
share of C = (xy / (xy + yz + zx)) * k

If A and B can do a piece of work in x days and y days, respectively and they received k as wages by working together, then share of A = (yk / (x+y)) and share of B = (xk / (x+y)). Wages are directly proportional to the work done and indirectly proportional to the time taken by the individual.

Some Other Formulae

  • If A and B can do a piece of work in x and y days, respectively. A and B started working together but A left the work t days before completing the work, then time taken to complete the work will be ((x+t)y / (x+y)) days.
  • If A and B do a piece of work in x and y days, respectively. Both begin together but after some days, A leaves the work and the remaining work is completed by B in x days. Then, the time after which A left is given by T = ((b-x)a / a+b).
  • If A and B can do a piece of work in x and y days, respectively. They start working together and after t days B leaves the work, then time taken to finish the whole work will be (x(y-t) / y) days.

If there are two pipes A and B takes 'a' h and 'b' h respectively to fill a tanker, then the two pipes together fill (1/a + 1/b) part of the tank in 1h and time taken to fill the tank will be (ab / a+b) h. If a pipe fills a tank in 'a' h, then in 1 h only 1/a of the tank is filled.

Rule 10

(i) If a pipe can fill a tank in 'a' h and another can fill the tank in 'b' h but a third pipe empties the filled tank in 'c' h, then in one hour (1/a + 1/b - 1/c) part of the tank will be filled (when all the three pipes are open) and time taken to fill the tank will be (abc / bc+ac-ab) h.

(ii) If a pipe can fill a tank in a1 h and another pipe can empty the filled tank in a2 h, then in one hour (1/a1 - 1/a2) part of the tank will be filled. (when both pipes are open) and time taken to fill the tank will be (a1*a2 / a2-a1) h.

Per Cent: Per cent is a fraction whose denominator is 100 and numerator of the fraction is called the rate per cent. Per cent is denoted by the symbol '%'.

Important Rules and Formulae:

  • Rule 1: For expressing a% as a fraction, we can write a% = a/100, i.e. divide 'a' by 100 and reduce it to the lowest form, e.g., 25% = 25/100 = 1/4.
  • Rule 2: For expressing a fraction a/b as a per cent, we can write a/b = (a/b * 100)%, e.g., 2/3 = (2/3 * 100)% = 200/3%.
  • Rule 3: To find how much per cent one quantity is of another quantity, we can write: Required percentage = (The quantity to be expressed in per cent / 2nd quantity (in respect of which the per cent has to be obtained)) * 100%.
  • Rule 4: Percentage increase or decrease in a quantity when it increases or decreases by some value: Percentage = (Increase or decrease in the value / Initial value) * 100%.
formulas: Required percentage = (The quantity to be expressed in per cent / 2nd quantity) * 100%
Percentage = (Increase or decrease in the value / Initial value) * 100%

text:
Interest: When money is borrowed by a person, then customarily the money lender used to charge some extra money in lieu of the money lent by him. This extra money earned by the money lender is called interest.

Terms related to interest:

  • Principal (P): The money which is borrowed from a money lender.
  • Amount (A): The sum of the principal and the interest. Amount (A) = Principal (P) + Interest (I).
  • Rate (R): The rate at which the interest is charged on Principal.
  • Time (T): The time period for which the money is lent or deposited or borrowed.

Simple Interest: If the interest is calculated on the original Principal for any length of time, then it is called simple interest.

text:
Rule 1: If a sum of money becomes n times in 'T' yr at simple interest, then rate of interest will be, R = (100(n-1))/T %.

Rule 2: If a certain Principal Amounts to A1 in t1 yr and to A2 in t2 yr, then the sum (P) is given by P = (A2*t1 - A1*t2)/(t1 - t2) and the rate per cent (R) per annum is given by ((100(A2 - A1))/(A1*t2 - A2*t1))%.

Rule 3: At the same rate of simple interest, if a sum of money becomes n1 times of itself in t1 yr and n2 times in t2 years, then t2 = ((n2 - 1)/(n1 - 1)) * t1 yr.

Compound Interest: When the interest is calculated on the amount of previous year, then it is known as compound interest. It will make a deposit or loan grow at a faster rate than simple interest.

Variables:

  • P = Principal (amount borrowed)
  • A = Amount (Principal + Interest)
  • R = Rate of interest per annum
  • n = Number of years

Rule 1: When interest is compounded annually

  • Amount = P(1 + R/100)^n
  • CI = A - P = P[(1 + R/100)^n - 1]

Rule 2: When interest is compounded half-yearly (every 6 months)

  • Amount = P(1 + r/(100*2))^(2n)
  • CI = [(1 + R/(100*2))^(2n) - 1]

Rule 4: When interest is compounded annually but time is given in fraction (say, t + a/b yr), then:

Amount = P(1 + R/100)^t * (1 + (a/b)R/100)

text:
Cost Price (CP): The price, at which an article is bought is called its cost price. All the overhead expenses in the transaction like freight, damage etc., are added to the cost price.

Selling Price (SP): The price at which an article sold is called its selling price.

  • Profit (SP > CP): When an article is sold at a price more than its cost price, then profit is earned.
  • Loss (CP > SP): When an article is sold at a price lower than its cost price, then loss is incurred.

Note: Profit and loss percentage is always calculated as the percentage of CP unless otherwise specified.

List Price/Marked Price: The price of an article which is displayed on the price tag is known as marked price. It is the normal price of the thing/products without a discount. Sometimes the shopkeeper increases or decreases the cost price, then this price is taken as the list price of the article.

details.summary: Introduction to fundamental concepts of Profit and Loss including definitions of Cost Price, Selling Price, Marked Price, and calculation formulas for profit and loss percentages.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Rule 1: If there is a profit of r%, then (i) SP = (100 + r) * CP / 100 (ii) CP = 100 * SP / (100 + r)

Rule 2: If there is a loss of r%, then (i) SP = (100 - r) * CP / 100 (ii) CP = 100 * SP / (100 - r)

Rule 3: When there are two successive profits or losses of x% and y%, then the resultant profit or loss percent is given by (±x ± y + (±x)(±y)/100)%.

  • Take positive for profit and negative for loss.
  • If the sign of result is positive, then there is a total gain.
  • If the sign of result is negative, then there is a total loss.

Rule 4: When two different articles are sold at the same selling price, getting gain/loss of x% on the first and gain/loss of y% on the second, then the overall % gain or % loss in the transaction is given by [100(x + y) + 2xy / (100 + x) + (100 + x)]%. The above expression represent overall gain or loss accordingly as its sign is positive or negative.

When two different articles are sold at the same selling price getting a gain of x% on the first and loss of x% on the second, then the overall % loss in the transaction is given by (x/10)^2 %.

Note: That in such questions there is always a loss.

details.summary: Covers fundamental profit and loss formulas including successive percentage changes and specific rules for selling two articles at the same price.

  • Cost price of item sold at gain = (S * (100 - r)) / ((100 - r) + (100 + R))

text:
A ratio is the comparison of two or more quantities of the same type (or kind) by division. If a and b are two quantities of the same kind (or same unit), then the fraction a/b is called the ratio a to b and we write it as a : b.

  • a is called the antecedent.
  • b is called the consequent.

Example: If a fruit box contains 8 oranges and 7 lemons then the ratio of oranges to lemons is 8 to 7 or 8:7.

Note: If both terms a and b of a ratio are multiplied or divided by the same quantity, then ratio remains unchanged.

i.e. a:b is same as na : nb => a/b = na/nb and a:b is same as a/n : b/n => (a/n) / (b/n) = a/b.

details.summary: Introduction to the definition of ratio, its components (antecedent and consequent), and the property of equivalent ratios.

mcq.question: If the ratio of 90 cm to 1.5 m is same as 3 : x, then x is
mcq.explanation: 1.5 m = 150 cm (units must be same). Ratio of 90 cm to 150 cm = 90/150 = 90/30 / 150/30 = 3/5. As this ratio is same as 3 : x, then 3/x = 3/5, which implies 3x = 15, so x = 5.

subject: Mathematics
text:
1. Compound Ratio: When two or more ratios are multiplied together, they are said to be compound ratio. If a/b, c/d and e/f are all ratios, then their compound ratio is ace/bdf. e.g., Compound ratio of 2/3, 4/7 and 1/3 = (2*4*1)/(3*7*3) = 8/63.

2. Duplicate Ratio: When a ratio is compounded with itself, the resulting ratio is called the duplicate ratio. So, a^2 : b^2 is duplicate ratio of a : b.

3. Triplicate Ratio: If a ratio is compounded three times with itself, then resulting ratio is called triplicate ratio. So, a^3 : b^3 is the triplicate ratio of a : b.

4. Subduplicate Ratio: If two numbers are in ratio, then the ratio of their square roots is called subduplicate ratio. If a : b is ratio, then the subduplicate ratio is sqrt(a) : sqrt(b). e.g., Subduplicate ratio of 9 : 16 is sqrt(9) : sqrt(16) = 3 : 4.

5. Subtriplicate Ratio: If two numbers are in ratio, then the ratio of their cube roots is called subtriplicate ratio. If a : b is ratio, then the subtriplicate ratio is cuberoot(a) : cuberoot(b). e.g., Subtriplicate ratio of 64 : 27 is cuberoot(64) : cuberoot(27) = 4 : 3.

6. Reciprocal Ratio: If a : b is a ratio, then 1/a : 1/b is its reciprocal ratio, i.e., b : a. e.g., Reciprocal ratio of 3 : 7 is 1/3 : 1/7 i.e., 7 : 3.

Important Points:

  • Usually, the ratio is expressed in its lowest terms.
  • Ratio exists only between quantities of the same kind.
  • Ratio is a fraction, so it has no units.
  • Ratio is taken only between positive quantities.
formulas: Compound ratio of a/b, c/d, e/f = ace/bdf

subject: Mathematics
text:
The equality of two ratios is called proportion. '::' is the sign of proportion. So, if a : b = c : d, we write it as a : b :: c : d and say that a, b, c and d are in proportion. The quantities a, b, c and d are called the first, second, third and fourth terms of proportion respectively. First and fourth terms are called extreme terms and second and third terms are called means or middle terms. If quantities a, b, c and d are in proportion, then a/b = c/d => ad = bc i.e., product of extreme terms = product of middle terms. This is also called cross-product rule.

Types of Proportion:

1. Continued Proportion: The non-zero quantities of same kind, a, b, c, d, e, f, ... are said to be continued proportion, if a/b = b/c = c/d = e/f = ...
formulas: Continued proportion: a/b = b/c = c/d = e/f

details.summary: Definition of proportion, identification of terms (extremes and means), the cross-product rule, and definition of continued proportion.

subject: Mathematics
text:
If a, b, c, d and e are in continued proportion, then a/b = b/c = c/d = d/e. This implies a/e = a/b * b/c * c/d * d/e = b^4/a^4.

Mean Proportional: If a, b and c are in continued proportion, then b is called the mean proportional of a and c. i.e., a/b = b/c => b^2 = ac => b = sqrt(ac).

details.summary: Definitions and properties of continued and mean proportion.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Third Proportional: If a : b :: b : c, then c is called the 3rd proportional to a and b. Calculated as c = b^2/a.

Fourth Proportional: If four numbers or quantities a, b, c and d are in proportion, then d is known as the fourth proportional. i.e., a : b :: c : d.

details.summary: Definitions for third and fourth proportional.

subject: Mathematics
text:
If four non-zero quantities a, b, c and d are in proportion, the properties are:

  • Invertendo: If a:b::c:d, then b:a::d:c (a/b = c/d => b/a = d/c)
  • Alternendo: If a:b::c:d, then a:c::b:d (a/b = c/d => a/c = b/d)
  • Componendo: If a:b::c:d, then (a+b):b :: (c+d):d
  • Dividendo: If a:b::c:d, then (a-b):b :: (c-d):d
  • Componendo and Dividendo: If a:b::c:d, then (a+b):(a-b) :: (c+d):(c-d)

details.summary: List of five fundamental properties of proportions.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Mixture or Alligation: If two or more quantities are mixed together in a certain ratio, then the product is called mixture.

Mean Price: Cost price of a unit quantity of the mixture is called the mean price.

Rule of Mixture or Alligation: It is the rule to find the ratio in which two or more ingredients are mixed or to be mixed. If two quantities are mixed in the ratio n1:n2, then n1/n2 = (P2 - Pm) / (Pm - P1), where P1, P2 and Pm are cheaper price, dearer price and mean price respectively.

Note: P1 < Pm < P2
image_descriptions: Alligation diagram showing Cheaper price (P1) and Dearer price (P2) branching to Mean price (Pm), with (P2-Pm) under P1 and (Pm-P1) under P2.

details.summary: Definition and rule for calculating mixture ratios using alligation.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Variations: When a change in a certain quantity leads to a certain change in another quantity then it is called variations.

Direct Variation: If x varies directly with y, then as x increases (decreases) y also increases (decreases). i.e., x ∝ y => x = ky, where k is the constant of variation.

Inverse Variation: If x varies inversely with y, then an increase in the value of x causes a decrease in the value of y. i.e., x ∝ 1/y => x = k'/y, where k' is the constant of variation.

details.summary: Definitions of direct and inverse variations.

If 'a' is a positive real number, other than 1 and 'b' is a rational number such that a^b = N, then we say that logarithm of N to base 'a' is b or 'b' is the logarithm of N to base 'a', written as log_a N = b.

So, a^b = N <=> log_a N = b

Examples: 7^0 = 1 <=> log_7 1 = 0, 81^(1/4) = 3 <=> log_81 3 = 1/4

  • log_a(a) = 1
  • x > y => log_a(x) > log_a(y) for a > 1
  • x > y => log_a(x) < log_a(y) for 0 < a < 1
  • log_a(n)(x) = (1/n) log_a(x)
  • log_b(x) = x log_b(a)
  • log_a(n) = log_a^2(n^2) = log_a^3(n^3) = log_a^m(n^m)

details.summary: Key identities and properties of logarithms.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Common Logarithm: Logarithm to the base 10. Also called Brigg's logarithm. e.g., log_10(100) = 2, log_10(1000) = 3.

Natural Logarithm: Logarithm to the base e. Also called Napier logarithm. Denoted by ln x. e is an irrational number between 2 and 3. ln x = y => e^y = x.

details.summary: Definitions of common (base 10) and natural (base e) logarithms.

subject: Mathematics
text: The positive number 'a' is called the antilogarithm of a number b, if log a = b. If 'a' is antilogarithm of b, it is written as a = antilog b. So, a = antilog b <=> log a = b.
formulas: a = antilog b <=> log a = b

details.summary: Definition of antilogarithm.

subject: Mathematics
topic: Characteristic and Mantissa of a Logarithm
text:
The logarithm of a positive real number 'n' consists of two parts:

  • The integral part is known as the characteristic. It is always an integer (positive, negative or zero).
  • The decimal part is called the mantissa. The mantissa is never negative and is always less than one.

To Find the Characteristic:

  • Case I: The characteristic of the log of a number greater than 1 is positive and numerically one less than the number of digits to the left of the decimal point.
  • Case II: The characteristic of log of a number less than 1 is negative and numerically one more than the number of zeroes immediately after the decimal point. It is represented by a bar over the digit.

Rules for Inserting Decimal Point:

  • Rule 5: When the characteristic of the logarithm is positive, we insert the decimal point after the (n + 1)th digit, where n is the characteristic.
  • Rule 6: When the characteristic of the logarithm is negative, we insert the decimal point such that the first significant figures is at nth place, where n is the characteristic.

Some Important Points:

  • The base of a logarithm is never taken as zero and negative.
  • Log of negative integers are not defined and also log_e 0 is not defined.
  • Logarithmic function is positive as well as negative but exponential function is always positive.

details.summary: Explanation of characteristic and mantissa components of logarithms, rules for determining characteristics based on number magnitude, and rules for decimal placement.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Algebraic Expressions: A combination of constants and variables connected by the four fundamental operations +, -, × and ÷ is called an algebraic expression.

Polynomials: A polynomial is an algebraic expression consisting of variables and coefficients, having non-negative integral powers. e.g. x^3 + 5x^2 - 1, 3x^3 + 4x^2y + 17 etc.

  • (i) 3x^2 + 9x - 1 + 7/x is not a polynomial as it contains a term, namely 7/x, having negative integral power of variable x.
  • (ii) 5x^2 - 7x^(7/2) + x - 1 is not a polynomial as the term -7x^(7/2) contains rational power of variable x.

Degree of a Polynomial: The exponent of the highest degree term in a polynomial, is known as degree of polynomial. e.g. (i) 4x^3 - 9x^2 + 7x + 9 is a polynomial with variable x of degree 3. (ii) 4x^3y - 3x^2 + 2xy + 1 is a polynomial of degree 4.

Various Types of Polynomials: Polynomials are classified on the basis of degree of polynomial and number of terms which are given below.

Based on Degree of Polynomial: (i) Constant polynomial: A polynomial of degree zero, is called constant polynomial. e.g. f(x) = 8. Note: The polynomial f(x) = 0 is called the zero polynomial. The degree of zero polynomial is not defined.

details.summary: Introduction to algebraic expressions, definition of polynomials, criteria for non-polynomials, definition of degree of a polynomial, and classification of polynomials based on degree.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Classification of Polynomials by Degree:

  • Linear polynomial: A polynomial of degree 1. e.g., 9x + 7, x - 9, x + 2 etc.
  • Quadratic polynomial: A polynomial of degree 2. General form: ax^2 + bx + c, where a, b, c are real and a ≠ 0. e.g., x^2 - 7x + 12, 5y^2 - 7, z^2 - 4 etc.
  • Cubic polynomial: A polynomial of degree 3. General form: ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d, where a, b, c, d are real and a ≠ 0. e.g., 3x^3 + 2x^2 + 7x - 1, 8y^3 + 5y + 2, x^3 - 8 etc.
  • Biquadratic polynomial: A polynomial of degree 4. General form: ax^4 + bx^3 + cx^2 + dx + e, where a, b, c, d, e are real numbers and a ≠ 0. e.g., 6x^4 + 3x^3 + 2x^2 + x + 2, x^4 - 8 etc.

Classification of Polynomials by Number of Terms:

  • Monomial: A polynomial containing only one term. e.g., 6x^2
  • Binomial: A polynomial containing two terms. e.g., 5x^3 + 7xy
  • Trinomial: A polynomial containing three terms. e.g., 7x^2y + 5x + 6

Factorisation: To express a polynomial as the product of other polynomials of degree less than that of the given polynomial. e.g., x^2 - 49 = x^2 - 7^2 = (x - 7)(x + 7)

Important Identities:

  • a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b)
  • (a + b)^2 = a^2 + b^2 + 2ab and (a - b)^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab
  • (a + b)^2 - (a - b)^2 = 4ab
  • (a + b)^2 + (a - b)^2 = 2(a^2 + b^2)
  • (a + b)^3 = a^3 + b^3 + 3ab(a + b)
  • (a - b)^3 = a^3 - b^3 - 3ab(a - b)
  • (a^3 + b^3) = (a + b)(a^2 + b^2 - ab)
  • (a^3 - b^3) = (a - b)(a^2 + b^2 + ab)
  • (a + b + c)^2 = a^2 + b^2 + c^2 + 2(ab + bc + ac)
  • a^3 + b^3 + c^3 - 3abc = (a + b + c)(a^2 + b^2 + c^2 - ab - ac - bc)
  • If a + b + c = 0, then a^3 + b^3 + c^3 = 3abc
  • a^4 + a^2b^2 + b^4 = (a^2 + ab + b^2)(a^2 - ab + b^2)

details.summary: Covers classification of polynomials by degree and number of terms, definition of factorisation, and a comprehensive list of algebraic identities.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Factorisation of Perfect Square Polynomials: If the polynomial is given as the perfect square quadratic polynomial, use the following identities:

  • a^2 + 2ab + b^2 = (a + b)^2
  • a^2 - 2ab + b^2 = (a - b)^2

Factorising the Difference of Two Squares: In case the polynomial is in the form of a^2 - b^2, use:

  • a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b)

Factorisation of Quadratic Polynomials: For polynomials of the type ax^2 + bx + c (where a != 0), factorise by splitting the middle term. Find two numbers p and q such that p + q = b and pq = ac, then: ax^2 + bx + c = ax^2 + (p + q)x + c = ax^2 + px + qx + c

Factorisation of Sum and Difference of Cubes:

  • a^3 + b^3 = (a + b)(a^2 - ab + b^2)
  • a^3 - b^3 = (a - b)(a^2 + ab + b^2)

Factorisation of Polynomial of form a^3 + b^3 + c^3 - 3abc:

  • a^3 + b^3 + c^3 - 3abc = (a + b + c)(a^2 + b^2 + c^2 - ab - bc - ac)
  • If a + b + c = 0, then a^3 + b^3 + c^3 = 3abc
formulas: ax^2 + bx + c = ax^2 + (p + q)x + c

details.summary: Covers algebraic factorisation techniques including perfect squares, difference of squares, splitting the middle term for quadratics, sum/difference of cubes, and the identity for a^3 + b^3 + c^3 - 3abc.

subject: Mathematics
text: Let p(x) be a polynomial of degree n greater than or equal to 1 (i.e. n >= 1) and a be any real number. If p(x) is divided by the linear polynomial (x - a), then the remainder is p(a). Remainder can be evaluated by substituting x - a = 0, i.e. x = a in p(x).

details.summary: Definition and application of the Remainder Theorem for polynomials.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Let p(x) be a polynomial, if degree n >= 1 and a be any real number. Then,

  • (i) If p(a) = 0, then (x - a) is a factor of p(x).
  • (ii) If (x - a) is a factor of p(x), then p(a) = 0.

details.summary: Definition of the Factor Theorem.

subject: Mathematics
text: If p(x) and g(x) are any two polynomials with g(x) != 0, then we can find polynomials q(x) and r(x) such that p(x) = g(x) * q(x) + r(x). i.e. Dividend = (Divisor * Quotient) + Remainder where, r(x) = 0 or degree of r(x) < degree of g(x), then we say that p(x) divided by g(x), gives q(x) as quotient and r(x) as remainder. If the remainder r(x) is zero, we say that divisor g(x) is a factor of p(x).

details.summary: Definition of the Division Synthetic Algorithm.

subject: Mathematics
topic: Factorisation of Polynomials Using Factor Theorem
text:
To factorise the polynomial, follow the following steps:

  • (i) Let p(x) be a given polynomial.
  • (ii) find all the possible factors of constant term in p(x).
  • (iii) Take any one of the factors, say (alpha) and find p(alpha). If p(alpha) = 0 the (x - alpha) is a factor of p(x).
  • (iv) Divide the polynomial p(x) by (x - alpha) to find its all other factors.

details.summary: Steps to factorise polynomials using the Factor Theorem.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Divisor: A polynomial d(x) is said to be a divisor of polynomial p(x) if d(x) is a factor of p(x) i.e., p(x) can be written as p(x) = d(x) * q(x), where q(x) is a quotient polynomial e.g. (x - 3) is a divisor of (x - 3)^2(x + 1).

HCF (GCD) of Polynomials: A polynomial h(x) is called the HCF or GCD of two or more given polynomials, if h(x) is a polynomial of highest degree dividing each one of the given polynomial without leaving any remainder.

Note: The coefficient of highest degree term is always taken as positive.

Example 1: The HCF of polynomials (x + 2)^2 (x - 3)^2 and (x + 1) (x + 2)^2 (x - 3) is:

  • a. (x + 2)(x - 3)
  • b. (x + 2)^2 (x - 3)
  • c. (x + 1)(x + 2)(x - 3)
  • d. (x + 2)^2 (x - 3)^2

Solution: Let p(x) = (x + 2)^2 (x - 3)^2 and q(x) = (x + 1) (x + 2)^2 (x - 3). The common factor between two polynomials is (x + 2)^2 (x - 3), therefore HCF = (x + 2)^2 (x - 3).

details.summary: Introduction to HCF and LCM of polynomials, defining divisors and the HCF (GCD) of polynomials with an illustrative example.

mcq.question: The HCF of polynomials (x + 2)^2 (x - 3)^2 and (x + 1) (x + 2)^2 (x - 3) is
mcq.explanation: The common factor between the two polynomials (x + 2)^2 (x - 3)^2 and (x + 1) (x + 2)^2 (x - 3) is (x + 2)^2 (x - 3).

subject: Mathematics
text:
HCF by Factorisation Method: Following are the steps for calculating HCF through factorisation method:

  • Step I: Resolve the given polynomials in the complete factored form.
  • Step II: Find the HCF of the numerical factors (if any) of given polynomial.
  • Step III: Find the factors of highest degree which is common to all given polynomials.
  • Step IV: The product of all such common factors and HCF of the numerical factors is the HCF of given polynomials.

details.summary: Step-by-step procedure to calculate the Highest Common Factor (HCF) of polynomials using the factorisation method.

subject: Mathematics
text:
To find the HCF of polynomials which cannot be factorised easily, we use successive division method.

  • Step I: Arrange the given polynomials in descending order of powers of its variables.
  • Step II: If any common factor is present in the terms of each polynomial, it should be taken out.
  • Step III: Divide the polynomial of highest degree by the polynomial of lowest degree. Or if both the polynomials are of the same degree then any one of them can be taken as divisor or dividend.
  • Step IV: After the first division take the remainder as the new divisor and first divisor as new dividend.
  • Step V: Continue this process of dividing the last divisor by the last remainder until the remainder becomes zero.
  • Step VI: The product of common factors obtained from step II and last divisor is the HCF of given polynomials.

Note:

  • If the first term of a remainder is negative at any stage, the sign of all of its term must be changed.
  • If at any stage, the remainder contains common factor it should be taken out.
image_descriptions: Long division process for finding HCF of polynomials: (x^3 - 11x - 6) divided by (x^2 - 3x - 2) resulting in a remainder of zero.

details.summary: Step-by-step procedure for calculating the Highest Common Factor (HCF) of polynomials using the division method.

subject: Mathematics
text:
A polynomial h(x) is called the LCM of two or more polynomials, if it is a polynomial of smallest degree which is divided by each one of the given polynomials without leaving any remainder.

LCM by Factorisation Method:

  • Step I: Resolve the given polynomials in the complete factored form.
  • Step II: Find the LCM of the numerical factors (if any) of given polynomials.
  • Step III: The required LCM is the product of LCM of numerical factors and each factor raised to the highest power.
formulas: LCM = (LCM of numerical factors) * (product of each factor raised to the highest power)

details.summary: Definition and methodology for calculating the Least Common Multiple (LCM) of polynomials using factorisation.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Key Property: For any two polynomials p(x) and q(x), the product of the two polynomials is equal to the product of their HCF and LCM.

p(x) * q(x) = (Their HCF) * (Their LCM)

details.summary: Explains the relationship between HCF, LCM, and the product of two polynomials with solved examples.

subject: Mathematics
text:
An expression in the form p(x)/q(x), where p(x) and q(x) are polynomials and q(x) ≠ 0 is called a rational expression.

  • In the rational expression p(x)/q(x), p(x) is called the numerator and q(x) is called the denominator.
  • Every polynomial is a rational expression. Since p(x) can be written as p(x)/1 and a constant function 1 is a polynomial of degree 0.
  • Every rational expression need not be a polynomial.

Working Rule to Reduce the Given Rational Expression in its Lowest Term:

  1. Firstly, factorize both the polynomials p(x) and q(x).
  2. Find the HCF of p(x) and q(x). If HCF of p(x) and q(x) is one, then rational expression p(x)/q(x) is in its lowest terms.
  3. If HCF is not equal to 1, then divide both p(x) and q(x) by their HCF and the rational expression is obtained in the lowest terms.

details.summary: Covers the definition of rational expressions and the step-by-step procedure to simplify them to their lowest terms.

subject: Mathematics
text:
1. Addition or Subtraction of Rational Expressions with like denominators: If p(x)/q(x) and h(x)/q(x) are two rational expressions then p(x)/q(x) ± h(x)/q(x) = (p(x) ± h(x))/q(x).

2. Addition or subtraction of Rational Expressions with unlike denominators: To add or subtract rational expressions with unlike denominators, follow the steps:

  • Step I: Write each denominator in the factor form.
  • Step II: Find the LCM of the denominators.
  • Step III: Rewrite each rational expression with LCM as the denominator.
  • Step IV: Add or subtract the numerators.

3. Multiplication of Rational Expressions: If p(x)/q(x) and g(x)/h(x) are two rational expressions, then their product is given by (p(x)/q(x)) * (g(x)/h(x)) = (p(x) * g(x)) / (q(x) * h(x)).

  • Multiplicative inverse of p(x)/q(x) is q(x)/p(x).
  • 1 is the multiplicative identity.

4. Division of Rational Expressions: If p(x)/q(x) and g(x)/h(x) are two rational expressions, then their division is given by (p(x)/q(x)) ÷ (g(x)/h(x)) = (p(x)/q(x)) * (h(x)/g(x)) = Product of p(x)/q(x) and the reciprocal of g(x)/h(x) i.e., h(x)/g(x).

details.summary: Covers arithmetic operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division) on rational algebraic expressions.

subject: Mathematics
text: A linear equation is an equation for a straight line. An equation which has degree 1, i.e., which has linear power of the variables, is called a linear equation.

details.summary: Definition of a linear equation based on degree.

subject: Mathematics
text:
A linear equation in one variable is an equation which can be written in the form ax + b = 0, or ax = c, where a, b, c are real numbers with a ≠ 0.

Examples: 5x + 8 = 9 - x, (2/3)y + 7 = y/2 and t + 3t = 9 - t are linear equations in one variable.

Steps for Solving a linear Equation in One Variable:

  • Simplify both sides of the equation.
  • Use the addition and subtraction properties to get all variables or terms on the LHS and all constant terms on the RHS.
  • Simplify and divide both sides of the equation by the coefficient of the variable.

details.summary: Definition and solving procedure for linear equations in one variable.

subject: Mathematics
text:
An equation which can be put in the form ax + by + c = 0, where a, b and c are real numbers and a, b both are not zero, is called a linear equation in two variables.

Examples: 2x + 3y = 5, sqrt(2)x + sqrt(3)y = 0 and 2a + 3b = 0 are linear equations in two variables.

details.summary: Definition of linear equations in two variables.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Two linear equations in the two same variables are called pair of linear equations in two variables. The general form is a1x + b1y + c1 = 0 and a2x + b2y + c2 = 0, where a1, a2, b1, b2 and c1, c2 are all real numbers and a12 + b12 ≠ 0, a22 + b22 ≠ 0.

Consistency Pair of Linear Equations: A pair of linear equations which has no solution is called an inconsistent pair. A pair of linear equations which has atleast one solution is called a consistent pair.
tables:
| Ratios | Consistency | Graphical Representation | Algebraic interpretation |
|---|---|---|---|
| a_1/a_2 != b_1/b_2 | Consistent | Intersecting lines | Exactly one solution (unique) |
| a_1/a_2 = b_1/b_2 = c_1/c_2 | Dependent (consistent) | Coincident lines | Infinitely many solutions |
| a_1/a_2 = b_1/b_2 != c_1/c_2 | Inconsistent | Parallel lines | No solution |
image_descriptions: Three small graphs showing: 1. Two intersecting lines, 2. Two coincident lines, 3. Two parallel lines.

details.summary: Definitions of consistent and inconsistent pairs of linear equations and their graphical/algebraic interpretations.

subject: Mathematics
text:
The pair a1x + b1y = 0, a2x + b2y = 0 has:

  • A unique solution, if a1/a2 != b1/b2 and the solution is x = 0, y = 0.
  • An infinite number of solutions, if a1/a2 = b1/b2.

This pair is always consistent.

details.summary: Conditions for unique and infinite solutions for homogeneous linear equations.

subject: Mathematics
text: 1. Substitution Method: In this method, we substitute the value of one variable in terms of other variable to solve the pair of linear equations. Step 1: Find the value of one variable x (or y) in terms of other variable i.e. y (or x) from an equation.

details.summary: Introduction to the substitution method for solving linear equations.

subject: Mathematics
text:
3. Cross-multiplication Method

Let us consider a general system of two simultaneous linear equations:

a1x + b1y + c1 = 0 ...(i)

a2x + b2y + c2 = 0 ...(ii)

where, a1/a2 ≠ b1/b2 then the solution of the system is given by,

x = (b1c2 - b2c1) / (a1b2 - a2b1) and y = (c1a2 - c2a1) / (a1b2 - a2b1)

∴ x / (b1c2 - b2c1) = y / (c1a2 - c2a1) = 1 / (a1b2 - a2b1)

This method is called cross multiplication method.

Remembering Technique (Cross-multiplication)

The following diagram helps in remembering the above solution. The arrows between the two numbers indicate that they are to be multiplied. The downward arrows indicate first product while upward arrows indicate the second product. The second product is to be subtracted from the first.
image_descriptions: A diagram showing the cross-multiplication mnemonic: x, y, and 1 are placed above columns of coefficients b1, c1, a1, b1 and b2, c2, a2, b2. Arrows connect b1 to c2, c1 to a2, a1 to b2, b2 to c1, c2 to a1, and a2 to b1 to indicate multiplication pairs.

details.summary: Explanation of the cross-multiplication method for solving simultaneous linear equations.

subject: Mathematics
text:
2. Elimination Method

In this method, one variable is eliminated from both equations to have an equation in one variable, so it is called elimination method.

Steps used in this method are given below:

  • Step I: Make the coefficient of one variable (x or y) numerically equal by multiplying both equations by some suitable non zero constant.
  • Step II: Now, add or subtract both equations, so that one variable is eliminated and the remaining equation is in one variable only.
  • Step III: Solve the equation in one variable to get the value of this variable (x or y).
  • Step IV: Substitute this value (x or y) in either of the given equations to get the value of other variable.

details.summary: Definition and steps for the elimination method to solve linear equations.

subject: Mathematics
topic: Equations Reducible to a Pair of Linear Equations
text: We have several situations when there are two equations that are not linear, but can be reduced to a pair of linear equations by making suitable substitutions.

details.summary: Explanation of how to solve non-linear equations by substituting variables to transform them into a pair of linear equations.

subject: Mathematics
text:
An equation in the form of ax + by + cz = r, where a, b, c and r are real numbers and a, b and c are not all zeros is called a linear equation in three variables.

Examples: 3x + 4y - 7z = 2, -2x + y - z = 6 and x + y + z = 2 are all linear equations in three variables.

Use substitution and elimination method to solve the system of three equations in three variables.

details.summary: Definition and examples of linear equations in three variables.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Application of Linear Equations

The application of linear equations is categorized into:

  • Problem Based on Ages: If the problem involves finding out the ages of two persons, take the present age of one person as x and the other as y. 'a' years ago, ages were (x - a) and (y - a). After 'b' years, ages will be (x + b) and (y + b).
  • Problem Based on Numbers: For a two-digit number, if the unit's place is x and ten's place is y, the number is 10y + x. On reversing, it becomes 10x + y.
  • Problem Based on Fractions: If the numerator is x and denominator is y, the fraction is x/y.

details.summary: Covers the methodology for solving word problems involving ages, numbers, and fractions using systems of linear equations.

subject: Mathematics
topic: Problem Based on Distance, Speed and Time
text:
Speed is the distance covered by an object per unit time.

i.e., Speed = Distance / Time

If the speed of boat in still water be x km/h and speed of stream be y km/h, then:

  • Speed of boat downstream = (x + y) km/h
  • Speed of boat upstream = (x - y) km/h

details.summary: Definitions and basic formulas for boat and stream problems.

subject: Mathematics
topic: Problem Based on Fixed and running Charges
text: Let the fixed charge of any commodity be ₹ x and rate of running charges be ₹ y, then total cost = x + total running charges.

details.summary: General formula for problems involving fixed and variable costs.

text:
Make use of given formulae to formulate the equation:

  • Area of rectangle = length × breadth
  • Perimeter of rectangle = 2(length + Breadth)
  • The sum of angles of a triangle is 180°
  • The sum of opposite angles of cyclic quadrilateral is 180°
  • In parallelogram, opposite angles are equal.
formulas: Sum of opposite angles of cyclic quadrilateral = 180

details.summary: Key geometric properties and formulas used to solve linear equations.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Example 17: The area of a rectangle is decreased by 28 m², if the length is increased by 2 m and the breadth is decreased by 2 m. The area of a rectangle is increased by 33 m², if the length is decreased by 1m and the breadth is increased by 2 m, then the area of rectangle is:

Solution: Let the length and breadth of a rectangle be x and y respectively. Original area = xy. Based on the conditions, two equations are formed and solved to find x=23 and y=11. The original area is 23 * 11 = 253 m².

details.summary: Example problem solving for dimensions of a rectangle using simultaneous linear equations.

mcq.question: The area of a rectangle is decreased by 28 m², if the length is increased by 2 m and the breadth is decreased by 2 m. The area of a rectangle is increased by 33 m², if the length is decreased by 1m and the breadth is increased by 2 m, then the area of rectangle is

subject: Mathematics
text:
A quadratic equation is an equation whose degree is 2, meaning that the highest exponent of variable is 2. The general form of a quadratic equation is ax^2 + bx + c = 0, where a, b and c are real numbers and a ≠ 0.

Examples: 2x^2 + 3x + 5 = 0, x^2 + x + 1 = 0 and 5x^2 + 6x + 8 = 0 are all quadratic equations.

details.summary: Definition and general form of quadratic equations.

subject: Mathematics
text:
A real number α is said to be a root of the quadratic equation ax^2 + bx + c = 0 (a ≠ 0), if it satisfies the equation i.e. aα^2 + bα + c = 0. We can also say that x = α is a solution of the quadratic equation.

Example: 2 is the root of the quadratic equation, x^2 - 6x + 8 = 0 since (2)^2 - 6(2) + 8 = 0.

Note: A quadratic equation has exactly two roots. If α be the root of the quadratic equation ax^2 + bx + c = 0, then (x - α) is the factor of ax^2 + bx + c.

details.summary: Definition of roots and the factor theorem for quadratic equations.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Solutions of quadratic equations can be determined by using any of the following two methods:

1. By Factorisation: In this method, the middle term of the quadratic equation is splitted and the given quadratic equation is converted into a product of two linear factors. Then, the roots of the equation are obtained by equating each factor equal to zero.

Let the quadratic equation be ax^2 + bx + c = 0 and its linear factors are (px + q) and (rx + s), then ax^2 + bx + c = (px + q)(rx + s).

Now, ax^2 + bx + c = 0 => (px + q)(rx + s) = 0 => px + q = 0 or rx + s = 0 => x = -q/p or x = -s/r.

Thus, -q/p and -s/r are the roots of the equation, ax^2 + bx + c = 0.

details.summary: Explanation of the factorisation method for solving quadratic equations.

subject: Mathematics
topic: Nature of Roots of Quadratic Equation
text:
Let D = b2 - 4ac be the discriminant of the quadratic equation, ax2 + bx + c = 0, where a ≠ 0. Then, the following cases arise:

  • (i) If D > 0, then the two roots are real and distinct.
  • (ii) If D = 0, then the two roots are real and equal and are given by α = β = -b / 2a.
  • (iii) If D < 0, then there are no real roots, i.e., given equation has imaginary roots.

IMPORTANT POINTS:

  • 1. If a, b, c ∈ Q and D is a perfect square, then equation has rational roots.
  • 2. If one root of quadratic equation is p + √q, then other root will be p - √q.

details.summary: Covers the discriminant method for determining the nature of roots of a quadratic equation and specific properties of roots under rational coefficients.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Consider the quadratic equation ax2 + bx + c = 0.

  • (i) Both roots are positive, if a and b are opposite in sign and a and c are same in sign, i.e., -b/a > 0 and c/a > 0.
  • (ii) Both roots are negative, if a, b and c are of same sign, i.e., -b/a > 0 and c/a > 0.
  • (iii) Roots are of opposite signs, if a and c are of opposite sign, i.e., -a/c > 0.
  • (iv) Roots are equal but opposite in signs, if b = 0.
  • (v) Roots are reciprocal to each other, if a = c.

details.summary: Conditions for the signs and relationships of roots based on coefficients a, b, and c.

subject: Mathematics
text:
1. Quadratic Equation

Let α and β be the roots of the equation ax2 + bx + c = 0 (a ≠ 0), then:

  • Sum of the roots = α + β = -b/a = -(Coefficient of x) / (Coefficient of x2)
  • Product of the roots = αβ = c/a = (Constant term) / (Coefficient of x2)

2. Cubic Equation

If α, β, γ are the roots of the cubic equation ax3 + bx2 + cx + d = 0, a ≠ 0, then:

  • Sum of the roots = α + β + γ = -b/a
  • Product of roots two at a time = αβ + βγ + γα = c/a
  • Product of three roots = αβγ = -d/a

details.summary: Definitions of relationships between coefficients and roots for quadratic and cubic equations.

subject: Mathematics
text:
An expression in α and β which remains same when α and β are interchanged is known as a symmetric function in α and β. To evaluate the value of symmetric function of the roots, express the given function in terms of (α + β) and αβ.

You can use the following results:

  • (α2 + β2) = [(α + β)2 - 2αβ]
  • (α3 + β3) = [(α + β)3 - 3αβ(α + β)]
  • (α - β)2 = [(α + β)2 - 4αβ]
  • (α3 - β3) = [(α - β)3 + 3αβ(α - β)]

details.summary: Identities for evaluating symmetric functions of roots.

text: If α, β are the roots of a quadratic equation, then the equation is (x - α)(x - β) = 0 ⇒ x^2 - (α + β)x + αβ = 0 i.e., x^2 - (sum of the roots)x + product of the roots = 0

subject: Mathematics
text:
The equations which at the outset are not quadratic equations, but can be reduced to quadratic equations by suitable substitutions or simplifications are called equations reducible to quadratic equations.

  • Rule 1: ax^(2n) + bx^n + c = 0, where n ≥ 2. Use substitution x^n = y ⇒ x^(2n) = y^2 and equation reduces to ay^2 + by + c = 0.
  • Rule 2: Px + Q/x = R. Reduce the given equation to a quadratic equation by multiplying both sides by 'x'. So, Px^2 + Q = Rx or Px^2 - Rx + Q = 0.
  • Rule 3: sqrt(x + b) + x = c or sqrt(a - x^2) = bx + c. Square both sides to get a quadratic equation without the radical. Solve the equation by factorisation or by quadratic formula.
  • Rule 4: sqrt(ax + b) ± sqrt(cx + d) = e or sqrt(ax + b) ± sqrt(cx + d) ± sqrt(ex + f) = 0. To solve such type of equations, follow the steps: Square both sides once, so that only one term containing radical is obtained. Keep the term containing radical on one side and all other terms on the other side. Square again to get, the quadratic equation and solve it.

details.summary: Covers rules for solving equations that can be reduced to quadratic form.

text: Rule 5: For equations of the form (x + a)(x + b)(x + c)(x + d) + k = 0, where a + b = c + d, the equation can be solved by substituting x^2 + (a + b)x = T.

details.summary: Method to solve quartic equations of a specific form by grouping factors.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Rule 6: To solve equations of the form:

  • (i) a(x^2 + 1/x^2) + b(x + 1/x) + c = 0: Put (x + 1/x) = y
  • (ii) a(x^2 + 1/x^2) + b(x - 1/x) + c = 0: Put (x - 1/x) = y

text:
Rule 7: For equations of the form ax^4 + bx^3 + cx^2 + bx + a = 0, we divide the equation by x^2 to obtain a(x^2 + 1/x^2) + b(x + 1/x) + c = 0, and then substitute y = x + 1/x.

Note: An equation of degree n has n roots.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Two real numbers or algebraic expressions related by symbols <, >, <=, or >= form an inequality.

Linear Inequalities: An inequality involving a linear function where each variable occurs in the first degree and there is no product of variables.

Examples: 5 < 7, x <= 2, x + y >= 11, ax + b <= 0, ax + by + c > 0, ax <= 4.

details.summary: Definition of inequalities and linear inequalities.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Linear inequality in one variable: A linear inequality which has only one variable is called linear inequality in one variable. e.g., ax + b < 0, where a != (-b/a), 4x + 7 >= 0.

Linear inequality in two variables: A linear inequality which has two variables, is called linear inequality in two variables. e.g., 3x + 11y <= 0, 4t + 3y > 0.

General Rules to Solve Linear Inequalities:

  • Equal numbers may be added or subtracted from both sides of an inequality without changing the sign of inequality. e.g., If a > b, then for any number c, a + c > b + c or a - c > b - c.
  • If both sides of an inequality are multiplied or divided by the same positive number, then the sign of inequality remains the same. e.g., If a > b and c > 0, then a/c > b/c and ac > bc.
  • If both sides of an inequality are multiplied or divided by the same negative number, then the sign of inequality is reversed. e.g., If a > b and c < 0, then a/c < b/c and ac < bc.

Graphical Solution of Linear Inequalities in Two Variables:

Let the inequality be ax + by + c >= 0.

  • Step I: Consider it as ax + by + c = 0 by changing the inequality sign to equality sign. Draw the graph of this equation.
  • Step II: Choose any point not on the line, (usually (0, 0)). Find whether this point satisfy the inequality or not. If it does, then shade the half-plane containing that point. Otherwise shade the other half-plane.

Note:

  • (i) If the inequality is strict (> or <), graph a dashed line. If the inequality is not strict (>= or <=), graph a solid line.
  • (ii) In order to solve a system of two or more linear inequalities with the same variables, graph each inequality on the same set of axes. The intersection of the region of all the inequalities is the required solution set.
image_descriptions: A Cartesian coordinate system showing a shaded region in the first quadrant bounded by the x-axis, y-axis, and a line passing through (0, 2) and (3, 0). The region represents the solution set of a system of inequalities.

details.summary: Covers definitions, rules for solving, and graphical methods for linear inequalities in one and two variables.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Quadratic Inequalities: An equation of the form ax^2 + bx + c >= 0 or ax^2 + bx + c <= 0 or ax^2 + bx + c > 0 or ax^2 + bx + c < 0, where a != 0 is called a quadratic inequality in one variable. It is same as quadratic equations except for the inequality sign.

Solution of Quadratic Inequalities: Solving the inequality means finding the values of x that make the inequality true. Solution sets of quadratic inequalities are expressed in the form of intervals. Here are the steps:

  • Replace the inequality symbol with an equal sign.
  • Solve the quadratic equation by factorisation or by quadratic formula and find the real roots of the equation.
  • Plot the two real roots on the numbers line. They divide the line into three sections or three intervals.

details.summary: Defines quadratic inequalities and outlines the step-by-step process for solving them using roots and intervals.

subject: Mathematics
text:
To solve quadratic inequalities:

  • Pick a number from each interval and test it in the original inequality.
  • If the inequality holds true for the chosen point, then that interval is the solution of the given quadratic inequality.

Note:

  • (i) If the quadratic equation does not have real roots, then the quadratic expression is always positive (or always negative) depending on the sign, meaning the solution set will either be empty or the entire real number line.
  • (ii) When the inequality has an additional '=' sign (≥ or ≤), use closed intervals like [a, b] to indicate that the two end points are also included in the solution set. If the inequality is strict (> or <), use open intervals like (a, b) as end points are not included.
