If a mistake is made in the first degree term, the roots are -9 and -1. The equation is (x+1)(x+9) = x^2 + 10x + 9.

If a mistake is made in the constant term, the roots are 8 and 2. The equation is (x-2)(x-8) = x^2 - 10x + 16.

subject: Mathematics
text:
A set is a well-defined collection of objects. The objects in a set are called its members or elements.

  • Sets are usually denoted by capital letters A, B, C, X, Y, Z etc.
  • Elements are denoted by small letters a, b, c etc.
  • If x is an element of set A, we write x ∈ A (x belongs to A).
  • If x is not an element of set A, we write x ∉ A.

Examples:

  • The collection of vowels in the English alphabet is a set A containing five elements: a, e, i, o, u, where a ∈ A but b ∉ A.
  • The collection of the first four prime numbers is a set A containing the elements 2, 3, 5, 7, where 3 ∈ A but 1 ∉ A.

details.summary: Definition and basic notation of sets.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Sets are generally represented in two ways:

1. Roster or Tabular form or listing method: In this method, all elements are listed within curly braces { } separated by commas.

  • If A is a set of first eight prime numbers, then A = {2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19}
  • If B is a set of squares of first five natural numbers, then B = {1, 4, 9, 16, 25}
  • If A is a set of vowels of English alphabets, then A = {a, e, i, o, u}

Note: The order in which elements are written makes no difference, and repeated elements are taken only once.

2. Set Builder form or Rule method: In this method, we write the set by some special property or properties satisfied by all its elements.

  • The set B of all even natural numbers can be written as B = {x : x is a natural number and x = 2n for n ∈ N} or B = {x : x ∈ N, x = 2n, n ∈ N}. The symbol ':' or '|' stands for 'such that'.
  • The set A = {3, 5, 7, 9, 11} is represented as A = {x : x = 2n + 1 where n ∈ N, n < 6}
formulas: B = {x : x is a natural number and x = 2n for n ∈ N}
A = {x : x = 2n + 1 where n ∈ N, n < 6}

details.summary: Methods of representing sets: Roster form and Set Builder form.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Types of Sets

  • Empty set: A set which does not contain any element is called an empty set or null set or void set. It is denoted by φ or { }. e.g., A = set of all odd numbers divisible by 2 and B = {x: x ∈ N and 5 < x < 6}. The sets which have atleast one element are called non void or non-empty set.
  • Singleton set: A set consisting of a single element is called a singleton set. e.g., (i) The set {5} is a singleton set. (ii) {x | x ∈ W and x + 6 = 6} = {0} which is a singleton set.
  • Finite set: A set which consists of a definite number of elements, is called a finite set. Empty set is also a finite set. e.g., (i) The set {1, 2, 3, 4} is a finite set. (ii) B = Set of vowels in English Alphabets = {a, e, i, o, u}. (iii) A = Set of even prime natural numbers => A = {2}. Note: The number of distinct elements contained in a set A is called the cardinal number of A and is denoted as n(A). If A = {a, e, i, o, u}, then n(A) = 5.
  • Infinite set: A set which consists of infinite number of elements is called an infinite set. e.g., (i) Set of square of natural numbers. (ii) Set of all points in a plane.
  • Equal sets: Two sets A and B are said to be equal, if they have exactly the same elements and we write A = B. Otherwise, they are said to be unequal and we write A ≠ B.
  • Equivalent sets: Two sets A and B are equivalent, if their cardinal numbers are same i.e. n(A) = n(B) and we write A ↔ B or A ~ B.

Subsets and Power Sets

  • Subsets: Let A and B be two sets. If every element of A is an element of B, then A is called a subset of B. If A is subset of B, then we write A ⊆ B. (i) Every set is a subset of itself i.e., A ⊆ A, B ⊆ B. (ii) Empty set is a subset of every set i.e., φ ⊆ A. Note: The total number of subsets of a finite set containing n elements is 2^n.
  • Super set: If A is a subset of B, then we say that B is superset of A and we write B ⊇ A.
  • Comparability of sets: Two sets A and B are said to be comparable, if either A ⊂ B or B ⊂ A or A = B, otherwise A and B are said to be incomparable.
  • Proper subset: If A ⊆ B and A ≠ B, then A is called a proper subset of B and we write A ⊂ B. Note: The total number of proper subset of a finite set containing n elements is (2^n - 1).
  • Universal set: If there are some sets under consideration, then there happens to be a set which is a superset of each one of the given sets. Such a set is known as the universal set and it is denoted by U.
  • Power set: The collection of all subsets of a set A, is called power set of A and it is denoted by P(A). In P(A), every element is a set. e.g., Let A = {1, 2, 3}, Then P(A) = {φ, {1}, {2}, {3}, {1,2}, {2,3}, {3,1}, {1,2,3}}.

details.summary: This section covers fundamental definitions in Set Theory including types of sets (Empty, Singleton, Finite, Infinite, Equal, Equivalent), subset relations, and power sets.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Properties of Power Sets:

  • Each element of a power set is a set.
  • If set A has n elements, then P(A) has 2^n elements.
  • If A is an empty set phi or {}, then P(A) has just one element i.e. P(A) = {phi}.
  • If A is a subset of B, then P(A) is a subset of P(B).
formulas: A is subset of B => P(A) is subset of P(B)

details.summary: Covers fundamental properties of power sets.

subject: Mathematics
text:
1. Union of Sets: Let A and B be any two sets. The union of A and B is the set of all the elements of A and all the elements of B, the common elements being taken only once. It is denoted by A U B and read as 'A union B'. Thus, A U B = {x : x is in A or x is in B}.

2. Intersection of sets: Let A and B be any two sets. The intersection of A and B is the set of all those elements which belongs to both A and B. It is denoted by A intersection B. Thus, A intersection B = {x : x is in A and x is in B}.

3. Disjoint sets: Two sets A and B are said to be disjoint, if they have no common element i.e. A intersection B = phi.

4. Difference of sets: Let A and B be two sets. The difference of two sets is the set of all those elements of A which do not belong to B. It is denoted by A - B and read as A minus B. A - B = {x : x is in A and x is not in B}.
formulas: A U B = {x : x is in A or x is in B}
A intersection B = {x : x is in A and x is in B}
A - B = {x : x is in A and x is not in B}

subject: Mathematics
topic: Symmetric Difference, Complement, and Laws of Algebra of Sets
text:
Symmetric Difference of Two Sets: Let A and B be two sets. The symmetric difference of sets A and B is the set (A - B) U (B - A) and is denoted by A Δ B. It is a set consisting of all those members of A which are not in B or all those which are in B but not in A. Thus, A Δ B = {x : x ∈ A but x ∉ B} U {x : x ∈ B but x ∉ A}. A Δ B = (A - B) U (B - A).

Complement of a Set: Let U be the universal set and A be any set such that A ⊂ U. The complement of A with respect to U is the set of all those elements of U which are not in A. It is denoted by A' or A^c or U - A. Thus, A' = {x : x ∈ U and x ∉ A}.

Laws of Algebra of Sets:

  • Idempotent laws: (i) A U A = A, (ii) A ∩ A = A
  • Identity laws: (i) A U φ = A, (ii) A ∩ U = A
  • Commutative laws: (i) A U B = B U A, (ii) A ∩ B = B ∩ A
  • Associative laws: (i) (A U B) U C = A U (B U C), (ii) (A ∩ B) ∩ C = A ∩ (B ∩ C)
  • Distributive laws: (i) A U (B ∩ C) = (A U B) ∩ (A U C), (ii) A ∩ (B U C) = (A ∩ B) U (A ∩ C)
  • De-Morgan's laws: (i) (A U B)' = A' ∩ B', (ii) (A ∩ B)' = A' U B'

More Results on Operations on Sets:

  • A - (B ∩ C) = (A - B) U (A - C)
  • A - (B U C) = (A - B) ∩ (A - C)
  • A ∩ (B - C) = (A ∩ B) - (A ∩ C)
  • A ∩ (B Δ C) = (A ∩ B) Δ (A ∩ C)
  • (A - B) U (B - A) = (A U B) - (A ∩ B)

Cardinality Results:

  • n(A U B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A ∩ B)
  • n(A U B) = n(A) + n(B) if A, B are disjoint sets.
  • n(A - B) = n(A) - n(A ∩ B)
  • n(A Δ B) = n(A) + n(B) - 2n(A ∩ B)
  • n(A U B U C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) - n(A ∩ B) - n(B ∩ C) - n(A ∩ C) + n(A ∩ B ∩ C)
formulas: A Δ B = (A - B) U (B - A)

subject: Mathematics
text:
An ordered pair consists of two objects or elements in a given fixed order.

If A and B are two sets and a ∈ A, b ∈ B, then the ordered pair of elements a and b is denoted by (a, b).

The natural numbers and their squares can be represented by ordered pair in the following way: (1, 1), (2, 4), (3, 9), (4, 16), ....

Two ordered pairs (a, b) and (c, d) will be equal, if and only if a = c and b = d.

Note: {a, b} = {b, a} but (a, b) ≠ (b, a).
formulas: (a, b) = (c, d) iff a = c and b = d

subject: Mathematics
chapter: Measurements of Angles and Trigonometric Ratios
text:
Trigonometry is the branch of Mathematics which deals with the measurements of sides and angles of triangles and the problems based on these angles.

Angle

An angle is considered as the figure obtained by rotating a given ray about its endpoint. The original ray is called the initial side and the ray into which the initial side rotates is called terminal side. In figure, OA is initial side and OB is the terminal side of ∠AOB. The point O is called its vertex.

Quadrants

Let XOX' and YOY' be two lines at right angles in the plane of paper. These two perpendicular lines divide the plane of the paper into four equal parts, these four parts are known as four quadrants and lines XOX' and YOY' are known as X-axis and Y-axis, respectively. The parts XOY, YOX', X'OY' and Y'OX are known as 1st, 2nd, 3rd and 4th quadrant, respectively.

Relation between Angles, Radius and Arc Length

If l is the length of a circle of radius r. And this arc subtends an angle θ radians at the centre of the circle, then l = rθ ⇒ θ = l/r.

subject: Mathematics
text:
A circle subtends an angle at the centre whose radian measure is 2π and its degree measure is 360°. It follows that:

  • 2π radian = 360°
  • π radian = 180°
  • 1 radian = 180/π degree = 57° 16' 22'' (approx)
  • 1 degree = π/180 radian = 0.01746 rad (approx)

Note: 1 radian is written as 1^c.

subject: Mathematics
text:
The ratio of the sides of a right-angled triangle with respect to its angle are called trigonometric ratios. The side opposite to the right angle is called the hypotenuse. Relative to the angle θ, the side opposite to θ is called the perpendicular side and the remaining side is called base.

For angle θ in right-angled triangle ABC:

  • sin θ = Perpendicular/Hypotenuse = BC/AC = P/H
  • cos θ = Base/Hypotenuse = AB/AC = B/H
  • tan θ = Perpendicular/Base = BC/AB = P/B
  • sec θ = Hypotenuse/Base = AC/AB = H/B
  • cot θ = Base/Perpendicular = AB/BC = B/P
  • cosec θ = Hypotenuse/Perpendicular = AC/BC = H/P

details.summary: Definitions of trigonometric ratios based on sides of a right-angled triangle.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Relation Between T-ratios:

  • sin θ = 1/cosec θ
  • cos θ = 1/sec θ
  • tan θ = 1/cot θ
  • tan θ = sin θ / cos θ
  • cot θ = cos θ / sin θ

Trigonometric Identities: A statement of equality involving trigonometric ratios of an angle is called a trigonometric identity. It is valid for all values of the angles. The three important identities are:

  1. sin² θ + cos² θ = 1
  2. 1 + tan² θ = sec² θ
  3. 1 + cot² θ = cosec² θ

Note: sin² A + cos² B cannot be equal to 1 because the angles are different.

topic: Sign of trigonometric ratios in different quadrants
text:
The sign of trigonometric ratios depends on the quadrant in which the angle lies:

  • I Quadrant (0 < θ < 90°): All trigonometric ratios are positive.
  • II Quadrant (90° < θ < 180°): sin θ and cosec θ are positive. All other trigonometric ratios are negative.
  • III Quadrant (180° < θ < 270°): tan θ and cot θ are positive. All other trigonometric ratios are negative.
  • IV Quadrant (270° < θ < 360°): cos θ and sec θ are positive. All other trigonometric ratios are negative.
image_descriptions: A Cartesian coordinate system showing the four quadrants with the signs of trigonometric ratios indicated for each.

details.summary: Overview of trigonometric signs in quadrants and domain/range of functions.

text: The behaviour of trigonometric functions across different quadrants is summarized below:
tables:

|---|---|---|---|---|
| sin θ | Increases from 0 to 1 | Decreases from 1 to 0 | Decreases from 0 to -1 | Increases from -1 to 0 |
| cos θ | Decreases from 1 to 0 | Decreases from 0 to -1 | Increases from -1 to 0 | Increases from 0 to 1 |
| tan θ | Increases from 0 to ∞ | Increases from -∞ to 0 | Increases from 0 to ∞ | Increases from -∞ to 0 |
| cot θ | Decreases from ∞ to 0 | Decreases from 0 to -∞ | Decreases from ∞ to 0 | Decreases from 0 to -∞ |
| sec θ | Increases from 1 to ∞ | Increases from -∞ to -1 | Decreases from -1 to -∞ | Increases from ∞ to 1 |
| cosec θ | Decreases from ∞ to 1 | Increases from 1 to ∞ | Increases from -∞ to -1 | Decreases from -1 to -∞ |

text:
The following trigonometric identities are essential for solving sum, difference, and product problems:

  • sin(A + B) = sin A cos B + cos A sin B
  • sin(A - B) = sin A cos B - cos A sin B
  • cos(A + B) = cos A cos B - sin A sin B
  • cos(A - B) = cos A cos B + sin A sin B
  • tan(A + B) = (tan A + tan B) / (1 - tan A tan B)
  • tan(A - B) = (tan A - tan B) / (1 + tan A tan B)
  • cot(A + B) = (cot A cot B - 1) / (cot A + cot B)
  • cot(A - B) = (cot A cot B + 1) / (cot B - cot A)
  • sin(A + B)sin(A - B) = sin^2 A - sin^2 B = cos^2 B - cos^2 A
  • cos(A + B)cos(A - B) = cos^2 A - sin^2 B = cos^2 B - sin^2 A
  • 2 sin A cos B = sin(A + B) + sin(A - B)
  • 2 cos A sin B = sin(A + B) - sin(A - B)
  • 2 cos A cos B = cos(A + B) + cos(A - B)
  • 2 sin A sin B = cos(A - B) - cos(A + B)
  • sin A + sin B = 2 sin((A + B)/2) cos((A - B)/2)
  • sin A - sin B = 2 sin((A - B)/2) cos((A + B)/2)
  • cos A + cos B = 2 cos((A + B)/2) cos((A - B)/2)
  • cos A - cos B = -2 sin((A + B)/2) sin((A - B)/2) = 2 sin((A + B)/2) sin((B - A)/2)
  • tan A + tan B = sin(A + B) / (cos A cos B)
  • tan A - tan B = sin(A - B) / (cos A cos B)
  • cot A + cot B = sin(A + B) / (sin A sin B)
  • cot A - cot B = sin(B - A) / (sin A sin B)

Formulas for trigonometric ratios of submultiple angles:

  • cos θ = cos²(θ/2) - sin²(θ/2) = 2 cos²(θ/2) - 1 = 1 - 2 sin²(θ/2)
  • (1 - cos θ) / sin θ = tan(θ/2)
  • (1 + cos θ) / sin θ = cot(θ/2)
  • (1 - cos θ) / (1 + cos θ) = tan²(θ/2)
  • (1 + cos θ) / (1 - cos θ) = cot²(θ/2)
  • sin θ = (2 tan(θ/2)) / (1 + tan²(θ/2))
  • cos θ = (1 - tan²(θ/2)) / (1 + tan²(θ/2))

Formulas for trigonometric ratios of multiple angles:

  • sin 2θ = (2 tan θ) / (1 + tan² θ)
  • cos 2θ = cos² θ - sin² θ = 2 cos² θ - 1 = 1 - 2 sin² θ = (1 - tan² θ) / (1 + tan² θ)
  • (1 + cos 2θ) / 2 = cos² θ
  • (1 - cos 2θ) / 2 = sin² θ
  • tan 2θ = (2 tan θ) / (1 - tan² θ)
  • sin 3θ = 3 sin θ - 4 sin³ θ
  • cos 3θ = 4 cos³ θ - 3 cos θ
  • tan 3θ = (3 tan θ - tan³ θ) / (1 - 3 tan² θ)

text:
Properties of Triangle

  • Circumcircle of a triangle: The circle passing through the vertices of a triangle ABC is called circumcircle. Its radius R is called the circumradius and its centre is known as circumcentre. Formula: R = a/(2sin A) = b/(2sin B) = c/(2sin C).
  • Sine rule: In a triangle ABC, if a, b, c be the sides opposite to the angles A, B, C respectively, then a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C.
  • Cosine rule: In a triangle ABC, if a, b, c be the sides opposite to the angles A, B, C respectively, then:
    • cos A = (b^2 + c^2 - a^2) / 2bc
    • cos B = (c^2 + a^2 - b^2) / 2ac
    • cos C = (a^2 + b^2 - c^2) / 2ab
formulas: R = a/(2sin A) = b/(2sin B) = c/(2sin C)
a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C

subject: Mathematics
text:
Height and Distance is an important application of trigonometry which helps us to find the height of any object and distance of that object from any point which are not directly measurable. If the angle of elevation/depression from a point is known.

Line of sight

A line of sight is the line drawn from the eye of an observer to the point, where the object is viewed by the observer.

Horizontal Line

The line of sight which is parallel to ground level is known as horizontal line.

ANGLE OF ELEVATION

Angle of elevation is defined as an angle formed by the line of sight with the horizontal line when an object is viewed in the upward direction. Let P be the position of the object above the horizontal line OA and O be the eye of the observer, then ∠AOP is called angle of elevation.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Angle of depression is defined as an angle formed by the line of sight with the horizontal line when an object is viewed in the downward direction.

Let P be the position of the object below the horizontal line OA and O be the eye of the observer, then ∠AOP is called angle of depression.

IMPORTANT POINTS

  • The angle of depression of a point P as seen from a point O is numerically equal to the angle of elevation of O as seen from P.
  • Angle of elevation and angle of depression are always acute angle.
  • Unless mentioned, the height of the observer is not considered.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Example solution for finding the height of a tower using trigonometry.

Given: Height of tower AB = 60m, distance BD = y.

In right-angled triangle ABD: tan(60) = AB/BD = 60/y => y = 60/sqrt(3).

In right-angled triangle AEC: tan(30) = AE/EC = AE/BD = 1/sqrt(3).

Substituting y: AE = (60/sqrt(3)) * (1/sqrt(3)) = 20m.

Height of tower x = AB - AE = 60 - 20 = 40m.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Point: The figure of which length, breadth and height cannot be measured is called a point. It is infinitesind.

Line Segment: The straight path between two points P and Q is called a line segment. This can be represented as PQ (with a bar over it).

  • P and Q are called the end points of the line segment.
  • The line segment has a definite length.
  • Distance between P and Q is called the length of the line segment PQ.

Line: A line segment extended endlessly on both sides, is called a line. It is denoted by PQ (with a double-headed arrow over it) or QP (with a double-headed arrow over it).

  • A line is a set of infinite number of points.
  • A line have no end points and no definite length.

Ray: A ray extends indefinitely in one direction. This is exhibited by an arrow i.e. PQ (with a right-pointing arrow over it).

  • P is called the initial point of the ray. The ray has no definite length.

Collinear Points: Three or more points are said to be collinear if a single straight line passes through them. Here, A, B and C are collinear.

Non-collinear Points: Three or more points not lying on a single straight line are called non-collinear points. Here, A, B and C are non-collinear.

Intersecting Lines: Two lines having a common point are called intersecting lines. This common point is the point of intersection i.e. O.

details.summary: Introduction to fundamental geometric concepts including points, line segments, lines, rays, collinearity, and intersecting lines.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Concurrent Lines: Three or more lines intersecting at the same point are said to be concurrent. This common point is the point of concurrence i.e. O.

Non Intersecting lines/Parallel Lines: If two lines lie in the same plane and do not intersect when produced on either side, then such lines are said to be parallel to each other. If l and m are two parallel lines, we write l || m and read it as l is parallel to m.

ANGLES: An angle is formed by two rays with a common initial point. Let 'O' is the initial point, then O is called the vertex. P is a point in the interior of angle AOB and R is a point in the exterior of angle AOB.

Types of Angle:

  • Acute angle: 0° < angle < 90°
  • Right angle: angle = 90°
  • Obtuse angle: 90° < angle < 180°
  • Straight angle: angle = 180°
  • Reflex angle: 180° < angle < 360°
  • Complete angle: angle = 360°

Pairs of Angle:

  • Complementary Angles: Two angles are said to be complementary, if the sum of their measure is 90°. Complement of x is (90° - x).
  • Supplementary Angles: Two angles are said to be supplementary, if the sum of their measures is 180°. Supplement of x is (180° - x).

text:
Two angles are said to be adjacent, if:

  • (i) they have a common vertex.
  • (ii) they have a common arm.
  • (iii) their non-common arms are on either side of the common arm.

Here, ∠POQ and ∠ROQ are adjacent angles.

text:
If the non-common arms of two adjacent angles form a line, then these angles are called linear pair of angles.

∠ROP and ∠ROQ form a linear pair of angles.

∴ ∠POQ = ∠ROP + ∠ROQ = 180°

subject: Mathematics
text:
Two angles are called a pair of vertically opposite angles, if their arms form two pairs of opposite rays.

If two lines PQ and RS intersect at a point O, then the pair of ∠POR and ∠QOS or pair of ∠POS and ∠ROQ is said to be a pair of vertically opposite angles.

  • Vertically opposite angles are always equal i.e. ∠POS = ∠ROQ and ∠POR = ∠SOQ.
  • Sum of the angles around a point is 360°.

subject: Mathematics
text:
1. Corresponding angles: Corresponding angle pairs are ∠1 and ∠5, ∠2 and ∠6, ∠4 and ∠8, ∠3 and ∠7 and all the corresponding pair are equal. i.e., ∠1 = ∠5, ∠2 = ∠6, ∠4 = ∠8 and ∠3 = ∠7.

2. Vertically opposite angles: Vertically opposite angles pairs are ∠1 and ∠3, ∠4 and ∠2, ∠8 and ∠6, ∠5 and ∠7 and all vertically opposite angles are equal. i.e., ∠1 = ∠3, ∠4 = ∠2, ∠8 = ∠6 and ∠5 = ∠7.

3. Alternate angles: Alternate angles pairs are ∠3 and ∠5, ∠4 and ∠6 and they are equal. i.e., ∠3 = ∠5 and ∠4 = ∠6.

  • The sum of interior angles on the same side of transversal is equal to 180°. i.e., ∠3 + ∠6 = 180° and ∠4 + ∠5 = 180°.
  • The sum of exterior angles on the same side of transversal is equal to 180°. i.e., ∠2 + ∠7 = 180° and ∠1 + ∠8 = 180°.

subject: Mathematics
topic: Definition and Properties of a Triangle
text:
A plane (closed) figure bounded by three line segments is called a triangle. It is denoted by Δ.

ΔABC has:

  • three vertices, namely A, B and C.
  • three sides, namely AB, BC and CA.
  • three angles, namely ∠A, ∠B and ∠C.
  • Sum of three angles of a triangle is 180°. i.e., ∠A + ∠B + ∠C = 180°
  • Area of a triangle = 1/2 × base × height = 1/2 × BC × AD

subject: Mathematics
topic: Classification of Triangle on the Basis of Angles
text:
1. On the Basis of Angles

  • (i) Right Angled Triangle: A triangle in which one of the angle measures 90° is called a right angled triangle. The side opposite to the right angle is called its hypotenuse and the remaining two sides are called as perpendicular and base depending upon conditions. Here, ΔABC is a right angled triangle in which ∠B = 90° and AC is hypotenuse.
  • (ii) Acute Angled Triangle: A triangle in which every angle measure more than 0° but less than 90° is called an acute angled triangle. Here, ΔABC is an acute angled triangle.
  • (iii) Obtuse Angled Triangle: A triangle in which one of the angle measures more than 90° but less than 180° is called an obtuse angled triangle. Here, ΔABC is an obtuse angled triangle and ∠ABC is the obtuse angle.

subject: Mathematics
topic: Classification of Triangles on the Basis of Sides
text:
Triangles are classified based on their sides:

  • Equilateral Triangle: A triangle having all sides equal. In triangle ABC, AB = BC = AC. All angles are equal and measure 60 degrees.
  • Isosceles Triangle: A triangle in which two sides are equal. In triangle ABC, AB = AC. The angles opposite to equal sides are equal, i.e., angle B = angle C.
  • Scalene Triangle: A triangle in which all sides are of different lengths. In triangle ABC, AB != BC != AC.

Note: The sum of the lengths of three sides of a triangle is called its perimeter. Perimeter of triangle ABC = AB + BC + AC.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Centroid: A line segment joining the mid-point of a side to the opposite vertex is called a median. Medians are concurrent. The point of intersection is the centroid (G). Centroid divides the median in the ratio 2:1. A median bisects the area of the triangle, i.e., Ar(ABD) = Ar(ADC) = 1/2 Ar(ABC).

Incentre: The point of intersection of all three angle bisectors is the incentre (I). The circle with centre I touching all sides is the incircle. Inradius (r) = 1/3 * Height = Side / (2 * sqrt(3)).

Circumcentre: The point of intersection of perpendicular bisectors of the sides is the circumcentre (C). The circle passing through vertices A, B, and C is the circumcircle. Circumradius (R) = 2/3 * Height = Side / sqrt(3).

subject: Mathematics
text:
Some Important Results of a Triangle:

  • If two angles of a triangle are equal, then the sides opposite to them are also equal.
  • In a triangle, the side opposite to a greater angle is the longest side.
  • The sum of all the three interior angles of a triangle is 180°.
  • If a side of a triangle is produced, then the exterior angle so formed is equal to the sum of the two interior opposite angles.
  • An exterior angle of a triangle is greater than either of the interior opposite angles.
  • A triangle must have atleast two acute angles.
  • If a perpendicular is drawn from the vertex of a right angled triangle to the hypotenuse, then the triangles on both sides of the perpendicular are similar to the original triangle and also to each other.
  • In a right angle triangle ABC, angle B = 90° and AC is hypotenuse. The perpendicular BD is dropped on hypotenuse AC from right angle vertex B, then: (i) BD = (AB * BC) / AC, (ii) AD = AB^2 / AC, (iii) CD = BC^2 / AC, (iv) 1/BD^2 = 1/AB^2 + 1/BC^2.
  • The area of the equilateral triangle described on the side of a square is half the area of the equilateral triangle described on its diagonal.
  • In triangle ABC, if angle B > 90° and AD is perpendicular dropped on BC, then AC^2 = AB^2 + BC^2 + 2BC * BD.
  • In triangle ABC, if angle B < 90° and AD is perpendicular to BC, then AC^2 = AB^2 + BC^2 - 2BC * BD.
  • In any triangle, the sum of the squares of any two sides is equal to twice the square of half of the third side together with twice the square of the median which bisect the third side. Here, AD is median, so AB^2 + AC^2 = 2AD^2 + 2(1/2 BC)^2.
  • In a triangle ABC, three times the sum of the squares of the sides of a triangle is equal to four times the sum of the squares of the medians of the triangle. So, in triangle, if AD, BE, FC are the medians, then 3(AB^2 + BC^2 + AC^2) = 4(AD^2 + BE^2 + CF^2).
  • In an equilateral triangle ABC, the side BC is trisected at D. Then, 9 AD^2 = 7 AC^2.
  • When the bisector of one internal base angle and the bisector of external angle meet at a point then the formed angle is equal to one half of the vertical angle. Here, angle BEC = 1/2 angle BAC.

text:
• The side BC of triangle ABC is produced to D. The bisector of angle A meets BC in L. Then angle ABC + angle ACD = 2 angle ALC.
  • In a triangle ABC, the bisector of angle B and angle C intersect each other at a point O. Then, angle BOC = 90 degrees + 1/2 angle A.
  • In a triangle ABC, the side AB and AC are produced to P and Q, respectively. The bisectors of angle PBC and angle QCB intersect at a point O. Then, angle BOC = 90 degrees - 1/2 angle A.
  • In a triangle ABC, angle B > angle C. If AN is the bisector of angle BAC and AM is perpendicular to BC, then angle MAN = 1/2 (angle B - angle C).
  • The bisectors of the base angles of a triangle can never enclose a right angle.
  • A triangle is an isosceles if and only if any two altitudes are equal.
  • If the three sides of a triangle be produced in order, then the sum of all the exterior angles so formed is 360 degrees. So, angle DAB + angle EBC + angle ACF = 360 degrees.
  • Sum of any two sides of a triangle is greater than its third side. Here, in triangle ABC, AB + AC > BC; similarly, AB + BC > AC, BC + AC > AB.
  • The difference between any two sides of a triangle is less than its third side. Here, in triangle ABC, AC - AB < BC. Similarly, BC - AC < AB, BC - AB < AC.
  • If the bisector of the vertical angle of a triangle bisects the base, then that triangle is an isosceles.
  • If the altitude from one vertex of a triangle bisects the opposite side, then the triangle is an isosceles.
  • The perpendiculars drawn from the vertices of equal angles of an isosceles triangle to the opposite sides are equal.
  • Medians of equilateral triangle are equal.
  • If D is the mid-point of the hypotenuse AC of a right angled triangle ABC. Then, BD = 1/2 AC.
  • The sum of any two sides of a triangle is greater than twice the median drawn to the third side.
  • Perimeter of a triangle is greater than the sum of its three medians. So, AB + BC + AC > AD + BE + CF.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Congruent Figures: The geometrical figures having the same shape and size are known as congruent figures. e.g. Two circles of the same radii and two squares of the same sides are congruent.

Congruent Triangles: Two triangles are said to be congruent, if both are exactly of same size i.e. all angles and sides are equal to corresponding angles and sides of other.

  • Every triangle is congruent to itself: ΔABC ≅ ΔABC
  • If ΔABC ≅ ΔDEF, then ΔDEF ≅ ΔABC
  • If ΔABC ≅ ΔDEF and ΔDEF ≅ ΔPQR, then ΔABC ≅ ΔPQR

In congruent triangles, corresponding parts are equal and we write in short ‘CPCT’, i.e. corresponding part of congruent triangles.

Criteria for Congruence of Triangles:

  • Theorem 1 (SAS criteria): Two triangles are congruent if two sides and the included angle of one triangle are equal to the corresponding sides and the included angle of other triangle.
  • Theorem 2 (ASA criteria): Two triangles are congruent if two angles and the included side of one triangle are equal to the corresponding two angles and the included side of the other triangles.
  • Theorem 3 (SSS criteria): Two triangles are congruent if three sides of one triangle are equal to the corresponding three sides of the other triangle.
  • Theorem 4 (RHS criteria): Two triangles are congruent if the hypotenuse and other side of one triangle are equal to the hypotenuse and the corresponding side of the other triangle.
  • Theorem 5 (AAS criteria): Two triangles are congruent if two angles and a side other than the included side of one triangle are equal to the corresponding two angles and a side other than the included side of other triangle.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Similar Figures: The geometrical figures having the same shape, but different sizes are known as similar figures. The congruent figures are always similar, but two similar figures need not be congruent. e.g., Any two circles are similar. Any two rectangles are similar.

Similar Triangles: Two triangles are said to be similar to each other, if (i) their corresponding sides are proportional, (ii) their corresponding angles are equal. If triangle ABC ~ triangle PQR, then angle A = angle P, angle B = angle Q, angle C = angle R and AB/PQ = BC/QR = AC/PR.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Theorem 1 (Basic Proportionality Theorem): If a line is drawn parallel to one side of a triangle to intersect the other two sides in distinct points, then it divides these sides in the same ratio. If DE || BC, then AD/DB = AE/EC.

Theorem 2: The internal bisector of an angle of a triangle divides the opposite sides internally in the ratio of the sides containing the angle. If AD is internal bisector of angle A, then AB/AC = BD/DC.

Theorem 3: The line joining the mid-points of any two sides of a triangle is parallel to the third side and is half of the third side. PQ = 1/2 BC.

Theorem 4: If two triangles are equiangular, then the ratio of their corresponding sides is the same as the ratio of the corresponding altitudes. BC/QR = AD/PS.

Theorem 5: If two triangles are equiangular, then the ratio of their corresponding sides is the same as the ratio of the corresponding angle bisector segments. BC/ST = AD/RP.

Theorem 6: If two triangles are equiangular, then the ratio of their corresponding sides is the same as the ratio of the corresponding medians. BC/QR = AD/PS.

Note: If two triangles are similar, then ratio of their corresponding sides is same as ratio of their perimeters.

subject: Mathematics
topic: Criteria for Similarity of Two Triangles
text:
Criteria for Similarity of Two Triangles:

  • AAA similarity: If the corresponding angles of two triangles are equal then their corresponding sides are proportional and hence the two triangles are similar.
  • Corollary AA similarity: If two angles of one triangle are equal to the corresponding two angles of another triangle, then the two triangles are similar.
  • SSS similarity: If the corresponding sides of two triangles are proportional, then their corresponding angles are equal, and hence the two triangles are similar.
  • SAS similarity: If one angle of a triangle is equal to the corresponding angle of the other triangle and the sides including these angles are proportional, then the two triangles are similar.
  • RHS similarity: If hypotenuse and one side of a right triangle are proportional to the hypotenuse and corresponding side of other right triangle then the two triangles are similar.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Theorem 1: The ratio of areas of two similar triangles is equal to the square of the ratio of their corresponding sides. If triangle ABC ~ triangle PQR, then Area(ABC)/Area(PQR) = AB^2/PQ^2 = BC^2/QR^2 = AC^2/PR^2.

Theorem 2: The areas of two similar triangles is equal to the ratio of the squares of corresponding altitudes. If triangle ABC ~ triangle PQR, then Area(ABC)/Area(PQR) = AD^2/PS^2.

Theorem 3: The areas of two similar triangles is equal to the ratio of the squares of the corresponding medians. If triangle ABC ~ triangle PQR, then Area(ABC)/Area(PQR) = AD^2/PS^2.

Theorem 5: If the areas of two similar triangles are equal, then the triangles are congruent. Equal and similar triangles are congruent.

Example 12: Two poles of heights 6m and 11m stand vertically on a plane ground at a distance of 12m from each other. The distance between their tops is:

  • Draw DL perpendicular to AB
  • Then, BL = AB - AL = AB - CD = (11 - 6)m = 5m
  • and DL = AC = 12m
  • In right angled triangle BDL, BD^2 = DL^2 + BL^2 = 5^2 + 12^2 = 169
  • BD = sqrt(169) = 13m

mcq.question: Two poles of heights 6m and 11m stand vertically on a plane ground at a distance of 12m from each other. The distance between their tops is
mcq.explanation: Using the Pythagorean theorem on the triangle formed by the difference in heights and the distance between the poles: sqrt((11-6)^2 + 12^2) = sqrt(5^2 + 12^2) = sqrt(25 + 144) = sqrt(169) = 13m.

In a right-angled triangle, the median to the hypotenuse is half the length of the hypotenuse.

Example: In triangle PQR, right-angled at Q, with PQ=5 and QR=12. By Pythagoras theorem, PR = sqrt(5^2 + 12^2) = 13. The median QL = 1/2 * PR = 6.5 cm.

subject: Mathematics
text:
A quadrilateral, in which opposite sides are parallel is called a parallelogram.

  • Area = Base × Height = b × h
  • Perimeter = 2(a + b)

Properties of Parallelogram:

  • (i) Diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.
  • (ii) Each diagonal of a parallelogram divides it into two congruent triangles.
  • (iii) Sum of any two adjacent angles is 180°.
  • (iv) A parallelogram inscribed in a circle is a rectangle.
  • (v) A parallelogram circumscribed about a circle is a rhombus.
  • (vi) Two parallelograms have equal areas if they are on the same base and between the same parallel lines.
  • (vii) Lines joining the midpoints of the sides of parallelogram is a parallelogram.
  • (viii) The opposite angles of parallelogram are equal. (∠A = ∠C and ∠B = ∠D) (from above figure)
  • (ix) The sum of the squares of the four sides is equal to the sum of squares of diagonal. AC² + BD² = AB² + BC² + CD² + AD²
formulas: AC^2 + BD^2 = AB^2 + BC^2 + CD^2 + AD^2

subject: Mathematics
text:
A Rhombus is a parallelogram with all 4 sides equal. The opposite angles in a rhombus are equal but they are not right angles.

  • Area = 1/2 * d1 * d2
  • Perimeter = 4a
  • Side (a) = 1/2 * sqrt(d1^2 + d2^2)
  • 4a^2 = d1^2 + d2^2

Properties of Rhombus:

  • The diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles (90°). But they are not necessarily equal.
  • Diagonals bisect the vertex angles.
  • The figure formed by joining the mid-points of the sides of rhombus is a rectangle.
  • All rhombus are parallelogram but reverse is not true.
  • A rhombus may or may not be a square but all squares are rhombus.
image_descriptions: Diagram of a rhombus with sides labeled 'a' and diagonals labeled 'd1' and 'd2'.

subject: Mathematics
text:
A Rectangle is a parallelogram with opposite sides equal and each angle is equal to 90°.

  • Area = Length * Breadth = L * B
  • Perimeter = 2(L + B)
  • Diagonal (d) = sqrt(L^2 + B^2)

Properties of Rectangle:

  • The diagonals of a rectangle are of equal lengths and they bisect each other.
  • All rectangles are parallelograms but reverse is not true.
  • Diagonal of a rectangle inscribed in a circle is equal to the diameter of the circle.
  • The figure formed by joining the mid-points of the sides of a rectangle is a rhombus.
  • A rectangle and a parallelogram have equal area if they are on the same base and between same parallel lines.

  • Area = (side)^2 = a^2 or 1/2 * d^2
  • Perimeter = 4 * side = 4a
  • Diagonal (d) = a * sqrt(2)

  • Diagonal of a square are equal and bisect each other at right angles (90°).
  • All square are rhombus but converse is not true.
  • Diagonal of square is the diameter of the circumscribing circle that circumscribes the square.
  • Side of a circumscribed square is equal to the diameter of the inscribed circle.
  • The figure formed by joining the mid-points of the sides of square is a square.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Trapezium: It is a quadrilateral with any one pair of opposite sides parallel.

Properties:

  • If the non-parallel sides are equal then the diagonals will also be equal to each other.
  • Diagonals intersect each other proportionally in the ratio of lengths of parallel sides.
  • If a trapezium is inscribed in a circle, then it is an isosceles trapezium with equal oblique sides.
  • The line joining the mid-points of non-parallel sides is half the sum of parallel side and is called median. i.e. Median = 1/2 * sum of parallel sides.

text:
A circle is a curved figure consisting of all points in a plane that are at a fixed distance from a fixed point. The fixed point is called the centre and the fixed distance is called the radius of the circle.

  • Circles are simple closed curves which divide the plane into two regions: an interior and an exterior.
  • In the given figure, O is the centre of the circle, OA is the radius of the circle and AB is the diameter of the circle.

Diameter is any line segment that passes through the centre of the circle and whose end points lie on the circle. The diameter of a circle is twice the radius. Here, AB and CD are the diameters of the circle.

text:
Any part of a circle between two points is called an arc of the circle. Any two points, say A and B of a circle divide it into two parts called arcs. The smaller arc APB is called minor arc and larger arc AQB is called major arc.

It is usually denoted by APB (with arc symbol) and AQB (with arc symbol).

subject: Mathematics
text:
Semi Circle: A diameter divides the circle into two equal parts. Each of the two is called a semi-circle.

Segment: The area enclosed by an arc and its corresponding chord is called a segment of the circle. The segment containing the minor arc is called minor segment. The segment containing the major arc is called major segment.

Sector: The area enclosed by any two radii and the arc determined by the end points of the radii is called a sector of the circle.

Circumference: The length of the complete circle is called its circumference.

Concentric Circles: Two or more circles having the same centre are called concentric circles.

Tangent: A tangent to a circle is a straight line that touches the circle at a single point. The distance between external point P from which tangent is drawn and the point of contact of the tangent is called length of tangent.

Properties of Tangent To a Circle:

  • Only two tangents can be drawn from a point outside the circle.
  • Only one tangent can be drawn through a point lying on the circle.
  • No tangent can be drawn from a point lying inside the circle.
  • A tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.

Relative Position of two Circles: Two circles will:

  • (i) be disjoint, when OO' > r1 + r2.
  • (ii) be touching externally, when OO' = r1 + r2.
  • (iii) be intersecting when OO' < r1 + r2.
  • (iv) be touching internally, when OO' = |r2 - r1|.
  • (v) one of the circle will lie inside the other, when OO' < |r2 - r1|.

text:
Theorem 1: If two arcs of a circle are congruent, then the corresponding chords are equal.

Theorem 2: Equal arcs (or chords) subtend equal angle at the centre. Here, if AB = PQ, then ∠AOB = ∠POQ.

Theorem 3: The perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord. Here, if OD ⊥ AB, then AD = DB.

Theorem 4: The line joining the centre to the mid-point of a chord is perpendicular to the chord. Here, if AD = DB, then ∠ADO = ∠ODB = 90°.

Theorem 5: The perpendicular bisectors of two chords of a circle intersect at its centre. Here, AB, CD are the chords and l, m are perpendicular bisector of AB and CD. So, l and m meet at centre ‘O’.

Theorem 6: There is one and only one circle passing through three non-collinear points.

  • An infinite number of circles can be drawn to pass through a single point.
  • An infinite number of circles can be drawn to pass through two given points.
  • A unique circle can be drawn to pass through three given non-collinear points.

Theorem 7: Equal chords of congruent circles are equidistant from the corresponding centres. Here, if AB = CD, then OP = O'Q. Conversely if OP = O'Q, then AB = CD.

Theorem 8: Equal chords of a circle are equidistant from the centre. Here, if AB and CD are equal chords of circle, then OP = OQ. Conversely, if OP = OQ, then also AB = CD i.e. chords at equal distance from the centre are equal.

text:
Theorem 14: Alternate Segment Theorem: In the given figure, if BAC is a tangent to a circle at point A and if AD is any chord, then ∠DAC = ∠APD and ∠PAB = ∠PDA.

Theorem 15: If two tangents are drawn to a circle from an external point, they subtend equal angles at the centre. These two tangents are equally inclined to the line segment joining the centre to that point. In the given figure, ∠AOP = ∠BOP and ∠APO = ∠BPO.

Theorem 16: Line joining centre and external point is perpendicular bisector of line joining of contacts of tangents to the circle. In the above figure, OP ⊥ AB and AC = BC.

Theorem 17: The length of two tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal. Here, PA = PB.

Theorem 18: Tangents drawn at the end points of a diameter of a circle are always parallel.

Cyclic Quadrilateral: A quadrilateral whose all vertices lie on a circle is called a cyclic quadrilateral.

Properties of Cyclic Quadrilateral:

  • The sum of either pair of opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral is 180°, i.e., the opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary.
  • If the sum of a pair of opposite angles of a quadrilateral is 180°, then quadrilateral is cyclic.
  • The exterior angle, formed by producing a side of a cyclic quadrilateral is equal to the interior opposite angle. Here, ∠BAD = ∠BCE.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Locus: The path traced by a point moving under a given condition is called locus. e.g., The locus of points (in a plane) equidistant from a fixed point (in a plane) is a circle with the fixed point as centre. The plural of locus is loci.

  • The locus may be a line segment or lines, straight or curved.
  • Every point which satisfies the given geometrical condition(s) lies on the locus and vice-versa.

Basic Locus Theorem:

  1. The locus of points at a fixed distance d from point p is a circle with the given point p as its centre and d as its radius.
  2. The locus of points at a fixed distance d from a line m is a pair of parallel lines at a distance of d from line m and located on either side of m.
  3. The locus of points equidistant from two points A and B is the perpendicular bisector of the line segment joining the two points.
  4. The locus of points equidistant from two parallel lines m1 and m2, is a line parallel to both m1 and m2 and midway between them.
  5. The locus of points in the interior of an angle equidistant from the sides of an angle is the bisector of the angle.
  6. The locus of points equidistant from two intersecting lines l1 and l2, is a pair of bisectors that bisect the angles formed by l1 and l2.

Locus in Some Standard Cases:

  1. The loci of all points d units from a circle having a radius r units are two concentric circles with radii of r-d and r+d units respectively.
  2. The locus of all points equidistant from two concentric circles is a third circle whose radius is the average of the radii of the given circles.
  3. The locus of the mid-points of all parallel chords of a circle is the diameter of the circle, which is perpendicular to the given chords.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Properties of Locus in Circles:

  • The locus of the mid-points of equal chords is a circle with the same centre as the given circle and radius equal to the distance from the centre of the given circle to the given chord.
  • The locus of the centre of a circle touching a given line at a given point is a line perpendicular to the given line through the given point.
  • The locus of the centre of all circles passing through two given points is the perpendicular bisector of the line segment joining the two points.
  • If A and B are fixed points, then the locus of a point P such that angle APB = 90 degrees is the circle with AB as diameter.

Formula for length of transverse common tangent:

Length = sqrt((distance between centres)^2 - (sum of radii)^2)

Example: distance = 10 cm, radii = 3.5 cm and 4.5 cm. Length = sqrt(10^2 - (3.5 + 4.5)^2) = sqrt(100 - 64) = sqrt(36) = 6 cm.

Problem 53: Angles in the same segment of a circle are equal.

  • Given: ∠XBY = ∠XAY = 45°
  • In ΔBXY, by angle sum property of a triangle: ∠BXY + ∠XBY + ∠BYX = 180°
  • 50° + 45° + ∠BYX = 180°
  • ∠BYX = 180° - 95° = 85°

Problem 54: Application of Pythagoras theorem in right-angled triangles ΔOPB and ΔAOP.

  • In ΔOPB: OB² = OP² + BP² => 15² = 12² + BP² => BP = 9 cm
  • In ΔAOP: OA² = OP² + AP² => 20² = 12² + AP² => AP = 16 cm
  • Hence, AB = AP - BP = 16 - 9 = 7 cm

text:
Problem 55: Properties of cyclic quadrilaterals and angle sum property.

  • Given x/3 = y/4 = z/5 = k. So x=3k, y=4k, z=5k.
  • ∠DCQ = ∠BCP = 3k (vertically opposite).
  • In ΔDCQ: ∠CDQ = 180° - (3k + 5k) = 180° - 8k.
  • By properties of cyclic quadrilateral: ∠CDQ = ∠CBA = 180° - 8k.
  • ∠PBC = 8k.
  • In ΔPBC: ∠P + ∠B + ∠C = 180° => 4k + 8k + 3k = 180° => k = 12°.

Properties of Tangents and Circles:

chapter: Area and Perimeter of Plane Figures
text:
Definition: Area of a plane figure is the amount of surface enclosed by its boundary. It is measured in square units. The perimeter of a plane figure is the total length of the sides enclosing the figure. The unit of perimeter is the same as the unit of sides of a given figure.

Square Properties: Let each side of a square be a unit.

  • Perimeter of square = 4(Side) = 4a units
  • Diagonal of square = sqrt(2) * (Side) = a*sqrt(2) units
  • Area of square = Side * Side = (a)^2 sq units = 1/2 * (Diagonal)^2 = 1/2 * d^2 sq units
image_descriptions: A square labeled ABCD with sides of length 'a'. The bottom side is labeled 'Side (a)'.

details.summary: Basic definitions and formulas for the area and perimeter of a square.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Let l and b be the length and breadth of a rectangle respectively, then:

  • Area of rectangle = Length × Breadth = l × b
  • Perimeter of rectangle = 2 (Length + Breadth) = 2(l + b) units
  • Diagonal of rectangle = sqrt(Length^2 + Breadth^2) = sqrt(l^2 + b^2) units
  • Area of track (Shaded region) = (l_1b_1 - l_2b_2) sq units
image_descriptions: Diagram of a rectangle with vertices A, B, C, D, labeled length (l) and breadth (b).
Diagram of a rectangular track showing an outer rectangle with dimensions l1, b1 and an inner rectangle with dimensions l2, b2.

(ii) Let d_1 and d_2 are two diagonals and θ is angle between them, then area of quadrilateral = 1/2 * d_1 * d_2 * sin(θ).

chapter: Area and Perimeter of Plane Figures
text:
Parallelogram

Let adjacent sides of a parallelogram be b and a respectively and h is the corresponding altitude (height) of side a, then:

  • (i) Area of the parallelogram = (Base × Height) = a × h sq units
  • (ii) Perimeter of a parallelogram = 2(Sum of adjacent side) = 2(a + b) units

Note: Each diagonal of a parallelogram divides it into two triangles of equal area.
image_descriptions: A parallelogram ABCD with base 'a' along the bottom side AB, and a vertical height 'h' dropped from point D to the base line.

details.summary: Definitions and formulas for the area and perimeter of a parallelogram.

subject: Mathematics
chapter: Area and Perimeter of Plane Figures
text:
Rhombus

Let the length of each sides of a rhombus be a and length of both diagonals are d1 and d2, then:

  • (i) Area of rhombus = 1/2 * d1 * d2 sq units
  • (ii) Side of rhombus = 1/2 * sqrt(d1^2 + d2^2) units => 4a^2 = d1^2 + d2^2
  • (iii) Perimeter of rhombus = 4 * (Side) units

Note: Diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other at right angles.
image_descriptions: A rhombus ABCD with diagonals d1 and d2 intersecting at point O at right angles. Each side is labeled 'a'.

details.summary: Definitions and formulas for the area, side length, and perimeter of a rhombus.

text:
Let the length of parallel sides of a trapezium be a and b and distance between them is h, then

Area of trapezium = 1/2 * (Sum of parallel sides) * (Distance between them)

Area = 1/2 * (AB + CD) * h = 1/2 * (a + b) * h sq units
image_descriptions: A diagram of a trapezium with parallel sides labeled 'a' and 'b', and height 'h' indicated by perpendicular lines from the top side to the base.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Let the sides of a triangle be a, b, c and h be the corresponding altitude to side a, then

  • (i) Perimeter of scalene triangle, 2s = (a + b + c) units
  • (ii) Semi-perimeter of scalene triangle, s = (a + b + c) / 2 units
  • (iii) Area of triangle = sqrt(s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)) sq units, where s = (a+b+c)/2 [Heron's formula]
  • or area of triangle = 1/2 * a * h sq units
  • (iv) The radius of incircle = (2 * Area) / Perimeter
  • (v) The radius of circumcircle = (abc) / (4 * Area)
image_descriptions: A triangle with sides labeled a, b, c and altitude h.

details.summary: Properties and formulas for a scalene triangle.

text:
A figure bounded by three straight lines is called a triangle. Let perpendicular, base and hypotenuse of a right angled triangle (ABC) be p, b and h, respectively, then

  • (i) Perimeter of right angled triangle = AB + BC + CA = (b + p + h) units
  • (ii) Area of right angled triangle = 1/2 * Base * Altitude = 1/2 * b * p sq units

text:
Isosceles Triangle: Let sides of an isosceles triangle be a, b, and b.

  • (i) Perimeter of isosceles triangle = a + b + b = a + 2b units
  • (ii) Area of isosceles triangle = (s - b) * sqrt(s - a) = 1/4 * a * sqrt(4b^2 - a^2) sq units, where a = Base, b = Equal sides, and s = semi-perimeter.
  • (iii) Area of a right isosceles triangle, in which equal sides from a right angle is given by: Area = 1/2 * a^2 sq units.
  • (iv) If theta is the angle between two equal sides of an isosceles triangle, then Area of triangle = 1/2 * a^2 * sin(theta).

Equilateral Triangle: Let a be the side of an equilateral triangle.

  • (i) Height (altitude) of an equilateral triangle = (sqrt(3) / 2) * a
  • (ii) Area of an equilateral triangle = (sqrt(3) / 4) * a^2
  • (iii) Perimeter of an equilateral triangle = 3 * Side = 3a
  • (iv) The radius of incircle = a / (2 * sqrt(3))

text: The radius of a circumcircle of an equilateral triangle with side 'a' is given by: radius = a / sqrt(3).

subject: Mathematics
text:
Let the radius of a circle be r.

  • Circumference of circle = 2 * pi * r = pi * D units (where D is diameter, D = 2r)
  • Area of circle = pi * r^2 sq units
  • Distance covered by a wheel in one revolution = Circumference of the wheel

subject: Mathematics
text:
A diameter divides a circle into two equal parts. Each of these two arcs is called a semi-circle. If r is the radius of a circle, then:

  • Area of semi-circle = (1/2) * pi * r^2 sq units
  • Perimeter of semi-circle = (pi * r + 2r) = (pi * r + D) units

If r is the radius of a circle, then:

If two diameters are perpendicular to each other, then they divide the circle into four quadrants.

text:
A polygon that has all sides equal and all interior angles equal is a regular polygon.

Let n = number of sides, a = length of side, r = radius of inscribed circle (inradius), R = radius of circumcircle.

  • Area of polygon = (1/4)na^2 cot(180/n) = nr^2 tan(180/n) = (1/2)nR^2 sin(360/n)
  • Perimeter of polygon = n * a = 2nr sin(180/n)
  • Inradius of polygon = (1/2)a cot(180/n)
  • Circumradius of polygon = (1/2)a cosec(180/n)
  • Area of regular pentagon = (1/4)sqrt(5(5+2sqrt(5)))a^2 sq units
  • Area of regular hexagon = (3sqrt(3)/2)a^2 sq units
  • Area of regular octagon = 2(sqrt(2)+1)a^2 sq units

This section provides solutions to various geometry problems involving rectangles, squares, circles, and triangles.

  • Rectangle: Area = l x b, Perimeter = 2(l + b).
  • Square and Semi-circle: Area between square and semi-circles is calculated by subtracting the area of the semi-circles from the area of the square.
  • Triangle: Area = 1/2 x base x height. For an equilateral triangle, Area = (sqrt(3)/4) * a^2.
  • Circle: Area of a sector = (theta/360) * pi * r^2. Area of a segment = Area of sector - Area of triangle.
  • Inscribed Rectangle: Area of a rectangle inscribed in a circle is maximum when the diameter of the circle is equal to the diagonal of the rectangle.

subject: Mathematics
chapter: Surface Area and Volume of Solids
text:
Solid Figures: The objects which occupy space (i.e. they have three dimensions) are called solid figures. The solid figures can be derived from the plane figures.

Surface Area of Solid Figure: Surface area of a solid body is the area of all of its surfaces together. It is always measured in square units. Surface area is also referred to as the total surface area. The area of four walls or the area excluding top and bottom is called curved surface area or lateral surface area.

Volume of Solid Figure: The measure of space occupied by a solid is called its volume. It is always measured in cubic units.

Cuboid: A figure which is surrounded by six rectangular surfaces, is called cuboid. It is also called rectangular parallelepiped.

  • A cuboid has 8 corners, 12 edges, 6 faces and 4 diagonals.

details.summary: Introduction to solid geometry, defining surface area, volume, and the properties of a cuboid.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Cuboid Properties:

  • Volume of cuboid = Area of base × height = l × b × h
  • Total surface area of cuboid = 2(lb + bh + lh)
  • Diagonal of the cuboid = sqrt(l^2 + b^2 + h^2)
  • Lateral surface area or Area of four walls = 2(l + b)h
image_descriptions: Diagram of a cuboid with vertices labeled A, B, C, D showing length, breadth, and height dimensions.
Diagram showing a rectangular sheet of 48cm by 36cm with 8cm squares cut from each corner to form an open box.

details.summary: Definitions and formulas for cuboid geometry.

subject: Mathematics
text:
A cuboid whose length, breadth and height are same is called a cube.

  • A cube has 6 surfaces, 12 edges, 8 corners and 4 diagonals.
  • Cube is a special case of cuboid which has 6 square faces.
  • Volume of a cube = (side)^3
  • Total surface area of a cube = 6 × (side)^2
  • Diagonal of a cube = sqrt(3) × edge
  • Lateral surface area or area of four walls = 4 × (side)^2
image_descriptions: Diagram of a cube with vertices labeled A, B, C, D.

details.summary: Definitions and formulas for cube geometry.

subject: Mathematics
text:
A right circular cylinder is a solid figure obtained by revolving the rectangle, say ABCD about its one side, say BC. Let base radius of right circular cylinder be r and its height be h. Then,

  • (i) Volume of the cylinder = (Area of base) × Height = πr^2h cu units
  • (ii) Curved surface area = Circumference of the base × Height = 2πrh sq units
  • (iii) Total surface area = Curved surface + Area of two ends = 2πrh + 2πr^2 = 2πr(h + r) sq units
image_descriptions: A diagram of a right circular cylinder with height labeled 'h', and points A, B, C, D marking the vertices of the rectangle used to generate the cylinder.

details.summary: Definitions and formulas for the volume and surface area of a right circular cylinder.

subject: Mathematics
text:
• Volume of prism = Area of base × height
  • Lateral surface area of prism = Perimeter of base × height
  • Volume of pyramid = 1/3 × Area of base × height
  • Lateral surface area = 1/2 × Perimeter of base × slant height
formulas: Volume of prism = Area of base × height
Lateral surface area of prism = Perimeter of base × height
Volume of pyramid = 1/3 × Area of base × height
Lateral surface area = 1/2 × Perimeter of base × slant height

subject: Mathematics
text:
A right circular cone is a solid, generated by the revolution of a right angled triangle about one of its sides containing the right angle. Let height of a right circular cone be h, and its radius be r. Then:

  • Slant height of the cone: l = AC = sqrt(r^2 + h^2) units
  • Volume of cone: 1/3 * pi * r^2 * h cu units
  • Curved surface area of a cone: pi * r * l sq units
  • Total surface area of a cone: Curved surface area + Base area = pi * r * (l + r) sq units
formulas: Curved Surface Area = pi * r * l
Total Surface Area = pi * r * (l + r)
image_descriptions: A diagram of a right circular cone showing height (h), slant height (l), and radius (r) with vertices labeled A, B, and C.

details.summary: Definitions and formulas for the geometry of a right circular cone.

subject: Mathematics
text:
A hollow cylinder is one which is empty from inside and has some difference between the internal and external radius. Let R and r be the external and internal radii of the hollow cylinder and h be its height. Then:

  • Volume of hollow cylinder: pi * (R^2 - r^2) * h cu units
  • Curved surface area: 2 * pi * R * h + 2 * pi * r * h = 2 * pi * (R + r) * h sq units
  • Total surface area: 2 * pi * R * h + 2 * pi * r * h + 2 * pi * (R^2 - r^2) = 2 * pi * (R + r) * (h + R - r) sq units
formulas: Curved Surface Area = 2 * pi * (R + r) * h
Total Surface Area = 2 * pi * (R + r) * (h + R - r)
image_descriptions: A diagram of a hollow cylinder showing external radius (R), internal radius (r), and height (h) with vertices labeled A, B, C, D.

details.summary: Definitions and formulas for the geometry of a hollow cylinder.

subject: Mathematics
text:
If a right circular cone is cut-off by a plane parallel to the base of the cone, then the portion of the cone between the cutting plane and base of the cone is called the frustum of the cone. Let R, r be the radii of base and top (R > r) of the frustum of a cone. Let height of frustum of a cone be h and slant height be l, then:

  • (i) Slant height of frustum of right circular cone = sqrt(h^2 + (R-r)^2) units
  • (ii) Volume of frustum of right circular cone = (pi * h / 3) * (R^2 + r^2 + Rr) cu units
  • (iii) Curved (lateral) surface area of frustum of right circular cone = pi * l * (R + r) sq units
  • (iv) Total surface area of frustum of right circular cone = Area of base + Area of top + Lateral surface area = pi * [R^2 + r^2 + l(R + r)] sq units
  • (v) Total surface area of bucket = pi * [(R + r)l + r^2] sq units (it is open at the bigger end)
image_descriptions: Diagram of a frustum of a cone showing height h, top radius r, and base radius R.

subject: Mathematics
text:
The set of all points in space, which are equidistant from a fixed point, is called a sphere. Let radius of sphere be r, then:

  • (i) Volume of sphere = (4/3) * pi * r^3 cu units
  • (ii) Surface area of sphere = 4 * pi * r^2 sq units
  • (iii) Volume of a hollow sphere = (4/3) * pi * (R^3 - r^3) cu units, where r = Inner radius and R = Outer radius
image_descriptions: Diagram of a sphere with radius r marked from the center O.

subject: Mathematics
text:
A plane passing through the centre cuts the sphere in two equal parts, each part is called a hemisphere.

Let the radius of hemisphere be r, then:

  • Volume of hemisphere = (2/3) * pi * r^3 cu units
  • Curved surface area of hemisphere = 2 * pi * r^2 sq units
  • Total surface area = 2 * pi * r^2 + pi * r^2 = 3 * pi * r^2 sq units
  • Volume of hemispherical shell = (2/3) * pi * (R^3 - r^3), where R = outer radius, r = inner radius
formulas: Volume of hemispherical shell = (2/3) * pi * (R^3 - r^3)
image_descriptions: A diagram showing a hemisphere with a radius line labeled 'r' extending from the center of the flat circular face to the edge.

details.summary: Definitions and formulas for the volume and surface area of a hemisphere and hemispherical shell.

subject: Mathematics
text:
• If the side of a cube is increased by x%, then its volume is increased by [(1 + x/100)^3 - 1] * 100%.
  • If the length, breadth and height of a cuboid are made x, y and z times respectively, then its volume is increased by (xyz - 1) * 100%.
  • If the length, breadth and height of a cuboid are increased by x%, y% and z% respectively, then its volume is increased by [x + y + z + (xy + yz + zx)/100 + xyz/(100)^2]%.
  • If the sides and diagonal of a cuboid are given, then the total surface area in terms of diagonal and sides is given by Total surface area = (Sum of the sides)^2 - (Diagonal)^2.
  • If the side of a cube is increased by x%, then the surface area is increased by [2x + x^2/100]%.

Total surface area = (Sum of the sides)^2 - (Diagonal)^2

subject: Mathematics
text:
Statistics is the branch of Mathematics which deals with the collection, analysis and interpretation of numerical data.

Collection of Data:

  • Primary data: The data collected actually in the process of investigation by the investigator. It is original and first hand information.
  • Secondary data: The data collected by someone and used by any other person.

Presentation of Data:

  • Raw or Ungrouped data: Data presented in random order, not prepared according to any order.
  • Grouped data: Data arranged in any manner like ascending or descending order, often presented in a frequency distribution table.

Key Definitions:

  • Class Intervals: Groups in which all observations are divided, bounded by two figures called class limits.
  • Class mark: The mid-point of the class interval.
  • Range or class size: The difference between the upper limit and the lower limit of a class.
  • Frequency of an observation: The number of times an observation occurs.
  • Frequency distribution: A tabular arrangement of data showing the frequency of each observation.
formulas: Class mark = (Lower class limit + Upper class limit) / 2

details.summary: Introduction to basic statistical concepts including data collection types, presentation methods, and fundamental definitions like class intervals, class marks, and frequency distribution.

subject: Mathematics
text:
1. Discrete frequency distribution: A frequency distribution is called a discrete frequency distribution, if data are presented in a way such that exact measurements of the units are clearly shown.

2. Continuous frequency distribution:

  • Exclusive form: A frequency distribution in which upper limit of each class is excluded and lower limit is included. e.g., In the class 0-10, a student who has obtained 10 marks is not included in this class; it will be counted in the next class i.e., 10-20.
  • Inclusive method: Classes are formed so that the upper limit of a class is included in that class. e.g., In class 1000-1099, we include workers having wages between 1000 and 1099. If income is exactly 1100, it will be included in the next class 1100-1199.

To convert inclusive to exclusive, subtract 0.5 from the lower limit and add 0.5 to the upper limit of each class.

Cumulative frequency: If the frequency of a class interval is added to the frequency of the second class and this sum is added to the third class and so on, then frequencies so obtained are known as cumulative frequency.
formulas: Class size = Upper limit - Lower limit
tables:
| Marks | Number of students (frequency) |
|---|---|
| 40 | 7 |
| 60 | 3 |
| 80 | 3 |
| 100 | 2 |
| Total | 15 |

details.summary: Explanation of discrete and continuous frequency distributions, inclusive vs exclusive methods, and cumulative frequency calculation.

subject: Mathematics
text:
An average or central value of a statistical series is the value of the variable which describes the characteristic of the entire distribution. The following are the five measures of central tendency:

  • (i) Arithmetic mean or mean
  • (ii) Geometric mean
  • (iii) Harmonic mean
  • (iv) Median
  • (v) Mode

Out of these measures of central tendency, Arithmetic mean, median and mode are sometimes known as measures of location.

Arithmetic Mean

The mean (or average) of number of observations is the sum of the observations divided by the total number of observations.

Mean = Sum of observations / Number of observation

Properties of Arithmetic Mean

  1. If every observation is increased by a constant, then the mean of the observations, so obtained also increases by the same constant.
  2. If every observation is decreased by a constant, then the mean of the observation, so obtained also decreases by the same constant.
  3. If each observation is multiplied by a constant, then the mean of the resulting observations can be obtained by multiplying the mean by the same constant.
  4. If each observation is divided by a constant, then the mean of the resulting observation can be obtained by dividing the mean by the same constant.
  5. The average of natural numbers from 1 to n is (n+1)/2.
  6. The average of odd numbers from 1 to n is [(Last odd number + 1)/2] and the average of even numbers from 1 to n is [(Last even number + 2)/2].
formulas: Mean = Sum of observations / Number of observation
Mean (x_bar) = A + (1/n) * sum(d_i), where d_i = x_i - A
Average of natural numbers from 1 to n = (n+1)/2

details.summary: Overview of measures of central tendency and properties of the arithmetic mean.

subject: Mathematics
topic: Mean of grouped or continuous observations
text:
Mean of grouped or continuous observations: If x1, x2, x3, ..., xn are n observations whose corresponding frequencies are f1, f2, f3, ..., fn, then:

  • (i) Direct Method: Mean (x_bar) = (x1f1 + x2f2 + ... + xnfn) / (f1 + f2 + ... + fn) = sum(fixi) / sum(fi)
  • (ii) Assumed Mean Method: Mean (x_bar) = A + (sum(fidi) / sum(fi)), where A = Assumed mean and di = xi - A.
  • (iii) Step Deviation Method: Mean (x_bar) = A + (sum(fiui) / sum(fi)) * h, where h = Difference between two consecutive class marks.

Weighted Arithmetic Mean: If corresponding weights of x1, x2, ..., xn are w1, w2, ..., wn respectively, then Weighted arithmetic mean = (w1x1 + w2x2 + ... + wnxn) / (w1 + w2 + ... + wn) = sum(wixi) / sum(wi).
image_descriptions: Table showing calculation of mean wage using assumed mean method with A=900.
Table showing calculation of mean using step deviation method with A=35 and h=10.

details.summary: Covers methods for calculating the mean of grouped data including Direct, Assumed Mean, and Step Deviation methods, along with the formula for Weighted Arithmetic Mean.

subject: Mathematics
text:
If two sets of observations are given, then the combined mean of both the sets can be calculated by the following formula:

x̄ = (n₁x̄₁ + n₂x̄₂) / (n₁ + n₂)

where, x̄ = Mean of sets of observations, x̄₁ = Mean of first set of observations, n₁ = Number of observations in first set, x̄₂ = Mean of second set of observations, n₂ = Number of observations in second set.

details.summary: Formula for calculating the combined arithmetic mean of two sets of observations.

subject: Mathematics
text: If a, G and b are in GP, then the geometric mean between a and b is, G = √ab.

details.summary: Definition of geometric mean for two numbers in a geometric progression.

subject: Mathematics
text: The harmonic mean of n positive numbers a₁, a₂, ..., aₙ is 1/H = 1/n (1/a₁ + 1/a₂ + ... + 1/aₙ), where H denotes the harmonic mean.

details.summary: Definition and formula for the harmonic mean of n positive numbers.

subject: Mathematics
text:
After arranging the given data in ascending or descending order of magnitude, the value of the middle most observation is called the median of the data.

  • Median of an individual series: If number of observations is n, arrange in order. If n is odd, Median = Value of the ((n+1)/2)th observation. If n is even, Median = [Value of (n/2)th observation + Value of (n/2 + 1)th observation] / 2.
  • Median of a discrete frequency series: Arrange data, find cumulative frequency, find N/2 where N = Σfᵢ. The median is the value corresponding to the cumulative frequency just greater than N/2.
  • Median of a continuous series: Find the median class corresponding to cumulative frequency just greater than N/2. Median = l + [(N/2 - c) / f] * h, where l is the lower limit of the median class.
formulas: Median = (Value of (n/2)th observation + Value of (n/2 + 1)th observation) / 2

details.summary: Methods to calculate the median for individual, discrete, and continuous series.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Median Calculation Formula:

  • f = Frequency of median class
  • h = Size of median class
  • c = Cumulative frequency of class before median class

Median = l + ((N/2 - c) / f) * h

details.summary: Example calculation for median of grouped data.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Mode: The data value which occurs maximum number of times in a data distribution is called mode.

  • Mode of individual series: The value which is repeated maximum number of times is called mode of the series.
  • Mode of a discrete frequency series: The value of the variate corresponding to the maximum frequency.
  • Mode of a continuous series: The class which has maximum frequency is called modal class or group. The mode is given by the formula:

Mode = l + ((f1 - f0) / (2f1 - f0 - f2)) * h

Where:

  • l = Lower limit of modal class
  • h = Size of class interval
  • f1 = Frequency of modal class
  • f0 = Frequency of the class preceding the modal class
  • f2 = Frequency of the class succeeding the modal class

details.summary: Definitions and formulas for calculating mode in individual, discrete, and continuous series.

subject: Mathematics
topic: Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Relation between Mean, Median and Mode: The empirical relationship between the three measures of central tendency is given by: Mode = 3 (Median) - 2 (Mean). In case, mean = median = mode, then distribution is said to be symmetric distribution.

Some Useful Formulae: If x1, x2, ..., xn are n observations with their mean M, then deviation di is given by di = |xi - M|.

  • Mean deviation for individual series is given by sum(|di|) / n
  • Mean deviation for discrete series is given by sum(fi * |di|) / sum(fi)
  • Standard deviation (sigma) for ungrouped data is given by sigma = sqrt(sum(|di|^2) / n)
  • Standard deviation for grouped data is given by sigma = sqrt(sum(fi * |di|^2) / sum(fi))
  • Variance = sigma^2
  • Coefficient of variation = (Standard deviation / Mean) * 100
  • Coefficient of mean deviation = (Mean deviation / Mean) * 100
formulas: Coefficient of mean deviation = (Mean deviation / Mean) * 100

Histogram: A chart showing frequency on the Y-axis (0 to 40) and adjacent rectangles representing class intervals.

details.summary: Covers empirical relationships between mean, median, and mode, and provides standard statistical formulae for mean deviation, standard deviation, variance, and coefficients of variation.

subject: Mathematics
text:
There are many ways of picturing a frequency distribution of continuous type:

  • 1. Bar Graph: Bars of uniform width are drawn with various heights representing the frequency of observation.
  • 2. Histogram: Graphical representation of a frequency distribution in the form of rectangles with class intervals as bases and frequencies as height. There is no gap between consecutive rectangles.
  • 3. Frequency polygon: Drawn by joining the mid-points of the respective tops of the rectangles of a histogram in case of equal class intervals.

Points to be remembered:

  • A histogram consists of a set of adjacent rectangles, whose bases are equal to class sizes and height are equal to class frequencies.
  • The total area of the histogram = Sum of areas of all rectangles. If class intervals are of same size (width), then area of histogram = NK, where K = Size of a class and N = Sum of frequencies of all classes.
  • If the frequency distribution is discontinuous (inclusive), change it to continuous (exclusive) and then construct a histogram.
image_descriptions: Bar Graph and Histogram diagrams illustrating frequency distribution.

details.summary: Explains graphical methods for data representation including Bar Graphs, Histograms, and Frequency Polygons.

subject: Mathematics
text: A frequency polygon for a grouped data can also be drawn independently by plotting the mid-points of the all classes along X-axis and frequencies along Y-axis and joining the plotted points by straight line.
image_descriptions: A line graph showing temperature on the Y-axis (ranging from 65 to 85) and time on the X-axis (9:00 to 15:00). The line connects points representing temperature at specific time intervals.

subject: Mathematics
text:
When we plot the upper or lower class limits along X-axis and cumulative frequencies along Y-axis, And on joining them we get a curve called an ogive.

We have two types of ogive curves:

  • (a) less than ogive (i.e. the rising curve): It is the graph between upper limits and cumulative frequencies of a distribution.
  • (b) more than ogive (i.e. a falling curve): It is the graph between lower limits and cumulative frequencies of a distribution.

Note:

  • If we have both ogive (i.e. less than type and more than type), then these two ogives intersect each other at a point.
  • From this point, draw a perpendicular on X-axis, the point at which it cuts the X-axis gives the median. i.e. the x-coordinate of intersection point gives the median.

text:
A type of graph in which a circle is divided into sectors such that each sector represents a proportion of the whole.

Thus, in a pie chart:

  • Data is represented by sectors of a circle.
  • Each part of data makes a certain central angle.
  • Sum of all the angles of sector is 360°.

Important Concepts:

  • Cumulative Frequency Polygon: Provides an equivalent representation of a frequency distribution table. It is a closed polygon with one horizontal and one vertical side, and the other sides have non-negative slopes.
  • Modal Class: The class which has the maximum frequency.

text: Histogram: A histogram is an equivalent graphical representation of the frequency distribution and is suitable for continuous random variables where the total frequency of an interval is evenly distributed over the interval. It consists of vertical rectangular bars with a common base such that there is no gap between consecutive bars and the height of the rectangle is determined by the frequency of the class it represents.

text:
Frequency Polygon: Can be drawn by joining the mid-points of the respective tops of the rectangle of a histogram in the case of equal class intervals.

Frequency Distribution: A comprehensive way to classify raw data of a quantitative variable. It shows how different values of a variable are distributed in different classes along with their corresponding class frequencies. It is an equivalent representation of original data.

Median Formula: Median = l + [(n/2 - cf) / f] * h

subject: Mathematics
text:
Median Calculation: For even number of terms, Median = (Value of (n/2)th term + Value of (n/2 + 1)th term) / 2.

Mode: The value with the maximum frequency.

Geometric Mean: If X = (x1 * x2 * ... * xn)^(1/n) and Y = (y1 * y2 * ... * yn)^(1/n), then the geometric mean of (x1/y1, x2/y2, ..., xn/yn) is X/Y.

Arithmetic Mean Properties: Uses all data, uniquely defined. Sum of deviations from mean is zero: Σfi(xi - x̄) = 0.

Histogram: Graphical representation where class intervals are on the X-axis and rectangles are proportional to frequencies.
formulas: Median = (Value of (n/2)th term + Value of (n/2 + 1)th term) / 2

subject: Mathematics
text:
This page provides detailed solutions for statistical problems involving mean, median, weighted arithmetic mean, and frequency distribution tables.

  • Median calculation for discrete values: Arrange in ascending order and find the middle term.
  • Weighted Arithmetic Mean: Calculated as the sum of products of values and their weights divided by the sum of weights.
  • Central Angle in Pie Charts: Calculated as (Value / Total) * 360 degrees.
  • Effect of constant subtraction: If a constant is subtracted from each observation, the mean and median decrease by that same constant.
  • Frequency Distribution: Median class is determined by N/2. Median formula: l + ((N/2 - C) / f) * h.
  • Geometric Mean (GM) and Median: For a geometric progression 1, λ, λ^2, ..., λ^10, the median is the 6th term (λ^5) and GM is also λ^5.
  • Harmonic Mean (HM) and Median: For a harmonic progression 1, 1/2, 1/3, ..., 1/11, the median is the 6th term (1/6) and HM is also 1/6.
