subject: History
text:
Under Ashoka, the empire reached its Zenith. In history, for the first time, the entire Indian sub-continent came under a single umbrella (except extreme Southern India). He fought a battle known as Kalinga War in 261 BC in the 8th year of his coronation, in which one lakh people died.

  • Ashoka sent peace missionaries inside India as well as abroad. Ashoka Dhamma was made up of tenets of most of famous sect of that time though tenets from Buddhism were predominant.
  • Ashoka used his policy of Dhamma to promote religious tolerance in society. He also used Dhamma based policy to promote Buddhism in foreign land and Dhamma as a foreign policy to promote peace.
  • A stone portrait of Emperor Ashoka has been found at Kanaganahalli. This is situated near Bhima river in Gulbarga district of Karnataka.

Ashoka's Edicts

Ashokan edicts are inscribed either on pillars of stone or on rocks. They consist of major and minor group. They give information on the life and reign of the king.

Major Rock Edicts

They are a set of 14 inscriptions found at 8 places: Dhauli, Girnar, Jauguda, Kalsi, Mansehra, Shahbazgarhi, Sopara and Yerragudi. The major rock edicts also include two separate edicts found at Kalinga. They deal with administration and ethics.

Minor Rock Edicts

These are spread over 13 places i.e. Bairat, Brahmagiri, Gavimath, Gujarra, Jatinga-Rameshwar, Maski, Palkigunda, Maadagiri, Rupanath, Sasaram, Siddhapur, Suvarnagiri and Yerragudi. Bhabru Inscriptions is located at Bairat in Rajasthan and deals with Ashoka's conversion to Buddhism.

Major Pillar Edicts

These are a set of 7 edicts found at Allahabad, Meerut, Sopara, Lauriya Areraj, Lauriya Nandangarh and Rampurva. These edicts are engraved on Monolithic pillars. Kausambi edicts are known as Queen's Edict. They indicate about donations given by queen Karuvaki.

Minor Pillar Edicts

  • Rummindei Pillar Inscription: It mentions the exemption of Lumbini (birth place of Buddha) from tax.
  • Nigalisagar Pillar Inscription: It is located in Kapilvastu. It informs about Ashoka increasing the size of stupa of Buddha Konakamana to double of its former size.
  • Scheism Edict: It is located at Kausambi, Sanchi and Sarnath. It appeals for maintaining unity in Buddhist order.
  • Barabara Cave Inscriptions: It is located in Bihar. They speak about Ashoka's donation of cave to the Ajivikas.

Later Mauryas

According to Buddhist tradition, Ashoka ruled for 27 years. The disintegration of the Mauryan empire seemed to have set in immediately after Ashoka's death. The tenth and the last of the Mauryas was Brihadratha, who was murdered by his General Pushyamitra Shunga. This was the end of Mauryan dynasty.

Mauryan Administration

The Mauryan state was a welfare state with highly Centralised Government. King was the Nucleus, assisted by Mantri Parishad, which included:

  • i. Yuvaraj: The crown prince.
  • ii. Gopa: The Purohit Chief Priest.
  • iii. Senapati: Commander-in-Chief of army and other ministers.

Coins of Mauryan Empire was called Pana and it was made up of silver and copper. The later Maurya's and Post Maurya Kingdom started votive inscription to record the religious offering made to institutions and land grants made to official or any other citizen.

Facts about Mauryans by Megasthene

According to Megasthene, the administration of army was carried by a board of 30 officers divided into six committees, each consisting of five members. They are as follow:

  • i. Army
  • ii. Cavalry
  • iii. Elephants
  • iv. Chariot
  • v. Navy
  • vi. Transport

Though, Megasthene said that there was no slavery in India, yet according to Indian sources slavery was a recognised institution during Mauryans reign. Tamralipti in the Gangetic delta was the most prosperous part on the East coast of India. Megasthene in his Indica had mentioned 7 castes in Mauryan society.

subject: History
text:
Mauryan art is classified into two groups:

  • Popular/Folk Art: Sculpture of Yaksha and Yakshini e.g. Yaksha of Parkham (Mathura), Yakshini from Vidisha (Madhya Pradesh) and Didarganj (Patna).
  • Royal/Court Art: Royal Palace of Chandragupta Maurya at Kumharar, Patna (Fa-hien referred it as the creation of God), city of Patliputra, Ashokan pillars, stupas and caves.

Key Features:

  • Mauryans introduced stone masonry on large scale. Pillars represent the masterpiece of Mauryan sculpture, e.g., Single lion capital at Rampurva and Lauriya Nandangarh, Four lion capital at Sarnath and Sanchi, Carved elephant at Dhauli and engraved elephant at Kalsi.
  • Stupas were built throughout the empire to enshrine the relics of Buddha e.g. Sanchi and Bharhut.
  • Varanasi was the best producer of silk.

details.summary: Overview of Mauryan art, architecture, and key cultural features.

subject: History
text: Mauryans were succeeded by many ruling dynasties from Central Asia in North-West India and by native rulers (Sungas, Kanvas, Satavahanas) in the Eastern, Central and Deccan region of India.

details.summary: Introduction to the political landscape following the Mauryan Empire.

subject: History
text:
Period: 185 BC-73 BC

  • Founder: Pushyamitra founded this dynasty. His dominions extended to South as far as the Narmada river and included cities of Patliputra, Ayodhya and Vidisha.
  • Key Figures: The fifth king was Bhagabhadra, to whose court Heliodorus, the Greek ambassador visited. A Shunga king, Agnimitra was the hero of Kalidasa's Malavikagnimitram.
  • Literature/Religion: This period saw the revival of Bhagvatism. Patanjali's classic Mahabhashya was written during this time. The famous book on Hindu Law, Manusmriti was compiled during this period.

details.summary: Details regarding the Shunga Dynasty, its rulers, and cultural contributions.

subject: History
text: The founder of this short-lived dynasty was Vasudeva, who killed the last Shunga king Devabhuti. They were swept away by Satavahanas of the Deccan.

details.summary: Brief overview of the Kanva Dynasty.

subject: History
text:
Founder: Simuka. They were the successors of the Mauryans in the Deccan and the Central India.

  • Important King: Gautamiputra Satakarni (AD 106-130) who raised the power and prestige of Satavahanas to greater heights. He set-up his capital at Paithan on the bank of river Godavari in Aurangabad district.
  • Land Grants: First evidence of land grants to Brahmins was found (started by Satavahanas). Satavahanas built Nagarjuna Konda stupa and Amravati Stupa.
  • Economy/Religion: Mostly issued lead coins (apart from copper and bronze). Acted as a bridge between North and South India. Satavahana rulers called themselves Brahmins. They performed Vedic rituals and worshipped Gods like Krishna, Vasudeva and others. However, they also promoted Buddhism by granting land to the monks.
  • Architecture/Administration: The two common religious constructions were the Buddhist temple that was called Chaitya and the monasteries, which was called Vibara. The most famous Chaitya is that of Karle in West Deccan. Their provinces were called Ahara, as it was in Ashoka's time. Their officials were known as amatyas and mahamatyas, as they were known in Mauryan times.

details.summary: Comprehensive details on the Satavahana dynasty, their administration, and religious policies.

subject: History
text:
Capital: Kalinganagara.

  • King: The greatest and the most powerful king of the dynasty was Kharvela.
  • Inscriptions: The only source of information about the king Kharvela is the Hathigumpha inscription written in Prakrit language and Brahmi script. In the 9th year of his reign Kharvela built Mahavijaya Prasad (place of Great Victory) on both the banks of the river Prachi, in order to commemorate his victories in the North.
  • Welfare: In the 13th year of his reign, Kharvela undertook many welfare schemes like building caves for the Jaina monks in the Udaigiri hills i.e. Hathigumpha and Ranigumpha caves.

details.summary: Details on the Chedi dynasty and King Kharvela.

subject: History
text: The Ikshavaku dynasty was founded by the legendary king Ikshavaku. The important personalities belonging to this royal house are Bharata, Harish Chandra, Dilipa, Sagara, Raghu, Rama and Paseuadi.

details.summary: Brief mention of the Ikshavaku dynasty.

subject: History
text:
Invasions: A number of invasions took place around 200 BC. The first to invade India were the Greeks, who were also called the Indo-Greeks or Bactrian Greeks (because they ruled Bactria).

  • Menander: The most famous Indo-Greek ruler was Menander (165-145 BC), also known as Milinda. He had his capital at Sankala (modern Sialkot) in Punjab. He was converted to Buddhism by Nagasena or Nagarjuna (described in Milindapanho or the Question of Milinda).
  • Currency: Greeks were the first to issue gold coins in India.

details.summary: Overview of the Indo-Greek invasions and the reign of Menander.

subject: History
text:
The Shakas or Scythians (90 BC)

  • The Greeks were followed by the Sakas, who controlled a larger part of India than the Greeks did. There were 5 branches of the Shakas with their seats of power in different parts of India and Afghanistan.
  • The most famous Shaka ruler in India was Rudradaman I (AD 130-150). He is famous for the repairs of Sudarshana lake in Kathiawar. His inscription was Junagarh inscription.
  • A king of Ujjain, who called himself Vikramaditya defeated Shakas in 58 BC and started Vikram era (58 BC).

The Parthians/Pahalvas (AD 1st-3rd Century)

Originally, they lived in Iran, invaded at the beginning of Christian era, from where they moved to India. In comparison to Greeks and Shakas, they occupied only a small portion in North-West India in the 1st century. The most famous Parthian King was Gondophernes (AD 19-45), in whose reign St Thomas is said to have come to India for the propagation of Christianity.

The Kushans (AD 45)

  • Came from North Central Asia near China. Their empire included a good part of Central Asia, a portion of Iran, a portion of Afghanistan, Pakistan and almost the whole of North India.
  • Kanishka was the most famous king. He patronised the following scholars:
    • Ashvaghosha (wrote Buddhacharita, which is the biography of Buddha and Sutralankar).
    • Nagarjuna (wrote Madhyamik Sutra).
    • Charaka (a physician, wrote Charakhsamhita).
  • Kanishka is known in history because of two reasons:
    • i. He started an era in AD 78, which is now known as Saka era and is used by the Government of India.
    • ii. He extended his whole-hearted patronage to Buddhism (held a Buddhist council in Kashmir). Some of the successors of Kanishka bore typical Indian names as Vasudeva.
  • During Kanishka's rule, foreign trade flourished and it was at peak. Trade flourished through silk routes and oceanic routes. During Kanishka reign, Gandhara School of Art and Mathura School of Art flourished and developed.

details.summary: Overview of Shaka, Parthian, and Kushan dynasties in ancient India.

subject: History
text:
Sangam Age (300 BC-AD 600)

The age of 3 Southern kingdoms Cheras, Pandyas, Cholas was known as Sangam Age. The word 'Sangam' means assembly. It was an assembly of Tamil poets and scholars.

The Three Sangam Kingdom

All the gathered information is based on Sangam literature. Sangam was a college or assembly of Tamil poets held probably under Royal patronage (especially Pandyas). Silappadikaram by Ilango Adigal (story of a married couple) and Manimekalai by sattanar are the famous epics of this time.

The Pandyas

First mentioned by Megasthenese, who says that their kingdom was famous for pearls and was ruled by a woman. Their capital was Madurai. Important king was Nedunjeliyan.

The Cholas

The kingdom was called Cholamandalam or Coromandal. The chief centre was Uraiyur, a place famous for cotton trade. Capital was Kaveripattanam/Puhar. A Chola king named Elara conquered Sri Lanka and ruled it over for 50 years. Karikala was their famous king.

The Cheras

Their capital was Vanji (also called Kerala country). It owed its importance to trade with the Romans. The Romans set-up two regiments at Vanji to protect their interests. Greatest king was Senguttuvan, the Red Chera. Fought against the Cholas about AD 150.

subject: History
text:
THE GUPTA PERIOD

After the decline of Mauryas, Guptas came into existence. Actually, we found two names related with Gupta dynasty, before Chandragupta I. These are Sri Gupta and Ghatotkacha.

Chandragupta I

He was the first prominent ruler of Gupta dynasty and assumed the title of Maharajadhiraja. He made his empire stronger by his own efforts and also by making marriage with Lichchavi princess. Lichchavi were a very powerful family or ruling class of Mithila at that time.

Samudragupta (AD 335-375)

  • Samudragupta has been called the 'Indian Napoleon' by VA Smith because of his extensive military conquests.
  • He assumed the titles of Vikramanka and Kaviraja.
  • Virasen was his commander-in-chief during Southern campaign. Vasubandhu, a famous Buddhist scholar was his minister.
  • He subjugated 5 kingdoms in lower Bengal, upper Assam, Nepal and the territories farther West as well as number of republican clans.

details.summary: Introduction to the Gupta dynasty, Chandragupta I, and Samudragupta.

subject: History
text:
Samudragupta: Advanced through the forest tract of Madhya Pradesh to the coast of Orissa and upto Kanchi, the capital of Pallavas. Some coins represent him playing the Veena. He performed Asvamedha sacrifice. He was a devotee of Vishnu but tolerant of other faiths, granting permission to the Buddhist king of Ceylon, Meghavarman, to build a monastery at Bodh Gaya.

Chandragupta II (AD 380-412) (Chandragupta Vikramaditya): Succeeded Samudra Gupta around AD 375. Some historians suggest Ramagupta ruled between them. In the play Devichandraguptam by Visakhadatta, Ramagupta is the elder brother of Chandragupta II. Chandragupta II saved the family honour by killing a Shaka chief and marrying Dhruvadevi. He used political marriages to strengthen his policy, notably marrying his daughter Prabhavati to Rudrasena II of the Vakatakas. He issued the first Gupta silver coins and adopted the title Vikramaditya and Sakari. The Mehrauli iron pillar inscription mentions a king called Chandra. The Chinese pilgrim Fa-Hein (399-414) visited India during his reign.

Navratnas in Chandragupta II's Court: Kalidas, Amarsimha, Dhanvantri, Varahamihira, Vararuchi (Vartika-a comment on Ashtadhyayi), Ghatakarna, Kshapranak, Velabhatt, and Shanku.

details.summary: Covers the reign of Samudragupta and Chandragupta II, including political policies, religious stance, and the Navratnas.

subject: History
text:
Kumaragupta I: Adopted the title Mahendraditya. Founded Nalanda University. Kalidas flourished during his and Chandragupta II's reign. He was a worshipper of Lord Kartikeya.

Skandagupta (Fall of Gupta Empire): Faced Hunas (fierce nomads of Central Asia) effectively. Weak successors could not check the growing Huna power, leading to the rise of feudatories in Bihar, Bengal, Madhya Pradesh, and Vallabhi.

Administration: Kings were called Parameshwara/Maharajadhiraja/Parambhattaraka. They issued the largest number of gold coins (Dinars) in Ancient India. The most important officer was the Kumaramatyas. The empire was divided into bhukti (provinces) under uparika, and further into vishayas (districts) under vishayapati. Village headmen were important. Lands gifted to brahmanas were known as Agraharas.

Social Development: Castes divided into sub-castes. Untouchability intensified (hatred for Chandalas). Fa-hien noted Chandalas lived outside the village. Varna-Shankar became highlighted.

Religion: Bhagavad Gita written; Buddhism declined. Vishnu temple at Deogarh and brick temple at Bhitargaon belong to this era.

Gupta Art and Crafts: Period referred to as the Golden Age of Ancient India due to unprecedented developments in art, architecture, sculpture, painting, and terracotta. Notable temples include Bhitargaon (Kanpur), Bhitari (Ghazipur), and Deogarh (Jhansi).

details.summary: Covers later Gupta rulers, administrative structure, social conditions, religious shifts, and the artistic achievements of the Golden Age.

subject: History
text:
The rock-cut architecture of the period is represented by the two conventional types - the Chaityas and the Vihara. They are mostly found at Ajanta, Ellora, Bagh and Udaigiri caves of Orissa.

Gupta age marks the beginning of the main style of temples architecture in India namely the Nagara style and Dravida style. The finest example of temple architecture is the Dasavatara temple at Deogarh. It is also an example of early stone temple with a Shikara. It has a square grabhagriha with exquisitely carved doorway. Other examples of temple architecture are Parvati temple at Nachna Kuthara, Shiva temple at Koh, Cave temple at Udaigiri etc.

Literature: Kalidas, the great Sanskrit dramatist, belonged to this period. His books are Abhigyanashakuntalam, Bhagwad Gita, Ritusamhara, Meghadutam, Kumarsambhavam, Malvikagnimitram, Raghuvamsa, Vikramovarshiyam etc.

subject: History
text:
• Aryabhatt the great Mathematician wrote the Aryabhattiya and the Suryasiddhanta. In the Aryabhattiya, he described the place value of the first nine numbers and the use of zero. He also calculated the value of π and invented Algebra. In the Suryasiddhanta, he proved that the Earth revolves around the Sun and rotates on its axis.
  • He discovered the cause of the solar and lunar eclipses and the methods for calculating the timings of their occurrence. He also said that the heavenly bodies, like the Moon, were spherical.
  • Lilavati of Bhaskara is written as standard text of mathematics.
  • Varahamihira wrote the Panchasidhantika and the Brihatsamhita. He said that the Moon moves around the Earth and the Earth, together with the Moon, move round the Sun.
  • Brahmagupta was a great Mathematician. He wrote the Brahma-sphutic Siddhanta in which he hinted at the 'Law of Gravitation.'
  • University of Nalanda was set-up during the rule of Kumaragupta I, who become king in AD 415. This University of Nalanda is called Oxford of Mahayan Buddhism.
  • Palakapya wrote the Hastyagarveda, a treatise on the disease of elephants. Kamandaka's Nitasara was written on the political morality.
  • Court language was Sanskrit. Dhanvantri was a physician famous for Ayurveda knowledge.
formulas: Law of Gravitation (hinted in Brahma-sphutic Siddhanta)

details.summary: Scientific and mathematical advancements during the Gupta period, including contributions by Aryabhatt, Varahamihira, and Brahmagupta.

subject: History
text:
POST GUPTAS: With the decline of the imperial Guptas at the end of 5th or the beginning of 6th century, Magadha and its capital Pataliputra, lost their importance. After the fall of the Guptas, five major centres of power and their centres emerged in North India.

The Age of Smaller Kingdoms: The disintegration of the Gupta empire gradually paved the way for the growth of many smaller kingdoms. The Maukharis started gaining political power towards the end of 5th century and hold over modern Uttar Pradesh and parts of Magadha. From the middle of 6th century till about AD 675 the kings who ruled Magadha were known as Later Guptas.

VARDHAN DYNASTY: Founder of Vardhan dynasty was Pushyabhuti Vardhan.

Harshavardhana (AD 606-647): Harshavardhana was the younger son of Prabhakaravardhana. Hiuen Tsang gave account of his reign, in his book, Si-Yu-Ki. Bana's Harshacharita, inscriptions, coins and Harsha's own writings i.e., Ratnavali, Priyadarshika and Nagananda, are other authentic sources of Harsha's era.

Shashanka, the ruler of Gauda killed Grahavarman (Maukhari ruler) in alliance with Devagupta and imprisoned his wife Rajyasri (Harsha's sister). Later Rajyavardhana killed Devagupta, but he was assassinated by Shashanka in AD 606. The news of the death of Rajyavardhana reached his younger brother Harshavardhana, who now coronated himself in AD 606 and proceeded to avenge his brother's death and release his sister. From this year started the Harsha era.

details.summary: Transition from the Gupta Empire to the Post-Gupta period, the rise of smaller kingdoms, and the history of the Vardhan Dynasty under Harshavardhana.

subject: History
text:
Beginning of the 7th century, the Chalukyas of Badami, the Vakatakas and the Ikshavakus emerged as the three major states in Deccan. While in South India after the fall of Satavahanas, the Pallavas established a powerful kingdom.

  • The kingdom was founded by Vindhyasakti, basically Brahmins. Most important king was Pravarsena-I who performed Ashwamedha Yajnas.
  • Chandragupta II married his daughter Prabhavati to a Vakataka king Rudrasenar-II and with his support succeeded in conquering Gujarat.
  • It is said that the magnificent caves of Ajanta, Vihara caves and Chaitya caves belong to the Vakataka age.

details.summary: Overview of the Vakataka dynasty, its origins, key rulers, and architectural contributions.

subject: History
text:
The Chalukyas grew powerful in Deccan in the middle of the AD 6th century. The dynasty had two branches viz. Vatapi (Badami) and Kalyani.

  • Pulakesin-I was the founder of the Chalukya dynasty, but the most important ruler of the dynasty was Pulakesin-II who ruled from AD 610-642. He sent an ambassador to the Persian king Khusro II. The greatest achievement of Pulakesin II was that, he inflicted a defeat on Harshavardhana.

details.summary: Overview of the Chalukyas of Badami, their branches, and the reign of Pulakesin-II.

subject: History
text: Simha Vishnu was founder of Pallavas dynasty. They set up their capital at Kanchi (identical with modern Kanchipuram). Pallava temples were usually free-standing. But one example of temple cut out of large rocks are the seven ratha temple (seven pagodas) at Mahabalipuram.

details.summary: Overview of the Pallava dynasty, their capital, and architectural style.

subject: History
text: First and famous king of Gangas of Odisha was Ananta Varman (1076-1147) who established his power over the whole territory between the Ganga and the Godavari. He built the famous temple of Lord Jagannath at Puri. Kesari who used to rule Odisha before Gangas, built the famous Lingaraja temple at Bhubhaneswar.

details.summary: Overview of the Gangas of Odisha and their architectural contributions.

subject: History
text:
Founder of Cholas was Vijayalya with Capital-Tanjore. Cholas were feudal of Pallavas. Important king was Rajaraj I. He built Brihadeshwar temple at Tanjore devoted to Shiva. This temple is also known as Rajrajeshwar Temple.

  • His son Rajendra I annexed the whole of Sri Lanka. In the Pala king Mahipala, he took title of Gangaikonda after that. The empire was divided into 6 mandalas or province administered by Governors. Mandalas were further divided into Valanadus, Valanadus into Nadus and Nadus into Taniyars.
  • The Gopuram style of art developed under Cholas. Local self-government was practiced during the reign of Cholas (concept of Panchayati Raj has been borrowed from it).

details.summary: Overview of the Chola dynasty, their administration, and architectural style.

subject: History
text:
The Rashtrakutas rose up against the Chalukyas under Dantidurga. Dantidurga founded this dynasty in AD 753 and made Manyakheta his capital.

  • King Krishna-I further expanded the kingdom, but is best remembered in history as the builder of the rock-cut Kailash temple at Ellora.
  • Rashtrakuta king Amoghavarsha I (814-880 AD) is compared to Vikramaditya in giving patronage to men of letters. He wrote the first Kannada poetry Kaviraj marg and Prashnottar Mallika.
  • The King Krishna-III set-up a pillar of victory and a temple at Rameshvaram.

details.summary: Overview of the Rashtrakuta dynasty, their rulers, and cultural contributions.

subject: History
text:
During AD 7th century, Bhakti Movement started in South India. Two prominent saints came to fore (i) Alvars and (ii) Nayanars.

  • Alvars: These saints were worshipper of Vishnu. They venerated vaishnavism and regard vishnu as supreme. Collection of their hymns are called Divya Prabandha.
  • Nayanars: These saints were bhakti saints who worshipped the Hindu god Shiva. Women’s participation was prominent in Nayanar. Both above bhakti movement started in present day Tamil Nadu.

details.summary: Overview of the origin of the Bhakti Movement in South India.

subject: History
text:
The powerful kingdom arose between AD 750-1000. The Rashtrakutas were ruling Northern Deccan, the Pratiharas in Avanti and parts of Southern Rajasthan and the Palas in Bengal. All three were engaged in a continual tripartite struggle.

The Rajputs:

  • Rajputs came into prominence in 9th and 10th centuries.
  • There is also a body of opinion claiming that some of them were foreign immigrants assimilated into Hindu fold over the centuries. Lastly there were the Agnikulas, the fire family. They were as follow:
    • The Pratiharas or Parihars, not the same as the main Pratiharas but with whom they had connections.
    • The Chahamanas or (Chauhans)
    • The Chalukyas (or Solankis)
    • The Paramaras (or Pawars)

details.summary: Overview of the tripartite struggle in Northern India and the rise of the Rajputs.

subject: History
text:
The Pratiharas (or Gurjara Pratihara)

  • The foundation of one branch of Pratiharas was laid down by Harichandra, a Brahaman near modern Jodhpur in the middle of the AD 6th century. Bhoj was the greatest ruler of this vast empire from Kannauj. He was also known as Adivaraha and Mihira.
  • Mahendrapala is believed to have started his reign about 893. His teacher was Rajashekhara a celebrated poet, dramatist and critic author. Rajashekhara has the literary work like Bal-Bharata, Bal Ramayan Bhuvanosh, Harvilas, Karpuramanjari, Kavya Mimansa, Prapanch Pandav, Vidhsaal etc.

The Chandellas

  • The Chandellas became rulers in Southern Bundelkhand under Nannuka early in the 9th century.
  • They had their capital at Kharjuravahaka (modern Khajuraho).
  • They were a patron of learning and fine arts and built Kandariya Mahadeva temple at Khajuraho in AD 1000.

Chauhan

  • Ruled over Shakambri (modern Sambhar-Rajasthan). Founder of Chauhan was Semharaja. Important king was Prithviraj Chauhan.
  • First Battle of Tarain, 1191 Prithviraj Chauhan defeated Mohammad Ghori. Second Battle of Tarain, 1192 Mohammad Ghori defeated Prithviraj Chauhan.
  • His court Poet was Chandbardai who composed Prithviraj Raso.

Gahadavals

  • They ruled over Kannauj. Important king was Jai Chand, he was defeated by Mohammad Ghori in 1194 in Battle of Chandawar.

The Chalukayas (Anhilwara)

  • The Chalukayas or Solankis were rulers of Gujarat and Kathiawar for about three and a half centuries.
  • Important ruler—Pulakesin II, Aihole inscription is associated with him, composed by his court poet Ravikirti.

The Paramaras

  • The dynasty was founded by Upendra or Krishnaraja. The main branch of the Paramaras comprised descendants of the Rashtrakutas who ruled Malwa.
  • Bhoja (1910-1055) is the best king of the Paramara rulers, also called as Kaviraj. He wrote the Samaraganasutradhar (a rare work on architecture) and the Ayurvedasaravasva (work on medicine).

Kingdoms in Bengal

The Palas of Bengal

  • In the middle of the AD 8th century, the Pala dynasty came into power. Its founder was Gopal (AD 750) who was elected to the throne as he had proved his valour and capability as a leader.
  • He was a Buddhist. He was succeeded by Dharmapala (AD 770-810) who won Kannauj.
  • Dharmapala was succeeded by Devapala who won Orissa and Assam and was followed by Mahipala I. Mahipala I attacked and defeated by Rajendra Chola.
  • Suleiman (an Arab merchant) visited them and was impressed. The Palas were patrons of Buddhism. Dharmapala founded the University of Vikramashila and revived Nalanda University.

The Senas

  • After the Palas, the Senas established an empire in Bengal. The earliest member of the Sena dynasty was Samanta Sena.
  • The greatest ruler of this dynasty was his grandson Vijayasena. Vijayasena was a devotee of Shiva. The muslim ruler Muhammad Bakhtyar Khilji attacked its capital Nadia and captured it.

Kingdoms in Kashmir

Karkota Dynasty

  • The Karkota dynasty was founded by Durlabh Vardhan in 7th century. Lalitaditya Muktapid was the most important ruler of this dynasty. He constructed the Martand temple in Kashmir.

Lohar Dynasty

  • Sangramraj was the founder of Lohar dynasty. Kalhan was the court poet of Harsha, Lohar king. He wrote 'Rajtarangiri' which contains the history of Kashmir.

details.summary: Overview of various regional dynasties in Medieval India including Pratiharas, Chandellas, Chauhans, Gahadavals, Chalukayas, Paramaras, Palas, Senas, and Kashmiri dynasties.

subject: History
text: In the early history of the far South in India, three tribal principalities are mentioned in Ashokan inscriptions of the 3rd century BC and in Kharavela inscription of the 1st century BC: Cholas, Pandyas and Cheras.

details.summary: Note on early South Indian tribal principalities.

subject: History
text:
As Harshvardhana and Pulakesin II were struggling for supremacy in India, a revolutionary change was taking place, i.e. the emergence of Islam in Arabia.

  • The Arabs, for long the carriers of Indian trade with Europe, were attracted by rich sea-ports of Sind. However, two expeditions sent by Al-Hajjaj the Governor of Iraq failed.
  • The third expedition under his nephew and son-in-law Mohammed-bin-Qasim, managed to acquire control over Sind in AD 712. Multan was conquered in AD 713.

details.summary: Overview of the Arab conquest of Sind during the 8th century.

subject: History
text:
• Mahmud came to the throne of Ghazni in AD 997. He moved towards India in AD 1001 by attacking and killing Jaipala, the King of Punjab in the First Battle of Waihind. The first attack was made against frontier post and many forts and districts were captured.
  • The sixth expedition (the Second Battle of Waihind) was against Anandapala (Hindu shahi ruler of Punjab) in AD 1008. The expedition in AD 1009 was against Nagarkot in the Kangra hills.
  • Ghazni led 17 expeditions between AD 1001 and AD 1027. He plundered Thaneshwar, Mathura, Kannauj and Somnath. The temple of Somnath dedicated to Shiva was plundered in 1025 situated on the sea coast of Kathiawar (Gujarat).
  • Utbi regarded as a great literary figure at that time, he was Mahmud's court historian. His Kitab-ul-Yamini or Tarikh-I-Yamini is a book on Mahmud's life and times.
  • Firdausi (Persian poet) known as the immortal Homer of the East wrote the Shahanama, Al Beruni a brilliant scholar from Central Asia wrote Tahqiq-i-hind. Farukhi was also court poet of Ghazni.

details.summary: Details regarding the 17 expeditions of Mahmud of Ghazni and his court scholars.

subject: History
text:
• Muizzuddin Mohammed-bin-Sam (known as Mohammed Ghori), the last Turkish conqueror of North India, had no son.
  • The King of Delhi Prithviraj Chauhan completely routed the Ghori's forces in AD 1191 at Tarain (First Battle of Tarain). But Prithviraj was defeated in the Second Battle of Tarain (AD 1192), Delhi and Ajmer were captured by Mohammed Ghori.
  • Fall of Delhi and Ajmer laid the foundation of Muslim Rule in India. Ghori also defeated Jaichand (Ruler of Kannauj) at Battle of Chandawar in 1194. Bakhtiyar Khilji, his general, annexed East India and destroyed Nalanda and Vikramshila University. Ghori died in 1206, leaving Qutub-ud-din Aibak in-charge.
  • Sufi Saint Khawaja Moin-ud-din Chisti came with him from Afghanistan. Tomb of Moin-ud-din Chisti is in Ajmer also known as Ajmer Sharif. He founded Chisti Silsila.

details.summary: Key battles and events involving Mohammed Ghori and the establishment of Muslim rule.

subject: History
text:
Qutub-ud-din Aibak was Turkish slave by origin. He was purchased by Mohammad Ghori who later made him his Governor. After the death of Ghori, Aibak became the master of Hindustan and founded the slave dynasty in 1206. The Delhi Sultanate (AD 1206-1526) had five ruling dynasties:

  1. The Ilbari (Slave)
  2. The Khilji
  3. The Tughlaq
  4. The Sayyid
  5. Lodhis

Of these five dynasties the first three were of Turkish origin and the Lodhis were Afghans.

details.summary: Introduction to the Delhi Sultanate and its five dynasties.

subject: History
text:
• The first dynasty of the Sultanate has been designated by various scholars as the Slave dynasty or the Mamluk dynasty or the Ilbari dynasty.
  • He was the founder of the Sultanate of Delhi. Qutub-ud-din Aibak was the first Muslim King of India. He began his reign with the modest little Malik and Sipahsalar, which had been conferred upon him by Mohammed Ghori. Lahore and later Delhi were his capitals.
  • He was famous for his generosity and earned the sobriquet of lakh-baksh (giver of lakhs).
  • He laid the foundation of Qutub Minar in Delhi after the name of the famous Sufi Saint Khwaja Qutub-ud-din Bakhtiyar Khilji. Aibak constructed the first mosque in India Quwat-ul-Islam (Delhi) and Adhai Din Ka Jhopara (At Ajmer).
  • Hasan Nizami and Fakhr-ud-din (whom Aibak patronised) were all praised for the qualities of head and heart of Aibak and sense of justice in their works Taj-ul Massir and Tarikhi Mubarik Shahi respectively.
  • His task was only half done, when he died of a sudden fall from a horse at Lahore in 1210 while playing Chaugan (Polo).

details.summary: Biography and achievements of Qutub-ud-din Aibak.

subject: History
text:
• Real founder of the Delhi Sultanate.
  • Made Delhi the capital.
  • Suppressed revolts of ambitious nobles and fought sons of Aibak.
  • Sent expeditions against Rajputs in Ranthambore, Jalor, and Mewar.
  • Governing class consisted of Turkish slave officers and Tazik.
  • Introduced silver coin (tanka) and copper coin (jital).
  • Organised the Iqta system and introduced reforms in civil administration and army.
  • Set up official nobility of slaves known as Turkan-i-Chalgani or Chalisa (group of forty powerful Turkish nobles).
  • On 18th February, 1229, the Khalifa sent emissaries from Baghdad with a decree registering the independent status of the Delhi Sultanate.
  • Called the father of Tomb building (built Sultan Garhi).
  • Completed Qutub Minar.
  • Saved Delhi Sultanate from Chengiz Khan by refusing shelter to Khwarizm Shah.

details.summary: Overview of Iltutmish's reign, administrative reforms, and military achievements.

subject: History
text:
• First and last Muslim woman ruler of medieval India.
  • First rebellion raised by Kabir Khan, Governor of Lahore.
  • Altunia, Governor of Bhatinda, revolted; Razia was defeated and taken prisoner, then married him.
  • Defeated by Bahram Shah (son of Iltutmish) while moving towards Delhi; deserted by soldiers and murdered by robbers.
  • Succession: Bahram Shah (1240-1242), Ala-ud-din Masud Shah (1242-1246), Nasir-ud-din Mahmud (1246-1266).
  • Nasir-ud-din was the grandson of Iltutmish.

details.summary: Life and reign of Razia Sultan and the subsequent succession of rulers.

subject: History
text:
• Ascended throne in 1266-67.
  • Separated military from Finance Department (Diwan-i-Wizarat) and placed it under a Minister for Military Affairs (Diwan-i-Ariz).
  • Impressed upon people that kingship was the vice regency of God on Earth (Niyabat-i-Khudai).
  • King was the shadow of God (Zil-i-Ilahi).
  • Abandoned the Chalisa.
  • Introduced Sijdah or Paibos and started Nauroz festival.
  • Took measures to safeguard North-West frontier against Mongol invasions.
  • His son Mohammed's death was a blow to his dynasty.
  • Last ruler of dynasty was Kaiqubad, killed by Jalal-ud-din Khilji.

details.summary: Balban's administrative policies, theory of kingship, and the end of his dynasty.

subject: History
text:
• Khilji Revolution: Marked the end of monopolisation of power by the Turkish nobility and racial dictatorship.
  • Jalal-ud-din Firoz Khilji: Came to throne at 70. Married his daughter to Mongol leader Ulugh Khan. Famous event: Invasion of Devagiri by Ala-ud-din.
  • Ala-ud-din Khilji: Conquered Gujarat (Vaghela King Karna). In 1299, army under Ulugh Khan and Nusrat Khan invaded Anhilwad. Commander Nusrat Khan acquired Hindu turned Muslim slave Kafur (Hazar Dinari). Conquered Ranthambore (1300-1301) and Chittor (1303) from Gahlot King Ratan Singh (Padmini committed Jauhar).

details.summary: Rise of the Khilji dynasty and key military conquests of Jalal-ud-din and Ala-ud-din.

subject: History
text:
Market Reforms: Established four separate markets in Delhi under Shahna-i-Mandi. Created Diwani Riyasat department and appointed Munhiyas (secret agents) to monitor market conditions.

  • Land Revenue: Introduced land measurement and cash revenue collection. Introduced dagh system (branding of horses) and huliya (list of soldiers).
  • Architecture: Built Hauz Khas, Mahal Hazar Satoon, Jamait Khana Mosque, Alai Darwaza, and Siri Fort. Adopted title Sikandar-i-Sani.
  • Culture: Patronised Amir Khusrau (Tuti-i-Hind).

details.summary: Overview of Ala-ud-din Khilji's administrative, military, and architectural contributions.

subject: History
text:
The Tughlaqs were a Muslim family of Turkish origin. Key rulers: Ghiyas-ud-din, Mohammed-bin-Tughlaq, and Firoz Shah Tughlaq.

Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq

  • Founded the third dynasty (real name Ghazi Malik).
  • Discarded Ala-ud-din's land measurement system.
  • Focused on canal construction and famine relief.
  • Built Tughlaqabad; conflicted with Sufi Saint Nizam-ud-din Auliya.

details.summary: Introduction to the Tughlaq dynasty and Ghiyas-ud-din Tughlaq's reign.

subject: History
text:
Real name Jauna Khan. Known for ambitious projects:

  • Capital Shift: Moved from Delhi to Devagiri (Daulatabad) in 1327, then back to Delhi.
  • Token Currency: Introduced bronze tankas (1329-30) to replace silver. Failed due to large-scale counterfeiting.
  • Military: Abandoned expeditions to Khurasan and Iraq.
  • Other: Ibn Battuta visited in 1334. Vijayanagara (1336) and Bahamani (1346) kingdoms were established during his period.

details.summary: Key events and administrative experiments of Mohammed-bin-Tughlaq.

subject: History
text:
Patron of arts and literature. Banned inhumane punishments.

Tax Reforms

Abolished 23 taxes, replaced with four:

  • Kharaj: 1/10 of land produce.
  • Jaziya: Tax on non-Muslims.
  • Zakat: 2.5% property tax.
  • Khams: 1/5 of war booty.

Other Reforms: Made posts hereditary. Built cities like Hissar, Fatehabad, Jaunpur, Firozabad, and Firoz Shah Kotla. Established Diwan-i-Bandagan (slaves) and Diwan-i-Khairat (charity). Built Dar-ul-Shafa (hospital).

details.summary: Administrative, social, and architectural reforms of Firoz Shah Tughlaq.

subject: History
text:
The Sayyids: Khizr Khan, the founder of the Sayyid dynasty, collaborated with Timur and was given the governorship of Lahore and Multan. His successors—Mubarak Shah (1421-33), Mohammed Shah (1434-43), and Ala-ud-din Alam Shah (1443-51)—were incapable rulers. During the 27 years of the Sayyid dynasty, the sultanate remained in trouble due to external invasions and internal intrigue. Yahya-bin-Ahmed-bin-Abdullah Sirhindi wrote the Tarikh-i-Mubarakshahi.

The Lodhis: The Lodhis were Afghans who ruled for 75 years. Bahlol Lodhi founded the dynasty and introduced coins called Sardar Masnad-i-Ali. Sikandar Lodhi was the ablest ruler; he set up an efficient coinage system, military spy network, and auditing of accounts. He repaired Qutub Minar, introduced the Gaz-i-Sikandari for measuring cultivated fields, wrote Persian verses under the name Gul-rukhi, founded Agra in 1504, and reimposed Jaziya.

Ibrahim Lodhi: Defeated and killed by Babur in the first Battle of Panipat (1526), ending the sultanate period.

details.summary: Overview of the Sayyid and Lodi dynasties, including key rulers, administrative reforms, and literary works.

subject: History
text:
The administration was divided into iqtas. The head of civil administration was the Wazir (finance). He was assisted by a deputy or Naib Wazir, an Accountant General (Mushrif-i-mumalik), and an Auditor General (Maustauji-i-mumalik). The chief justice was Qazi-i-mumalik. The officer-in-charge of royal correspondence was Ariz-i-mumalik (also responsible for military recruitment and inspection). Barid-i-Mumaliks were in charge of the royal post and news agency. Provinces were divided into shiqs (headed by munsifs). The iqta system provided land to soldiers, officers, and nobles.

Important Departments:

  • Diwan-i-Insha: Department of correspondence
  • Diwan-i-Ariz: Military department
  • Diwan-i-Risalat: Department of appeals
  • Diwan-i-Qaza-i-Mumalik: Department of Justice
  • Diwan-i-Ishtikak: Department of pensions

details.summary: Administrative structure and key departments of the Delhi Sultanate.

subject: History
text:
• Founded by Harihara I and Bukka I (Sons of Sangama), who were feudatories of Kakatiyas and later ministers in the court of Kampili.
  • Harihara and Bukka were brought to Delhi by Mohammed-bin-Tughlaq, converted to Islam, and sent back to the South to control rebellion.
  • Founded the Vijayanagara Empire in 1336 on the advice of Vidyaranya, who converted them back to Hindu.
  • Rulers believed in divinity and ruled by the will of God Virupaksha.
  • Colonel Colin Mackenzie brought Hampi into light in the AD 19th century.

details.summary: Founding and early religious context of the Vijayanagara Empire.

subject: History
text:
Harihara I

Made Anagundi his capital. Annexed the Hoyasala State in AD 1364 after defeating and killing Vir Ballal III.

Bukka I

Made Gutti his capital. War with Bahmanis started in AD 1367. His son Kumara Kampan annexed Madurai (mentioned in Madura Vijayam by Ganga Devi).

Harihara II

Embarked on a policy of expansion towards the Eastern sea coast, leading to fresh conflicts.

details.summary: Key rulers and military expansions of the Sangama Dynasty.

subject: History
text:
Deva Raya I

  • Assumed the title of Maharajadhiraja.
  • Defeated by Bahmani ruler Firoz Shah; paid indemnity and married his daughter to the Sultan.
  • Constructed a dam across the Tungabhadra for agriculture.
  • Visited by Nicolo De Conti (Italian), who described the city's circumference as 96 km and 90000 potential soldiers.

Deva Raya II

  • Greatest ruler of the Sangama dynasty.
  • Inducted Muslims into his army to teach archery.
  • Crossed the Tungabhadra to recover Mudkal and Bankapur.
  • Called Immadi Devaraya or Gajabetakara (the elephant hunter).
