details.summary: Reign details of Deva Raya I and II and a list of foreign travellers.

subject: History
text:
Deva Raya II: A great patron of literature and an accomplished scholar in Sanskrit. Credited with the authorship of two Sanskrit works: Mahanataka Sudhanidhi and a commentary on the Brahma Sutras of Badarayana. He showed tolerance in religious views, appointing people of different religions as ministers and constructing a mosque in Vijayanagara.

The Saluva Dynasty

Vijayanagara witnessed chaos after 1465. The situation was saved by the Governor of Chandragiri, Narasimha Saluva, who seized the throne in 1485 (First Usurpation). He was succeeded by his minors, Timma and Imadi Narasimha, with Narsa Nayak as the Reagent.

The Tuluva Dynasty

Founded by Vira Narasimha in 1505 after deposing Imadi Narasimha (Second Usurpation). Krishnadeva Raya (1509-1529) is considered the greatest ruler of the Tuluva Dynasty.

Krishnadeva Raya

  • Maintained friendly relations with Albuquerque (Portuguese Governor).
  • Gave permission to build a Fort at Bhatkal.
  • Built the Vijaya Mahal (House of Victory), expanded the Hazara Rama temple and Vithal Swami temple.
  • Took the title Yavanaraja Sthapanacharya (restorer of the Yavana kingdom).
  • Known as Andhra Pitamaha and Andhra Bhoja.
  • Authored the Telugu work on polity Amuktamalyada and the Sanskrit drama Jambavati Kalyanam.

Krishnadeva Raya's Ashtadiggajas (The eight celebrated poets)

  • Peddana: Manucharitam and Harikathasaramu.
  • Timma: Parijatapahara-vam.
  • Madaya: Raja Shekarcharitam.
  • Dhurjate: Kalahasti Mahatyam.
  • Surona: Raghav Pandaviyam and Prabhavati Pradyuman.
  • Tenali Ramalingam: Ponduranga Mahatyam.
  • Ayyalaraju Ramabhadra: Sakalamata sara Sangraha.
  • Rama Raja Bhushan: The eighth poet.

After Krishnadeva Raya, Achyuta Rai and Sadasiva Raya ruled until 1570.

The Aravidu Dynasty

Founded by Thirumala II. He shifted the capital to Penugonda. During his rule, the Nayaks became independent, and he divided his empire into three linguistic sections for his sons.

details.summary: Overview of the later Vijayanagara dynasties (Saluva, Tuluva, Aravidu) and the reign of Krishnadeva Raya.

subject: History
text:
Bahamani Kingdom

Founded by Hasan Gangu (original name Ismail Mukh). Capital was Gulbarga. He took the title Ala-ud-din Hasan Bahaman Shah (AD 1347-58). He renamed Gulbarga as Ahsanabad. At his death, the dominion had four provinces: Gulbarga, Daulatabad, Berar, and Bidar.

  • Mahmud Shah I (1358-75): Son of Bahaman Shah, established a council of eight ministers.
  • Firoz Shah (1397-1422): Remarkable figure, made Deccan a cultural centre. Inducted Hindus into administration. Built an observatory at Daulatabad and the city of Firozabad on the bank of river Bhima. Defeated Devaraya I.
  • Ahmed Shah I (1422-36): Brother of Firoz Shah, shifted capital to Bidar. Known as Wali or saint due to association with Gesu Daraz.
  • Later Rulers: Humayun, Nizam Shah (1461-63), and Mohammed Shah III (1463-82).
  • Mahmud Gawan: Prime Minister under Mohammed Shah III. Under his guidance, the kingdom saw a resurgence. His military conquests included Konkan, Goa, and the Krishna-Godavari Delta. Nikitin, a Russian merchant, visited Bidar during his reign.

details.summary: History of the Bahamani Kingdom from its foundation by Hasan Gangu to the era of Mahmud Gawan.

subject: History
text:
Regional Kingdoms

  • Adilshahi of Bijapur (1490-1686): Founded by Yusuf Adil Shah. Ibrahim Adil Shah was the greatest ruler. Introduced 'Dakhini' in place of Persian. Mohammed Adil Shah built the Gol Gumbaz. Annexed by Aurangzeb.
  • Imad Shahis of Berar (1490-1574): Founded by Fatehullah Khan II Mad-ul-Mulk with Daulatabad as capital. Annexed by Nizam Shahi rulers of Ahmednagar.
  • Qutub Shahis of Golconda (1518-1687): Founded by Quli Qutub Shah. Built Golconda fort. Mohammed Quli Qutub Shah was the greatest ruler; founded Hyderabad and Charminar. Masulipatnam was the most important port. Annexed by Aurangzeb (1687).
  • Barid Shahis of Bidar (1528-1619): Founded by Ali Barid. Annexed by Adil Shahis of Bijapur.

details.summary: Overview of regional kingdoms in the Deccan and their annexation history.

subject: History
text:
The Sufis

  • Sufism is a mystical Islamic belief seeking divine love and knowledge through direct experience of God.
  • Appealed to both Muslims and Hindus in India.
  • Ziyarat: Pilgrimage to sites associated with Sufi saints.
  • Khanqah: The abode of a Sufi.
  • Divided into 14 silsilas by the 13th century.

The Chistis

  • Founder: Khwaza Abu-e-Chisti. Popularised in India by Moin-ud-din Chisti (tomb in Ajmer).
  • Khwaza Qutub-ud-din Bakhtiyar Kaki: Main disciple of Moin-ud-din; Qutub Minar is named after him.
  • Nizam-ud-din Auliya: Saw the reign of seven Delhi Sultans. Known as Mahboob-i-Ilahi (beloved of God) and Sultan-ul-Auliya (king of the saints). Tomb in Delhi.
  • Sheikh Nasir-ud-din (Chirag-i-Delhi): Disciple of Mahboob-i-Illahi.
  • Amir Khusrau and Al-Biruni were followers of Chisti.

Qadiri

  • Founder: Sheikh Mohi-ud-din Qadir Zilani.
  • Popularised by Shah Nizamat Ullah and Makhdum Zilani Dara Shikoh (son of Shah Jahan).
  • Dara Shikoh: Wrote Safinat-ul-Auliya, Sakinat-ul-Auliya. Translated Sir-e-Akbar and Sir-e-Asrar.

Naqshabandi

  • Founder: Khwaza Baha-ud-din Naqshabandi. Popularised by Khwaza Khwand Mahmud.
  • Other saints: Baqi-Billah, Shahwali ullah, Khwaza Mir Dard (wrote Dard-e-Dil, Sham-e-Mahfil, Ilm-ul-Khitab).

details.summary: Detailed breakdown of Sufi orders (Silsilas) including Chisti, Qadiri, and Naqshabandi.

subject: History
text:
Bhakti Movement

  • Devotional worship of God to attain Moksha or Salvation.
  • Started in South India (Alvar and Nayanar) and spread to North India in the 13th century.
  • Opposed casteism, ritualism, and religious sacrifices. Promoted equal participation of women.
  • Branches: i. Nirguna, ii. Saguna.

Nirguna Saints

  • Guru Nanak: Born in Talwandi (Lahore). Propagated Monotheism and Hindu-Muslim unity. Denounced idol worship. Teachings in Guru Granth Sahib.
  • Dadu Dayal: Born in Ahmedabad. Founded Brahma sect or Param Brahma Sampradaya.
  • Kabir: Opposed caste, creed, and idol worship. Promoted Hindu-Muslim unity. Works: Sabada Doha, Holi, Rekhtal. Included in Adi Granth.

details.summary: Core principles of the Bhakti movement and key Nirguna saints.

subject: History
text:
Tulsidas: Contemporary to Akbar. Works- Ramcharitamanas, Gitawali, Parvati Mangal, Janki Mangal, Vinay Patrika etc.

Ramananda: Propagated Bhakti in North India. Organised a group of cadres called Bairagi.

Surdas: He was disciple of Vallabhacharya. He was a blind poet from Agra. He sang the glory of Krishna in his Sursagar.

Gorakhnath: Founder of Nath Hindu monastic movement in India. His followers are mostly found in Himalayan states. Followers are called yogis.

Mirabai: Rathor princess of Merta and daughter-in-law of Rana Sanga of Mewar (husband-Bhoja Raja). She wrote the verse Padavali. She believed in Krishna.

Chaitanya: He was known as Gaudiya Mahaprabhu. He was founder of Gaurang or Bengal Vaishnavism. His teacher was Ishwapuri.

Shankara Deva: He established EK Sharan Sampradaya or Mahapurushiya Sampradaya. He divided universe into two parts Aswatantra and Swatantra.

Chaitanya Mahaprabhu: He was also a great saint. There had been Vaishnavism in Bengal long before his birth, but Chaitanya accepted that Krishna alone is the most perfect God. 'Kirtan' system was given by Chaitanya.

details.summary: Overview of prominent Saguna Bhakti saints and their contributions.

subject: History
text:
Namdev: By profession he was a tailor. Earlier he believed in Saguna stream, but later on diverted towards Nirguna branch. He was poet saint of Maharashtra. Earlier he was influenced by Vaishnavism. He worshipped Vithoba. He formed a varkari sect of Hinduism.

Tukaram: Tukaram was contemporary of Shivaji. He was part of varkari devotionalism tradition, he is also known for Abhanga devotional poetry. His poetry was devoted to vithoba (avatar of Vishnu).

Ramdas: A noted spiritual poet of Maharashtra. He is famous for his Advaita vedantist text and Dashbodh. He was spiritual guru of Shivaji.

Eknath: He was famous religious Marathi poet of Varkari Sampradaya. He wrote Bhavarth Ramayan and a variant of Bhagvata Purana.

Taneshwara: He was 13th century Marathi saint, poet, philosopher and yogi. He wrote Dnyaneshwari (commentary on Gita) and Amrutobhava. His works are considered gem of Marathi language.

details.summary: Overview of Bhakti saints from the Maharashtra region.

subject: History
text:
Shankaracharya: He was born at Kalodi, Kerala. He taught concepts of Maya (illusion), Advaita and importance of Vedanta. He established four Mathas at Badrinath, Puri, Sringeri and Dwarka. He wrote commentaries on Upanishads, Bhagwad Gita and Brahmasutras of Badrayana. He is also known as Pseudo-Buddhist as many of his doctrines were similar to that of Buddhist doctrines.

Abhinava Gupta: He was a philosopher, mystic and aesthetican from Kashmir. His most famous work is Tantraloka, a treatise on all philosophical and practical aspects of Kashmir Shaivism.

Ramanuja Acharya: He was Tamil Vaishnavite saint. He gave philosophy of Visist-advait. Wrote Vedanta Samgraha, commentaries on Brahmasutras and Bhagwad Gita.

Madhavacharya: He was Kannada Vaishnavite saint. He gave philosophy of Dvaita.

Nimbarka: Telugu Vaishnavite saint, contemporary of Ramayana. Concept of Dvaitadvaita was promoted by him.

Vallabhacharya: He was a Telugu Vaishnavite saint. He was born at Varanasi in 1479 and went to Vrindavan, where he resided permanently. He established the philosophy of Shuddhadvaita. Vallabhacharya's teachings are also known as Pushtimarga. He was the contemporary of Vijayanagara King Krishna Deva Raya.

Raghunandan: He belonged to Nabadwip (Nadia) in Bengal. He was considered to be the most influential writer in the Dharamashastras.

details.summary: Biographical details of major Indian philosophers and Bhakti saints.

subject: History
topic: The Sikh Gurus and Their Contribution
text: Overview of the ten Sikh Gurus and their historical contributions.
tables:
| Guru | Contribution |
|---|---|
| Guru Nanak (1469-1539) | First Guru of Sikhs, Founder of Sikhism. |
| Guru Angad (1504-1552) | Compiled the biography of Guru Nanak Dev, known as Janam Sakhi introduced Gurumukhi Script; 63 hymns of Guru Angad Dev included in Guru Granth Sahib. |
| Guru Amar Das (1479-1574) | He promoted inter-caste dining at his kitchen. Akbar granted villages to finance the scheme, out of which grew Amritsar. |
| Guru Ram Das (1534-1551) | Son-in-law of Guru Amar Das. |
| Guru Arjun Dev (1563-1606) | Son of Guru Ram Das died after torture in Mughal (Jahangir) detention for sheltering rebellious Mughal prince Khusrau. |
| Guru Hargobind (1595-1644) | Son of Guru Arjun Dev, put on two words-one signifying Miri (secular power) and other Piri (spiritual power), Built the Akal Takht in 1608. |
| Guru Har Rai (1630-1661) | Son of Guru Hargobind supported Dara's claim in the wars of succession between Shah Jahan's sons. |
| Guru Harikishan (1656-1664) | Son of Guru Har Rai, Gurudwara Bangla Sahib in New Delhi, was constructed in his memory. |
| Guru Tegh Bahadur (1621-1675) | Son of Guru Hargobind, Gurudwara Rakab Ganj Sahib in New Delhi, is where Guru's body was cremated. He was executed on Mughal orders. |
| Guru Govind Singh (1666-1700) | Son of Guru Tegh Bahadur, tenth and the last sikh guru. Guru Granth Sahib was finally completed. |

details.summary: Chronological table of Sikh Gurus and their key contributions.

subject: History
text:
The Mughal empire was founded by Zahir-ud-din Muhammad Babur, a Turk. In 1523, he was invited by Daulat Khan Lodhi (Governor of Punjab) and Alam Khan (uncle of Sultan Ibrahim Lodhi) to invade India.

  • First Battle of Panipat (1526): Defeated Ibrahim Lodhi. Babur introduced gunpowder and artillery to India.
  • Battle of Khanwa (1527): Defeated Rana Sangram Singh of Mewar.
  • Battle of Chanderi (1528): Defeated Rajput Chief Medini Rai.
  • Battle of Ghaghra (1529): Defeated the Afghan Chief under Mahmud Lodhi.
  • Death: Tomb of Babur is situated in Kabul.

details.summary: Foundation of the Mughal Empire by Babur and his major military campaigns.

subject: History
text:
Babur's eldest son, Humayun, inherited the empire and divided it among his brothers: Kamran, Hindal, and Askari.

  • Capital: Built Dinpanah at Delhi as his second capital.
  • Conflicts: Attacked by Sher Shah at Chausa (1539) and defeated. Defeated again at the Battle of Kannauj (1540).
  • Exile and Return: After 15 years of wandering, regained his kingdom in 1555 by defeating Sikander Shah with Bairam Khan's help.
  • Death: Died in 1556 after an accidental fall from the stairs of his library, Sher Mandal, Delhi.
  • Literature: Humayunnama, written by his half-sister Gulbadan Begum, chronicles his life.

details.summary: Reign of Humayun, his struggles with Sher Shah, and his eventual return to power.

subject: History
text:
Akbar (1556-1605) was the son of Humayun and Hamida Banu. Born in 1542 at Amarkot.

  • Accession: Coronated at Kalanaur at age 13 under Bairam Khan's guardianship.
  • Second Battle of Panipat (1556): Defeated Hemu.
  • Administration: Introduced the Mansabdari system (rank/position of government officials).
  • Reforms: Abolished pilgrim tax (1564) and Jaziya. Implemented Zabti (land revenue system) under Todar Mal.
  • Religion: Formulated Din-i-Ilahi (Divine Monotheism) in 1582.
  • Literature: Abul Fazal wrote Ain-i-Akbari.
  • Navratna: Birbal, Todar Mal, Abul Fazal, Tansen, Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khana, Mullado Pyaja, Hakim Hukkam, Faizi, Maan Singh.
  • Other: Built Buland Darwaza in 1601 at Fatehpur Sikri.
tables:
| Year | Territory | Specific |
|---|---|---|
| 1561 | Malwa | The ruler of Malwa was Baz Bahadur. |
| 1564 | Garhkatanga (Gondwana) | Rani Durgawati and her minor son, Bir Narayan, died fighting Mughals. The Mughal army was led by Asaf Khan. |
| 1567 | Chittor | The storming of the fortress of Chittor was one of the most famous military feats of Akbar. Rana Udai Singh was its ruler. |
| 1572-73 | Gujarat | Akbar built the famous Buland Darwaza at Fatehpur Sikri in commemoration of this victory. |
| 1574-76 | Bihar and Bengal | Akbar personally marched against Bihar and drove out Daud from Patna and Hajipur. |
| 1576 | Battle of Haldighati | Rana Pratap, the son of Udai Singh of Mewar, was severely defeated by the Mughal army under Maan Singh and Asaf Khan. |
| 1581 | Kabul | Mirza Hakim was defeated. |
| 1586 | Kashmir and Baluchistan | - |
| 1591 | Sindh | - |
| 1592 | Orissa | The Mughal army was led by Maan Singh. |
| 1595 | Qandhar | The Mughal army in this battle was commanded by Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khanan. |
| 1601 | Asirgarh | The capture of Asirgarh marked the climax of Akbar's career of conquest. |

details.summary: Comprehensive overview of Akbar's reign, administrative reforms, and military conquests.

subject: History
text:
• Akbar’s eldest son Salim assumed the title ‘Nur-ud-din Mohammed Jahangir’ and ascended the throne. He mostly lived in Lahore, which he adorned with gardens and buildings. A few months after his accession, his eldest son Khusrau revolted against him.
  • Jahangir’s first political success was against the Mewar Rana Amar Singh (1615). In 1620, Prince Khurram conquered Kangra. Jahangir followed the policy of his father with regard to the Deccan.
  • In 1617, Ahmednagar fell and Khurram was rewarded with the title ‘Shah-Jahan’. Jahangir married Mehr-u-nisa, whom he gave the title ‘Nur-Jahan’.
  • Nur-Jahan was a politically shrewd and ambitious woman who dominated the royal household especially when Jahangir fell ill. She had great influence on Jahangir’s life as she had the status of Pad Shah Begum, coins were struck in her name and on all farmans her name was attached to the imperial signature.
  • Nur Jahan’s influence secured high positions for her father I’timad-ud-Daulah and for her brother Asaf Khan. She married Asaf’s daughter Mumtaz Mahal to Khurram.
  • Problem arose, when Nur Jahan married her daughter Sher Afghani to Jahangir’s youngest son, Shaharyar. Now, Nur Jahan supported him for the heir-apparent.
  • The Mughal court was divided into Pro-Nur Jahan and Anti-Nur Jahan. These events hampered the military operation for the recovery of Kandahar.
  • Captain Hawkins (1608-11) and Sir Thomas Roe (1615-19) visited his court to gain favourable concessions for English trade with India. As a result of the efforts of Thomas Roe, English factories were established at Surat, Agra, Ahmedabad and Broach.
  • Many foreign travellers visited India during the reign of Shah Jahan. Two Frenchman Bernier and Travenier and an Italian adventurer Manucci, the author of the Storio Dor Magor are specially noteworthy.

details.summary: Overview of Jahangir's reign, the influence of Nur Jahan, and early English trade relations.

subject: History
text:
• Shah Jahan, the third son of Jahangir, ascended the throne in AD 1628 and married Mumtaz in 1612.
  • He was an able general and administrator. In the first year of his reign Shah Jahan had to overcome the revolts of the Bundela chief, Juzhar Singh and the Afghan noble named Khan Jahan Lodhi an ex-viceroy of the Deccan.
  • Shah Jahan’s reign of 30 years is regarded as the Golden age of Mughal in art and architecture during which monument like the famous Taj Mahal at Agra in the memory of his wife Mumtaz, the Red fort at Delhi with its Diwan-i-Khas and Diwan-i-Aam, the Jama Masjid and the famous Jewel-studded peacock throne were built among other numerous pieces of architecture.
  • At the time of Shah Jahan’s sickness in 1657 his eldest son was in Agra, Shuja was Governor in Bengal, Aurangzeb was viceroy in the Deccan and the youngest Murad was Governor in Gujarat.
  • Aurangzeb took control of the fort and crowned himself at Delhi, after defeating his brothers. Shah Jahan was kept in strict confinement at Agra fort till his death in 1666.

details.summary: Details on Shah Jahan's reign, architectural achievements, and the war of succession.

subject: History
text:
• Aurangzeb ascended the throne with the title of Alamgir (conqueror of the world) and ruled for almost 50 years.
  • During his reign the Mughal empire reached territorial climax. He first defeated the Imperial army at Dharmatt and then defeated a force led by Dara in the Battle of Samugarh.
  • He ordered the arrest and later executed the ninth Sikh Guru, Guru Teg Bahadur. He discontinued the practice of inscribing the Kalima on the coins and abolished the celebration of the new year’s day (Nauroz). He was constantly involved in trying to curtail the rising maratha power, however he failed to subdue them.
  • Aurangzeb’s reign was marked by growing agrarian crisis and popular rebellions, such as those of the Jats, the Satnamis, the Sikhs and the Rajputs (when Jodhpur was annexed).
  • His religious policies were great setback to the standards of tolerance and liberalism set by his predecessors. Mulhtasib (regulator of moral conduct) was appointed in the reign. Aurangzeb was called a Darvesh or Zinda Pir. He also forbade Sati. He patronised the greatest digest of Muslim law in Indian Fatawa-i-Alamgiri. He was a diplomat and capable general.
  • He imposed Jaziya on the Hindus in 1679. He banned music and dancing. He died in 1707 in the Deccan.

details.summary: Aurangzeb's reign, religious policies, military campaigns, and decline of the empire.

subject: History
text:
• Bahadur Shah: He was generous, learned and pious without any bigotry. He assumed the title of Shah Alam and was known as Shah-i-Behkhabar.
  • Jahandar Shah: Jahandar Shah’s three brothers namely Azim-us-Shan, Rafi-us-Shan and Jahan Shah lost their lives in the Battle of successions. He became king with the help of Zulfikar Khan. He abolished Jaziya.
  • Farrukhsiyar: He had succeeded the throne with the help of Sayyid Brothers Abdullah Khan and Hussain Ali. In 1717, Farrukhsiyar gave tax free trade permission to British East India Company to trade through Bengal. This Royal farman became Magna Carta for British East India Company. In 1719, Sayyid Brothers killed him with the help of Maratha Peshwa Balaji Vishwanath.
  • Mohammed Shah: Nadir Shah invaded India in 1738-39. Nadir Shah defeated him in the Battle of Karnal (1739) and took away peacock throne and Kohinoor diamond. He was the most pleasure loving ruler of loose morals and therefore, called Mohammed Shah Rangeela.

details.summary: Brief overview of the Later Mughal rulers and the decline of the empire.

subject: History
text:
• Ahmed Shah: Succeeded by his only son Ahmed Shah, born through a dancing girl. During this period, Safdarjung the nawab of Awadh was the Wazir of the empire. Ahmed Shah Abdali invaded India twice in 1749 and 1752, marching up to Delhi.
  • Alamgir II: Aziz-ud-din, a grandson of Jahandar Shah, was placed on the throne with the title Alamgir II.
  • Shah Alam II: Joined hands with Mir Qasim of Bengal and Shuja-ud-Daula of Awadh in the Battle of Buxar (1764) against the British and were defeated.
  • Akbar II: Gave the title of Raja to Ram Mohan Roy. Started the Hindu-Muslim unity festival Phool-Walon-Ki-Sair.
  • Bahadur Shah II: During the revolt of 1857, he was proclaimed the emperor by the rebels. He was confined by the British to the Red Fort.

details.summary: Overview of later Mughal rulers from Ahmed Shah to Bahadur Shah II.

subject: History
text:
Key Administrative Posts:

  • Vakil: Prime Minister (post lost importance after Bairam Khan).
  • Wazir or Diwan: Head of revenue department.
  • Mir Bakshi: Military department.
  • Mir Saman: Household department and Karkhanas.
  • Chief Qazi: Judicial department.
  • Sadr-us-Sadr: Charitable and religious endowments.
  • Mustaufi: Auditor-General.
  • Amil: Judicial officer in civil court.
  • Kanungo: Head accountant.
  • Lambardar: Head of village.
  • Patwari: Accountant of village.
  • Sipah Salar: Commander of the force.
  • Kotwal: Chief of city police.

Administrative Features:

  • Mansabdari system: Introduced by Akbar.
  • Empire division: Divided into 15 Subas.
  • Land classification: Khalisa, Jagirs, and Inam.
  • Zabti system: Based on measurement and assessment of land.
  • Tins-i-Kamil: Refers to cash crop and earning from cash crop.

details.summary: Detailed breakdown of Mughal administrative hierarchy and land revenue systems.

subject: History
topic: The Afghan Interlude - Sher Shah Suri
text:
Sher Shah Suri:

  • Founded the second Afghan dynasty (1st was Lodhi). Original name was Farid.
  • In 1522, served under Babur Khan Lohani (Governor of Bihar).
  • Ruled Agra and Delhi. Defeated Raja Maldev of Marwar in the Battle of Sammel (1544).
  • Divided empire into 47 Sarkars; each Sarkar divided into parganas.
  • Died in 1545 in an explosion during the conquest of Kalinjar fort.

Central Administration:

  • Diwan-i-Wijarat: Financial matter.
  • Diwan-i-Ariz: Military department (Headed by Ariz-i-mumalik).
  • Diwan-i-Insha: Secretariat.
  • Diwan-i-Rasalat: Foreign affairs (Headed by Sadar).
  • Qazi: Judicial administration.

Sarkar Level Officials:

  • Shiqdari-i-Shiqadaran: Law and order.
  • Munshif-i-Munshifan: Revenue collection.

Other Contributions:

  • Constructed the Grand Trunk Road (Indus to Sonargaon).
  • Built Sarais (rest houses) and introduced Dak-Chowki.
  • Introduced coins of unalloyed gold, silver, and copper (Silver 'Rupaya', Copper 'Dam').
  • Built a tomb at Sasaram (Bihar) and a new city on the bank of Yamuna (Purana Qila).
  • Abbas Khan Sarwani wrote Tarikh-i-Sher Shahi.

details.summary: Comprehensive notes on Sher Shah Suri's administration, military, and architectural contributions.

subject: History
topic: Rise of Shivaji and Maratha Administration
text:
Shivaji, the son of Shahaji, was the creator of the Maratha nation. He united the Maratha chiefs from Malwa, Konkan and Desh regions to carve out a small kingdom. He took control of the hereditary Jagir after the death of his guardian Konadev in 1647.

  • Shivaji was born in the hill fort of Shivner in 1627.
  • Captured the fort of Toran in 1656.
  • Raided Bijapur; killed Afzal Khan using a Baghnakh (tiger's claw).
  • Attacked Mughal territories; outwitted Shaista Khan in 1663.
  • Visited Mughal Court of Agra, put in detention, escaped in 1666.
  • Coronated as 'Chhatrapati' in 1674 at Raigarh; died in 1680.
  • Sambhaji succeeded him, followed by Rajaram and later Tara Bai.
tables:
| Pradhan | Post/Responsibility |
|---|---|
| Peshwa or Chief Minister/Mukhya Pradhan | Prime Minister, he looked after general administration and later assumed great importance. |
| Pratinidhi | Rajaram created the new post of Pratinidhi, thus, taking the total number of Ministers to nine. |
| Amatya or Majumdar | Accountant general, he later became Revenue and Finance Minister. |
| Sachiv or Surunavis (Surnis) | Also called Chitnis, he looked after the royal correspondence. |
| Sumant or Dabir | Foreign affairs and the master of royal ceremonies. |
| Senapati or Sar-i-Naubat | Military Commander, he looked after the recruitment, training and discipline of the army. |
| Mantri or Waqianavis | Personal safety of the king, he looked after the intelligence, posts and household affairs. |
| Nyayadhish | Administration of justice. |
| Pundit Rao | Looking after charitable and religious affairs of the state. He worked for the moral upliftment of the people. |

| Kingdom | Territory |
|---|---|
| Scindia | Gwalior |
| Holkar | Indore |
| Pawar | Dhar |
| Gaekwad | Baroda |
| Bhonsle | Nagpur |
| Peshwa | Puna |

details.summary: Overview of the rise of the Maratha Empire under Shivaji, the administrative structure (Ashta Pradhan), and the subsequent decline under the Peshwas.

subject: History
text:
Revenue Administration: Shivaji abolished the Jagirdari system and replaced it with the Ryotwari system. He reduced the powers of hereditary officials like Deshmukhs, Deshpandes, Patils, and Kulkarnis. Revenue was assessed based on land quality and yield, fixed at two-fifths of the gross produce, payable in cash or kind. Annaji Datto completed a new revenue assessment in AD 1679.

The Peshwas: The period of Peshwa domination began with Balaji Vishwanath in 1713. Key events include the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) where the Maratha Army was defeated by Ahmed Shah Abdali. The empire eventually declined after the Treaty of Bassein (1802) signed by Baji Rao II.

details.summary: Details on the Maratha revenue system and the political trajectory of the Peshwa era.

subject: History
topic: Advent of the Europeans in India
text:
In the AD 17th-18th centuries India became a centre of attraction for many European nations, who were inspired by the new spirit of adventure and discovery. Following is the order in which Europeans came to India.

  • Portuguese
    • Vasco da Gama was sent in 1498 from Lisbon to find the direct sea-route from Europe to India.
    • Francisco Almeida was the first Governor of Portuguese in India (1505-09). He introduced ‘The Policy of Blue Water’.
    • Albuquerque, the next Governor, built a great territorial power in India.
    • They established trading settlements at Calicut, Cochin and Cannanore. Cochin was the early capital of the Portuguese in India.
    • The Portuguese maritime empire acquired the name of Estado da India which intended to monopolise the pepper and spice trade of the East.
    • The Portuguese were able to establish their settlements near the sea in Diu, Daman, Salsette, Bassein, Chaul and Bombay on the Western coast and San Thome near Madras and Hooghly in Bengal.
  • Dutch
    • In 1602, the Dutch East India Company was formed by the Dutch Parliament through a charter which gave them powers to fight wars.
    • The Dutch gradually set-up factories at Masulipatnam, Pulicat, Surat, Bimilipatnam, Karikal, Chinsura, Kasimbazar, Boranagore, Patna, Balasore, Nagapatnam and Cochin.
    • In 18th century, Dutch power in India began to decline and finally, collapsed with their defeat by English in the Battle of Bedara in 1759.
  • English
    • English East India Company was founded in AD 1600 by the merchants of London, for trade with India. It was chartered on 31st December, 1600 by Queen Elizabeth and granted the monopoly of Eastern trade.
    • Jahangir permitted the East India Company to establish factories at several places in the empire. Gradually, the company established factories at Agra, Ahmedabad, Baroda, Broach, Bombay, Surat, Madras, Masulipatnam and different parts of Orissa, Bihar, Bengal.
    • The Island of Bombay was acquired by the East India Company from the British Government in 1668 and was immediately fortified. The first factory of English was established at Surat (1608).
  • Danes
    • Danes East India Company was founded in AD 1616. They established their settlement at Bengal (Serampur), Tranqueber (Tamil Nadu).
    • They were forced to sell their settlements to the British in 1854.
  • French
    • ‘Compagnie des Indes Orientales’ popularly known as the French East India Company was formed by Colbert, under state patronage in AD 1664.
    • In AD 1667, an expedition was sent under Francois Caron, who established the first French factory India at Surat.
    • In AD 1669, Marcara founded another French factory at Masulipatam by securing patent from the Sultan of Golconda.
    • In July 1672, French squadron under De La Haye occupied San Thome near Madras.
    • In 1673, Francois Martin, director of the Masulipatam factory, obtained from Sher Khan Lodi, Governor of Valikondapuram, a site for a factory, which later developed into Pondicherry and its first governor was Francois Martin.
    • In Bengal, the French laid the foundation of their famous settlement of Chandranagar in AD 1690 on a site granted to them by Shaista Khan.

The European Commerce

India had maintained its trade relations with the foreign merchants even during the earlier centuries. There was a great difference between the foreign merchants who had earlier settled in and conducted brisk trade from India and the Europeans who came to India in the 16th and 17th centuries.

Governor-General of Bengal

Warren Hastings (1773-85)

  • He became Governor of Bengal in 1772 and first Governor-General of Bengal in 1773, through the Regulating Act. He abolished the dual system of administration.
  • He divided Bengal into districts and appointed collectors and other revenue officials. He established India’s first Supreme Court in Calcutta.
  • He founded Asiatic Society of Bengal with William Jones in 1784 and wrote introduction to the first English translation of the Gita by Charles Wilkins.
  • Started Diwani and Faujdari adalats and the district level Sadar diwani and Nizmat adalats (appellate courts).

details.summary: Overview of European arrival and settlements in India during the 17th-18th centuries, including key figures, establishments, and administrative changes under Warren Hastings.

subject: History
text: Lord Cornwallis (1786-93) was the first Governor-General to codify laws in India. He introduced the Izaredari System in 1773 and started the permanent settlement of Bengal. He created the post of District Judge and is considered the father of the Civil Services in India. He also undertook police reforms and codified laws separating revenue administration from justice administration. His tenure saw the First Anglo-Maratha War, Second Anglo-Mysore War, and the Rohilla War. He was impeached in Britain on charges of bribery but was acquitted after a seven‑year trial.

details.summary: Lord Cornwallis codified laws, introduced Izaredari System, permanent settlement, created District Judge, father of Civil Services, reforms, wars, impeachment.

subject: History
text: Sir John Shore (1793-98) played an important role in planning the permanent settlement and introduced the First Charter Act of 1793. He was known for his policy of non‑interference and oversaw the Battle of Kharla between the Nizam and Marathas in 1759.

details.summary: Sir John Shore: permanent settlement planning, First Charter Act, non‑interference, Battle of Kharla.

subject: History
text: Lord Wellesey (1798-1803) introduced the Subsidiary Alliance system and saw the formation of the Madras Presidency. His tenure included the Fourth Anglo‑Mysore War (1799) where Tipu Sultan died, the first subsidiary treaty with the Nizam of Hyderabad, and the Second Anglo‑Maratha War. In 1800 he established Fort William College in Calcutta and was known as the Bengal Tiger. He also enacted the Censorship of Press Act, 1799.

details.summary: Lord Wellesey: Subsidiary Alliance, Madras Presidency, Fourth Anglo‑Mysore War, Fort William College, Bengal Tiger, Press Act.

subject: History
text: Sir George Barlow (1805-07) presided over the Vellore Mutiny of 1806, a mutiny by soldiers, and saw the end of the Second Anglo‑Maratha War.

details.summary: Sir George Barlow: Vellore Mutiny, end of Second Anglo‑Maratha War.

subject: History
text: Lord Minto I (1807-13) signed the Treaty of Amritsar (1809) with Ranjit Singh and saw the Charter Act of 1813, which ended the monopoly of the East India Company in India.

details.summary: Lord Minto I: Treaty of Amritsar, Charter Act 1813.

subject: History
text: Lord Hastings (1813-23) adopted a policy of intervention and war, overseeing the Anglo‑Neepal War (1813-23).

details.summary: Lord Hastings: intervention policy, Anglo‑Neepal War.

subject: History
text: Lord William Bentinck (1828-35) was the most liberal and enlightened Governor-General, known as the Father of Modern Western Education in India. He abolished Sati in 1829 (Regulation XVII), suppressed Thuggee in 1830, and passed the Charter Act of 1833. He annexed Coorg (1834) and Central Cachar (1831), deposed the Raja of Mysore (1831), and opened the first medical college in Calcutta (1835). He signed the Treaty of Friendship with Ranjit Singh (1831).

details.summary: Lord Bentinck: liberal reforms, abolition of Sati, suppression of Thuggee, Charter Act 1833, annexations, medical college.

subject: History
text: Sir Charles Metcalfe (1835-36) passed the famous Press Law, liberating the press in India, earning him the title of the liberator of press.

details.summary: Sir Metcalfe: Press Law, press freedom.

subject: History
text: Lord Auckland (1836-42) initiated the construction of the Grand Trunk Road from Calcutta to Delhi in 1839 and renamed Sher Shah Suri Marg as the Grand Trunk Road (GT Road).

details.summary: Lord Auckland: Grand Trunk Road construction and renaming.

subject: History
text: Lord Ellenborough (1842-44) ended the Afghan War (1842) and annexed Sindh to the British Empire in 1843. He replaced Charles Napier with Major Outram as the resident in Sindh.

details.summary: Lord Ellenborough: end of Afghan War, annexation of Sindh, change of resident.

subject: History
text: Lord Hardinge (1844-48) oversaw the First Anglo‑Sikh War and the Treaty of Lahore.

details.summary: Lord Hardinge: First Anglo‑Sikh War, Treaty of Lahore.

subject: History
text: Lord Dalhousie (1848-56) led the Second Anglo‑Sikh War (1848-49) and annexed Punjab. He abolished titles and passed the Widow Remarriage Act (1856). He introduced the Doctrine of Lapse, the Woods Educational Despatch of 1854, and the Railway, Telegraph, and Postal System in 1853. He also oversaw the Second Anglo‑Burmese War (1852) and the Santhal uprisings (1855-56). The Charter Act of 1853 was passed during his tenure.

details.summary: Lord Dalhousie: Second Anglo‑Sikh War, annexation of Punjab, Widow Remarriage Act, Doctrine of Lapse, educational despatch, infrastructure, wars, uprisings.

subject: History
text: The Doctrine of Lapse was planned by Lord Dalhousie to deal with succession in princely states. According to the doctrine, if a ruler of a princely state under the Company's jurisdiction died without a natural heir, the state would automatically be annexed to the British Empire. The Company took over Satara (1848), Jaitpur and Sambalpur (1849), Nagpur and Jhansi (1854), Tanjore and Arcot (1855), Udipur (Chhattisgarh) and Oudh (1856) under this doctrine.

details.summary: Doctrine of Lapse: succession rule, annexation of multiple princely states.

subject: History
text:
Lord Canning (AD 1858-62)

  • The last Governor-General and the first Viceroy.
  • Withdrew Doctrine of Lapse.
  • Transfer of control from East India Company to the Crown under the Government of India Act, 1858.
  • ‘White Mutiny’ by European troops in 1859.
  • Indian Councils Act of 1861 was passed.

Lord Elgin (AD 1862-63)

  • Wahabi Movement took place.
  • Inauguration of High Court judicature in Bengal.
  • Transfer of Indian Navy to the Admiralty.

Lord John Lawrence (AD 1864-69)

  • Created the Indian Forest Department.
  • Bhutan War of 1865 took place.
  • Setting up of the High Courts at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras in 1865.
  • Opened telegraphic communication with Europe.

Lord Mayo (AD 1869-72)

  • Opening of the Rajkot College in Kathiawar and the Mayo College at Ajmer for political training of Indian princes.
  • Establishment of Statistical Survey of India.
  • Establishment of Department of Agriculture and Commerce.
  • Started the process of financial decentralisation in India.

Lord Northbrook (AD 1872-76)

  • Kuka Movement, Trial of Gaekwad of Baroda and Bihar Famine occurred.
  • Abolished income tax.

Lord Lytton (AD 1876-80)

  • Royal titles in 1876; Queen Victoria assumed the title ‘Kaiser-i-Hind’ (Queen Empress of India).
  • The Arms Act of 1878 was passed.
  • Famine of 1876-78 affecting Madras, Bombay, Mysore, Hyderabad, parts of Central India and Punjab; Famine Commission appointed under Richard Strachey in 1878.
  • Vernacular Press Act passed in 1878 to curtail freedom of the Indian language press.
  • He was called the Viceroy of reverse characters.

Lord Ripon (AD 1880-84)

  • The first Factory Act in 1881 to improve labour conditions.
  • Continuation of financial decentralisation.
  • Government resolution on local self‑government in 1882.
  • Education Commission appointed under Sir William Hunter in 1882.

Lord Dufferin (AD 1884-88)

  • Establishment of the Indian National Congress.
  • Punjab Affair (1884).
  • Celebrated the silver jubilee of Queen Victoria on 16 February 1887.

Lord Lansdowne (AD 1888-94)

  • Second Factory Act of 1891 passed, granting a weekly holiday.
  • Categorisation of civil services into imperial, provisional and subordinate.
  • Indian Councils Act of 1892 passed.
  • Durand Commission set up in 1893 to define the Durand Line between India and Afghanistan (now Pakistan‑Afghanistan).

Lord Elgin II (AD 1894-99)

  • British officials assassinated by Chapekar brothers in 1897.
  • Lyall Commission appointed after the famine of 1896-97.

Lord Curzon (AD 1899-1905)

  • Police Commission appointed in 1902 under Sir Andrew Frazer to review police administration.
  • Universities Commission appointed in 1902; Indian Universities Act passed in 1904.
  • Establishment of Department of Commerce and Industry.
  • Indian Coinage and Paper Currency Act (1899) passed; India placed on a gold standard.

Lord Minto II (AD 1905-10)

  • Establishment of Muslim League by Aga Khan in 1906.
  • Split of Congress in the annual session of 1907 in Surat.
  • Indian Councils Act of 1909 (Morley‑Minto Reforms) passed.
  • Popularisation of anti‑partition and Swadeshi Movement.

Lord Hardinge II (AD 1910-16)

  • Annie Besant announced the Home Rule Movement.
  • Coronation durbar of King George V held in Delhi in 1911.
  • Creation of Bengal Presidency (like Bombay and Madras) in 1911; partition of Bengal cancelled.
  • Transfer of capital from Calcutta to Delhi in 1911.
  • Establishment of Hindu Mahasabha in 1915 by Madan Mohan Malaviya.
  • Gandhiji returned to India from South Africa in 1915.

Lord Chelmsford (AD 1916-21)

  • Formation of Home Rule Leagues by Annie Besant and Tilak in 1916.
  • Lucknow Pact between the Congress and Muslim League in 1916.
  • Saddler’s Commission appointed in 1917 for reforms in educational policy.
  • Jallianwala Bagh massacre of 1919.
  • Launch of Non‑cooperation and Khilafat Movements.
  • SP Sinha appointed Governor of Bihar (first Indian governor).
  • Death of Tilak on 1 August 1920.

Lord Reading (AD 1921-26)

  • Moplah rebellion in Kerala in 1921.
  • Communist Party founded in 1920 by M.N. Roy.

details.summary: Chronological list of Viceroys of India from Lord Canning (1858) to Lord Reading (1926) with key events and reforms during each tenure.

subject: History
text:
Events of 1922-1925

  • Chauri Chaura incident on 5th February, 1922 and subsequent withdrawal on non-cooperation movement.
  • Vishwabharati University started in 1922.
  • Establishment of Swaraj party by CR Das and Motilal Nehru in 1922.
  • Decision to hold simultaneous examinations for the ICS both in Delhi and London, with effect from 1923.
  • Kakori train robbery of 1925.

details.summary: Key historical events between 1922 and 1925 including Chauri Chaura, establishment of Vishwabharati University, Swaraj Party, ICS exam changes, and Kakori train robbery.

subject: History
text:
Lord Irwin (AD 1926-31)

  • Appointment of the Harcourt Butler Indian States Commission in 1927.
  • Visit of Simon Commission to India in 1928 and boycott of the Commission by the Indians.
  • An All-Parties Conference held at Lucknow in 1928 for suggestions for the (future) Constitution of India, the report of which was called the Nehru Report or the Nehru Constitution.
  • Murder of Saunders, the assistant superintendent of police of Lahore, bomb blast in the Assembly Hall of Delhi in 1929, the Lahore conspiracy case and bomb accident in train in Delhi in 1929.

details.summary: Events during the tenure of Viceroy Lord Irwin, including the Harcourt Butler Commission, Simon Commission boycott, Nehru Report, and various incidents in Lahore and Delhi.

subject: History
text:
Lord Willingdon (AD 1931-36)

  • Second Round Table Conference in 1931 and failure of the conference, resumption of Civil Disobedience Movement.
  • Announcement of Communal Award in 1932 under which separate communal electorates were set-up.
  • ‘Fast unto death’ by Gandhiji in Yervada prison, broken after the Poona Pact in 1932.
  • Third Round Table Conference of 1932. The Government of India Act of 1935. Burma separated from India in 1935.
  • Establishment of All India Kisan Sabha in 1936 and Congress Socialist party by Acharya Narendra Dev and Jaya Prakash Narayan in 1934.

details.summary: Events during the tenure of Viceroy Lord Willingdon, including Round Table Conferences, Communal Award, Poona Pact, Government of India Act 1935, and separation of Burma.

subject: History
text:
Lord Linlithgow (AD 1936-44)

  • First general elections in 1936-37, Congress attained absolute majority in 6 states.
  • Resignation of the Congress ministries after the outbreak of the World War II in 1939.
  • Escape of Subhash Chandra Bose from India in 1941 and organisation of the Indian National Army.
  • Cripps Mission and Cripps plan to offer dominion status to India and setting up of a Constituent Assembly, its rejection by the Congress.
  • Passing of the ‘Quit India Resolution’ by the Congress in 1942. Outbreak of ‘August Revolution’ or Revolt of 1942 after the arrest of national leaders.

details.summary: Events during the tenure of Viceroy Lord Linlithgow, including 1937 elections, WWII impact, Subhash Chandra Bose's escape, Cripps Mission, and Quit India Movement.

subject: History
text:
Lord Wavell (AD 1944-47)

  • Wavell Plan and the Shimla Conference in 1942. C Rajagopalachari’s CR formula in 1944, failure of Gandhi-Jinnah talks in 1944. End of World War II in 1945. Proposals of the Cabinet Mission Plan in 1946 and its acceptance by the Congress.
  • Observance of ‘Direct Action Day’ on 16th August, 1948 by the Muslim League. Announcement of the end of British Rule in India by Clement Atlee (Prime Minister of England) on 20th February, 1947.

details.summary: Events during the tenure of Viceroy Lord Wavell, including Wavell Plan, CR Formula, Cabinet Mission, Direct Action Day, and announcement of end of British rule.

subject: History
text:
Lord Mountbatten (AD March 1947-August 1947)

  • Last Governor-General of India.
  • Introduction of Indian Independence Bill in the House of Commons.
  • India Independence Act passed by the British Parliament on 4th July, 1947 by which India became independent on 15th August, 1947.

details.summary: Events during the tenure of Lord Mountbatten, including the Indian Independence Act and India's independence on August 15, 1947.

subject: History
text:
C Rajagopalachari (AD 1948-50)

  • The last Governor General of free India (The first being Mountbatten).
  • The only Indian Governor General, remained in office till January, 1950.

details.summary: Tenure of C. Rajagopalachari as the last Governor General of free India and the only Indian to hold the position until 1950.

subject: History
text:
Permanent Settlement

  • Introduced in Bengal, Bihar-Orissa, districts of Banaras and Northern districts of Madras by Lord Cornwallis in 1793. Sir John Shore planned this settlement.
  • It declared zamindars as the owners of the land. Hence, they could keep 1/11th of the revenue collected to themselves while the British got a fixed share of 10/11th of the revenue collected. The zamindars were free to fix the rate. Assured of their ownership, many zamindars stayed in towns and exploited their tenants.
  • The zamindars collected the rents of land through different intermediate collectors. As a result of such practice there had been creation of multi-level ranks of collector under the zamindar.

details.summary: Details of the Permanent Settlement system introduced in 1793, including regions, key figures, revenue distribution between zamindars and British, and social impact.

subject: History
text:
Ryotwari Settlement

  • It was introduced in Bombay, Madras and Assam. Munro and Charles Reed recommended it. In this system, the direct settlement was made between the Government and the Ryots. The revenue was based on the basis of the quality of the soil and the nature of the crop.
  • The revenue was fixed for a period not exceeding 30 years. It was based on the Scientific Rent Theory of Ricardo. The position of the cultivator became more secure.

details.summary: Details of the Ryotwari Settlement system, including regions, key figures, direct settlement with ryots, revenue basis, and theoretical foundation.

subject: History
text:
Mahalwari System

  • It was introduced in the area of Ganga valley NWFP, parts of Central India and Punjab. Revenue settlement was to be made by village or estates with landlords.
  • In this system, a settlement was made with the village which maintained a form of common ownership known as Bhai Chara or with Mahals, which were group of villages. Revenue was periodically revised.

details.summary: Details of the Mahalwari System, including regions, settlement with villages/mahals, concept of Bhai Chara, and periodic revision of revenue.

subject: History
text:
The Mahalwari system did not cover the whole of the Uttar Pradesh. In the district of Oudh, there existed another system known as Taluqdari system. Under it a number of villages were put under the Taluqdari system. The government entered into an agreement with the Taluqdar for a period of 30 years.

  • The Taluqdar collected the stipulated revenues from different villages put under his charge and deposited them with the government, after deducting the cost of collection of the revenues and his own remuneration for the arduous work.
  • Unlike the Bengal Zamindars the Oudh Taluqdars had no real rights over the lands under their charge. Moreover, they worked as revenue collectors for the fixed period of the settlement, and not in perpetuity.

details.summary: Overview of the Taluqdari revenue collection system in Oudh.

subject: History
text:
Causes of the Revolt

  • Political Cause: Nana Sahib was refused pension as he was the adopted son of Peshwa Baji Rao‑II. He later led the revolt from Kanpur.
  • Awadh (Lucknow) was annexed in 1856, on charge of maladministration and Jhansi was annexed owing to Doctrine of Lapse.
  • Military Discrimination: Indian soldiers were paid low salaries, they could not rise above the rank of Subedar and were racially insulted.
  • Religious Discrimination: The social reforms by British were against the people’s will (widow remarriage, abolition of sati, school for girls, Christian missionaries etc). Soldiers were asked to use the Enfield Rifles with greased (by pork or beef) cartridges.
  • Economic Grievances: Heavy taxations, discriminatory tariff policy; destruction of traditional handicrafts that hit peasants, artisans and small zamindars.

Outbreak of the Revolt

  • Bengal Resentment in 19 native infantry of Behrampur, which refused to use the newly introduced Enfield Rifle.
  • Mangal Pandey 34th native infantry fired at the sergeant major of his regiment. Known as a part of Mutiny of Barrackpur.
  • Where the rulers were loyal to the British, the soldiers revolted, as in Gwalior and Indore. In some places, people revolted before the sepoys.
  • In the beginning, the rebels were successful. Europeans were killed, police stations and law courts were attacked and revenue records were destroyed. But, the revolt was soon suppressed.

Suppression of the Revolt

  • John Lawrence remarked, “Had a single leader of ability arisen among them we must have been lost beyond redemption.” Delhi was recaptured on 20th September, 1857 by John Nicholson and Bahadur Shah II was deported to Rangoon, where he died in 1862. His sons were shot dead at Delhi.
  • Jhansi was recaptured by Hugh Rose on 17th June, 1858. Rani Lakshmi Bai died in the battlefield.
  • Kanpur was recaptured on 6th December, 1857 by Colin Campbell. Lucknow was recaptured on 21st March, 1858 by Colin Campbell, Havelock and Outram.
  • Nana Sahib and Hazrat Mahal both escaped to Nepal.
  • William Taylor and Edgre suppressed the revolt at Arrah.
  • Tantia Tope was betrayed by a friend. He was captured and executed on 15th April, 1859.

Causes Behind the Failure of the Revolt

  • Lack of unity and poor organisation of the revolt. All the classes of the society were not effected or participated in the revolt. Lack of common motive for participating in the revolt.
  • Some of the rulers like Scindhias, Nizam and Holkars helped Britishers in repressing the revolt.
  • The military equipment of rebels was inferior.
