subject: Geography
text:
LIVESTOCK FARMING/ANIMAL HUSBANDRY

  • It refers to rearing of animals for food and other human uses. The world ‘Livestock’ applies primarily to cattle, chickens, goats, pigs, horses and sheeps.
  • Poultry farmers keep chickens, turkeys, geese and other birds for meat and eggs.
  • Top Beef producer of world are USA, Brazil, European Union, China and India.
  • India is the world’s largest producer of milk. It is the leading exporter of skimmed milk powder. The world’s largest exportes of milk and milk products are New Zealand, the European Union, Australia and the United States.

details.summary: Livestock farming involves rearing animals for food and other uses, with leading producers of beef, milk, and related products.

subject: Geography
text:
DAIRY FARMING

  • It is highly capital intensive and advanced form of farm activity.
  • It is practised mainly near urban and industrial centres.
  • Denmark and Sweden have witnessed the maximum development of this type of farming.
  • Some animals like sheeps, goats and rabbits reared for wool production also. Australia is the leading producer of wool followed by New Zealand and China.
  • Temperate grasslands like Steppes in Russia, Prairies in North America, Pampas in Argentina, Veldt in South Africa and Downs in Southern Australia supports highly intensive livestock industry.

details.summary: Dairy farming is capital-intensive, practiced near urban/industrial centres, with leading development in Denmark and Sweden; also notes on wool production and temperate grasslands supporting livestock.

subject: Geography
text:
Fisheries

  • Fisheries constitute an important economic activity in the coastal regions of the world, especially in the temperate latitudes. Fisheries can be classified into two groups – fresh water fisheries and marine fisheries.
  • Around 90% of the fishes are caught from the sea while remaining is obtained from fresh water. The top ten largest fish producing countries in the world are China, Peru, India, Indonesia, USA, Chile, Japan, Thailand, Vietnam and Russia.
  • Major exporters of fish and fishery products in the world are China, Norway, Thailand, USA and Denmark and major importers of fish and fishery products are Japan, USA, Spain, France and Italy.
  • There are four major fishing grounds in the world :
    • i. North-East Atlantic Region Dogger Bank located in the North Sea is one of the most important fishing ground. Important species of this region are Cod and Herring.
    • ii. North-West Atlantic Region Grand Bank and Georges Bank are important fishing grounds. Important species of this region are Cod, Lobster, Oyster and Herring.
    • iii. North-West Pacific Region Countries involved in fishing in this region are China, Japan, Russia, North and South Korea.
    • iv. North-East Pacific Region This region include coastal regions of Canada and USA. Important species of this region are Halibut, Sardine, Salmon and Tuna.

details.summary: Fisheries overview: classification, top producers, exporters/importers, and major fishing grounds with key species.

subject: General Knowledge
text:
A naturally occurring substance that has a definite chemical composition and physical properties is called mineral.

Minerals are formed in different types of geological environments, under varying conditions. They are created by natural processes without any human interference.

Minerals

Countries in Decreasing Order of Production

  • Iron ore – China, Australia, Brazil, India, Russia
  • Manganese – China, South Africa, Australia, Brazil, Gabon
  • Bauxite – Australia, China, Brazil
  • Aluminium – China, Russia, Canada, UAE, India
  • Copper – Chile, China, Peru, USA, Congo
  • Silver – Mexico, China, Peru, Russia, Australia
  • Gold – China, Australia, Russia, USA, Canada
  • Tin – China, Indonesia, Peru, Bolivia, Brazil
  • Zinc – China, Peru, Australia, USA, Canada
  • Uranium – Kazakhstan, Canada, Australia, Niger, Namibia

Energy resources are generally defined as anything that can be used as a source of energy. Some energy resources are coal, petroleum and natural gas etc.

Resources – Major Producer Countries

  • Coal – China, USA, Australia, India
  • Petroleum – USA, Saudi Arabia, Russia, China
  • Natural Gas – USA, Russia, Qatar, Iran
  • Uranium – Kazakhstan (First), Canada, Australia, Niger, Namibia
  • Wind Energy – China, USA, Germany, Spain, India
  • Solar Energy – Germany, China, Italy, Japan, USA, Spain, France
  • Hydro‑electricity – China (First), Canada, Brazil, USA, Norway, New Zealand, India

Industries

All economic activities namely; primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary, revolve around obtaining and utilising resources necessary for survival. Among all, these secondary activities add value to natural resources by transforming raw materials into valuable products.

Industries – Major Countries

  • Iron and Steel Industry – Russia, China, USA, Japan, India, Britain
  • Cotton Textile – China, India, USA
  • Jute Industry – India, Bangladesh, China
  • Woolen Textile – Australia, China, USA
  • Paper Industries – China, USA, Germany, Japan
  • Ship Building – China, South Korea, Japan
  • Aircraft Building – USA, Britain, Russia, France
  • Automobile Industry – China, USA, Japan, Germany, South Korea, India
  • Petro Chemical – USA, Belgium, Japan, Netherlands, China, South Korea, Taiwan

Transport

Transport along with communication is considered as lifeline of an economy. The principal modes of transportation includes land transport, waterways, airways and pipelines.

Road Transport

  • Roadways are the most universal and accessible form of transportation. It is also very economical for short distances.
  • Germany was the first country in the world to establish a nationwide highway network.
  • USA has world’s longest and biggest road network followed by China, India, Brazil and Russia.
  • Pan‑American Highway is the longest highway in the world.

Rail Transport

  • It is preferred mode of land transport for bulky goods passengers over long distances.
  • The first train was started on 27th September, 1825 between Stockton to Darlington in England.
  • United States has world’s longest rail network, followed by Russia and China.
  • Trans‑Siberian Railway is the longest railway line in the world.

Air Transport

  • Air transport is the fastest but costliest mode of transport. The development of air transport started after the World I. But the actual development of this transport took place after the World II.
  • Three types of services are performed by air transport :

i. Inter‑Continental Global – includes the longest services e.g. services between the continents.

ii. Continental Air Route – services performed among the countries within a continent e.g. India‑China.

details.summary: Comprehensive notes on minerals, energy resources, related industries and transport modes with major producing countries and key facts.

subject: Geography
text:
National Air Route performs services for long distance within the country, e.g., Mumbai-Delhi.

International Air Transport Authority (IATA) is an international trade body created over 60 years ago by a group of airlines. Today, IATA represents 240 airlines comprising 84% of total air traffic. The organisation also represents, leads and serves the airline industry in general.

details.summary: Overview of national and international air transport and the role of IATA.

subject: Geography
text: Water transport includes both ocean water transport and inland transport. Waterways are the most suitable and cheapest mode of transport for carrying international trade.

details.summary: Definition and importance of water transport.

subject: Geography
text:
Important Sea Routes of the World:

  • North Atlantic Sea Route (Big Trunk) – links North‑Eastern USA and North‑Western Europe; busiest route in the world.
  • South Atlantic Sea Route – connects North America and Europe with South America.
  • Mediterranean‑Indian Ocean Sea Route – connects highly industrialised West European region with East Africa, South Africa, South‑East Asia and Australia and New Zealand.
  • Cape of Good Hope Route – connects West European and West African countries with Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay in South America.
  • North Pacific Sea Route – links the ports of West‑coast of North America with those of Asia.
  • South Pacific Sea Route – important connecting link between South and North America with Australia, New Zealand and various Pacific islands via Panama Canal.

details.summary: List of major international sea routes and their connections.

subject: Geography
text:
Major Canal System of the World:

  • Suez Canal – constructed in 1869; largest canal in the world, connecting Port Said in North and Port Suez in South, linking Red Sea and Mediterranean Sea.
  • Panama Canal – constructed across the Panama Isthmus between Panama City and Colon, connecting the Pacific Ocean and the Caribbean Sea.
  • Kiel Canal – in Germany, connects the North Sea with the Baltic Sea.
  • Manchester Shipping Canal – connects Manchester with Eastham.
  • North‑Sea Canal – joins North Sea with Amsterdam.

details.summary: Description of major canals and their geographical significance.

subject: Geography
text:
Major Inland Waterways of the World:

  • Rhine Waterways – navigable for 700 km from Rotterdam (Netherlands) to Basel (Switzerland); world’s most heavily used waterways.
  • Danube Waterway – Danube river rises in Black Forest and flows Eastward in Eastern Europe; navigable up to Taurna Severin.
  • Volga Waterways – important waterways of Russia; navigable for 11,200 km. The Volga‑Moscow Canal connects it with Moscow region and Volga‑Don canal with Black Sea.
  • Great Lakes‑St. Lawrence Seaway – Great Lakes of North America (Superior, Huron, Erie, Ontario) connected by Soo Canal and Welland Canal; along with estuary of St. Lawrence River form the waterways.
  • Mississippi Waterways – Mississippi‑Ohio waterway connects interior part of USA with Gulf of Mexico.

details.summary: Overview of major inland waterways and their routes.

subject: Geography
text: Race is a term used for large group of people with some basic inherited physical characteristics common. e.g., skin colour, hair, facial features, eye colour, head shape etc. Four major human races are Caucasoid, Australoid, Mongoloid and Negroid.

text: Definition: Population refers to the whole number of people living in country or region. Demography is the scientific study of human population.

details.summary: Definition of population and demography.

subject: Geography
text:
• Population is not distributed evenly in all parts of the world. Some places have sparse (scattered) population and some have dense population.
  • Sparsely populated places tend to be difficult places to live. These are usually places with hostile environment e.g. desert areas of the world.
  • More than 75% of the world’s population lives in the continents of Africa and Asia.

details.summary: Factors affecting population distribution and global population concentration.

• Density is defined as number of persons in per unit area. The density varies not only from one country to another within a continent but also from one part to the other within a country.
  • The highest densities are found in North- Eastern USA, North-West Europe, South Asia, South-East Asia and East Asia.
  • The lowest densities are found in hot and cold deserts, areas around pole, high rainfall area near equator.

subject: Geography
text:
• Birth Rate: Number of live births per 1000 population in a given year. High birth rate found in Africa while lowest is in Europe.
  • Death Rate: Number of deaths per 1000 population in a given year.
  • Infant Mortality Rate: The number of deaths of infants under per 1000 live births in a year.
  • Maternal Mortality Rate: The number of women who die as a result of pregnancy and child birth complications per 100000 live births in a year.
  • Total Fertility Rate: The average number of children that would be born alive to a women.

subject: Geography
text: Doubling Time is the number of years required for the population of an area to double itself, at the current rate of population growth.

details.summary: Time taken for population to double at current growth rate.

subject: Geography
text: The Age-Dependency Ratio is the ratio of persons in the ages defined as dependent (under 15 years and over 64 years) to persons in the ages defined as economically productive (15-64 years).

details.summary: Ratio of dependent to productive population.

subject: Geography
text: Demographic Transition refers to the shift of birth and death rates from high to low levels. The decline in fertility is always delayed, leading to population growth.

details.summary: Stages of demographic transition and its impact on population growth.

subject: Geography
text:
Migration means the movement of people from one place to another.

  • Domestic migration can be either in-migration (entering one administrative sub-division from another) or out-migration (leaving one sub-division to reside in another).
  • International migration includes emigration (leaving one country to settle in another) and immigration (entering a country to settle).
  • Refugee: a person residing outside his/her country of origin due to fear of persecution for reasons of race, religion, nationality or political opinion.
  • Internally Displaced Person: a person forced to leave his/her home region due to unfavorable conditions but does not cross any boundary.

details.summary: Types and definitions of migration.

subject: Geography
text: Human Development refers to qualitative change that is always positively valued. Dr. Mahbub-ul-Haq introduced the concept, describing it as development that enlarges people’s choices and improves their lives. The four pillars of human development are equality, sustainability, productivity, and empowerment.

details.summary: Definition and pillars of human development.

subject: Geography
text: The Human Development Report is an annual publication by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP). It was first launched in 1990 by Pakistani economist Mahbub-ul-Haq and Indian Nobel laureate Amartya Sen. Human development is measured in terms of life expectancy at birth, education, and per capita income. Norway has the highest HDI ranking; India ranks 130th (131 in 2016).

details.summary: HDI measurement and rankings.

subject: Geography
text:
General Position: India occupies a South-Central position in the Asian continent, looking across the Arabian sea to Arabia and Africa on the West and across Bay of Bengal to Myanmar, Malaysia and the Indonesian Archipelago on the East. Geographically, the Himalayan ranges keep India apart from the rest of Asia. India derives her name from river Indus.

Location: India is often described as a tropical country although a large part of India lies in sub-tropics. The territorial limits of the Indian mainland extend between 8° 4´ N and 37° 6´ N latitudes and 68° 7´ E and 97° 25´ E longitudes.

Area and Extent:

  • India ranks 7th in the world in terms of area after Russia, Canada, USA, China, Brazil and Australia.
  • It has a total land area of about 3287263 sq km, i.e. about 33 lakh sq km.
  • It is second largest in terms of population and holds 17.4% of the total world population, the land area of India amounts only to 2.4% of the total world landmass.
  • India is the second largest country in Asia both in terms of area as well as population, after China.

Extremes and Coastline:

  • State with longest coastline is Gujarat.
  • Active volcanoes are in Barren island in Andaman and Nicobar islands.
  • Northern most point of India is Indira Col.
  • Southern most point is Indira point or Pygmalion point in Great Nicobar.
  • Southern most tip of mainland is Kanyakumari.
  • Eastern most point is Kibithu, Arunachal Pradesh.
  • Western most point is Guhar moti in Kutch, Gujarat.

Indian Standard Time (IST):

  • India has only one standard time.
  • India is 5.5 hours ahead of GMT/UTC, 4.5 hours behind Australian Eastern standard time and 10.5 hours ahead of American Eastern standard time.
  • The 82.5° E longitude that passes through Allahabad city is chosen as standard longitude for Indian standard time.

subject: Geography
topic: Relief and Physiographic Divisions: The Himalayas
text:
Physiography: Physiography is the branch of geography, which studies the present relief features of the Earth’s surface or of natural features in their causal relationships. The physiographic diversity of India embraces fold mountains, flat plains and one of the oldest plateaus of the world. India is divided into five physiographic units.

1. The Himalayas: The Northern mountain wall is a series of high mountain ranges stretching over the Northern borders of India.

  • The geologically young and structurally fold mountain ranges, the Himalayas run in West-East direction from the Indus to the Brahmaputra.
  • They form an arc, which covers a distance of about 2400 km. Their width varies from 400 km in Kashmir to 150 km in Arunachal Pradesh.
  • The altitudinal variations are greater in the Eastern half than those in the Western half.

Classification of Himalayas: The Himalayas range is classified into four longitudinal series of mountains:

  1. Trans-Himalayas: North of the Greater Himalayas lie the Trans-Himalayas or the Tibet Himalayas. This section is older than Himalayas. This range acts as a watershed between rivers flowing towards South and those flowing towards North. These ranges are about 40 km wide and rise in height upto 5000 m. They include the Karakoram, Zanskar and Ladakh ranges.
  2. Greater Himalayas or Himadri: The Northern most important range is known as the Great or Inner Himalayas or the Himadri.
  3. Himachal Himalayas: The range lying to the South of the Himadri, forms the most rugged mountain system and is known as Himachal or Lesser Himalayas or Middle Himalayas.

details.summary: Defines physiography and details the Himalayan range, including its extent, width, direction, and classification into Trans-Himalayas, Greater Himalayas (Himadri), and Himachal Himalayas.

subject: Geography
text: The outermost range of the Himalayas is called the Shivaliks. They extend over a width of 10-50 km and have an altitude varying between 900 and 1100 m. These ranges are composed of unconsolidated sediments brought down by rivers from the main Himalayan ranges located in North.

details.summary: Shivaliks are the outermost Himalayan range, 10-50 km wide, 900-1100 m altitude, composed of unconsolidated sediments.

subject: Geography
text: After crossing the Dihang Gorge, the Himalayas take a sudden Southward turn and form a series of comparatively low hills in the shape of a crescent with its convex side pointing towards the West. These hills are known as Purvanchal.

details.summary: Purvanchal are low hills formed after the Himalayas turn southward, crescent-shaped.

subject: Geography
text:
• To the South of Himalayas and North of Peninsula lies the Great Plain of North India. It is an aggradational plain formed mainly by the work of 3 rivers systems viz, the Indus, the Ganga and the Brahmaputra.
• This is the largest alluvial tract of the world, extending for a length of 3200 km and width varies between 150 to 300 km.
• Regional division of Great Plain of India are as follows :
• Punjab-Haryana Plain – The western part of the Northern Plain is known as Punjab-Haryana Plain. Its Eastern boundary in Haryana is formed by the Yamuna river. It also includes North-Eastern part of Rajasthan.
• Depositional processes by the rivers continuing since long, has united these doabs. However, this mass of alluvium is broken by bluffs, locally known as Dhayas.
• Ganga Plain – This is the largest unit of Great Plain of India. Depending upon its geological variations, this plain can be further sub-divided into the following three divisions :
• (i) Upper Ganga Plain – Compacting the upper part of Ganga plain, this plain is delimited by 300 m contour in Shiwaliks in the North, the Peninsular body in the South and course of Yamuna river in the West and 100 m contour in East. The gradient is comparatively steeper in the North.
• (ii) Middle Ganga Plain – To the East of upper Ganga plain, lies middle Ganga plain occupying Eastern part of Uttar Pradesh and Bihar. This plain is drained by the Ghaghara, the Gandak and the Kosi rivers.

details.summary: Description of the Great Indian Plain, its divisions, and geographical features.

subject: Geography
text:
• Major unit of this plain are Ganga‑Ghaghara doab, Ghaghara‑Gandak doab and Gandak‑Kosi doab (Mithila plain).

• Lower Ganga Plain: Some districts of Bihar and whole of West Bengal are part of this plain. The Northern part of this plain has been formed by sediment deposited by the Tista, Jaldhaka and Torsa.

• This area is marked by drawn and barren plain, a tract of old alluvium between Kosi‑Mahananda corridor in the West and the river Sankosh in the East.

• The delta formation accounts for about two‑thirds of this plain. This is the largest delta in the world. Large part of the coastal deltas is covered by thick inaccessible tidal forests called Sunderbans.

details.summary: The Ganga Plain comprises major doabs and the Lower Ganga Plain, characterized by alluvial deposits and the world's largest delta, the Sunderbans.

subject: Geography
text:
• Western boundary of these plains are formed by Indo‑Bangladesh border as well as boundary of lower Ganga plain.

• The Brahmaputra river enters this plain near Sadiya and flows further to Bangladesh after turning Southwards near Dhubri.

• There are large marshy tracts in this region and Southern tributaries of Brahmaputra also have meandering course and there are good number of bhils and ox‑bow lakes.

details.summary: The Brahmaputra Plain is bounded by the Indo‑Bangladesh border, features the Brahmaputra river, marshy tracts, and ox‑bow lakes.

subject: Geography
text:
• The Peninsular plateau is a tableland composed of mainly Archean gneisses and schists. It was formed due to the breaking and drifting of the Gondwana land and thus making it a part of the oldest landmass.

• This region of the country is surrounded on three sides by water and thus is a Peninsular plateau.

• The plateau has broad and shallow valleys and rounded hills. Narmada river, which flows into a Rift valley, divides the region into two parts namely, the Central Highlands in its North and the Deccan plateau in its South.

details.summary: The Peninsular Plateau is an ancient tableland of Archean rocks, surrounded by water, with broad valleys and the Narmada Rift dividing it into Central Highlands and Deccan Plateau.

subject: Geography
text:
• It is the largest unit of the Peninsular plateau of India with an elevation of 600 m. It is higher in the South than in its North.

• It generally slopes from West to East and various big rivers of Southern India like Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri etc flow through it.

• Karnataka plateau with Archean formations lies to the South of Maharashtra plateau having rocks of lava origin in Northern Karnataka called Malnad region and the rest of the red soil region of the plateau called Maidan.

details.summary: The Deccan Plateau is the largest part of the Peninsular plateau, higher in the South, sloping West to East, and traversed by major rivers.

subject: Geography
text: • It is extension of peninsular plateau, which has been separated by huge fault. Fault is between Rajmahal hills and Meghalaya plateau.

details.summary: The Meghalaya Plateau is an extension of the Peninsular plateau, separated by a major fault between Rajmahal hills and Meghalaya plateau.

subject: Geography
text:
• It lies East of Baghelkhand in the state of Jharkhand covering some parts of Chhattisgarh and West Bengal. Its average elevation is 700 m above sea level.

• It is the storehouse of minerals and a large scale mining of iron, manganese, coal, uranium etc is done in this region.

• Damodar river valley is well‑known for its coal deposits.

details.summary: The Chotanagpur Plateau is a mineral-rich region in Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and West Bengal, known for iron, manganese, coal, uranium and the Damodar river valley.

subject: Geography
text: • Largely in Western Madhya Pradesh and South‑Eastern Rajasthan forms a triangular shape and is typical for having two systems of drainage.

details.summary: The Malwa Plateau is a triangular region in Western Madhya Pradesh and South‑Eastern Rajasthan with dual drainage systems.

subject: Geography
text: • The Marwar uplands of Eastern Rajasthan lie to the East of Aravalli ranges. They are made up of sandstones and limestones of the Vindhyan period.

details.summary: The Marwar Uplands are eastern Rajasthan uplands composed of Vindhyan sandstones and limestones.

subject: Geography
text:
• It runs North‑East to South‑West for 800 km from Delhi through Rajasthan to Palanpur in Gujarat.

• It has a lower elevation between Delhi and Ajmer, where it is characterised by a chain of discontinuous ranges.

• Gurushikhar (1722 m) is the highest peak of the range, located in Abu hills of Rajasthan.

details.summary: The Aravalli Ranges stretch 800 km from Delhi to Gujarat, with lower elevations near Delhi‑Ajmer and Gurushikhar as the highest peak.

subject: Geography
text: • It runs parallel to the Narmada Rift valley as an escarpment in an East‑West direction from Jobat in Gujarat to Sasaram in Bihar for a distance of 1200 km.

details.summary: The Vindhyan Ranges run east‑west parallel to the Narmada Rift valley, spanning 1200 km from Gujarat to Bihar.

subject: Geography
text:
• It is a series of seven mountains that run in the East‑West direction in between Narmada and Tapi rivers. It is an example of block mountain.

• Amarkantak is meeting point of Vindhyan and Satpura range.

details.summary: The Satpura Ranges are seven east‑west mountains between Narmada and Tapi rivers, with Amarkantak as the junction with Vindhyan range.

subject: Geography
text:
• These are discontinuous and irregular and dissected by rivers draining into the Bay of Bengal.

• The Eastern ghats stretch from the South of Mahanadi valley to the Nilgiris in the South. The Eastern ghats are comparatively broader and do not form a continuous water divide.

details.summary: The Eastern Ghats are discontinuous, irregular ranges dissected by rivers, stretching from Mahanadi valley to Nilgiris, lacking a continuous water divide.

subject: Geography
text:
• Sahyadris form the Western edge of the Deccan plateau and lie parallel to the Western coast.

• They form a continuous water divide.

• It run continuously for 1600 km from Maharashtra to Kanyakumari and can be crossed through passes only.

• Highest mountain peak in Western ghat is Annaimudi. The Western ghats are higher than the Eastern ghats.

details.summary: The Western Ghats (Sahyadris) are a continuous 1600 km range along the western coast, forming a water divide, with Annaimudi as the highest peak.

subject: Geography
text:
The plains along the Bay of Bengal, i.e. the Eastern coastal plains are wide and level.

  • In the Northern part, they are referred to as the Utkal plains and Northern Circars, while the Southern part is known as the Coromandel coast.

details.summary: Description of the Eastern Coastal Plains along the Bay of Bengal.

subject: Geography
text:
It run almost parallel between Sahyadris and Arabian sea, from Kanyakumari to Surat.

  • North to South it has seen classified as Kathiawar plain, Konkan plain, Karnataka plain and Malabar plain along the Kerala coast.

details.summary: Description of the Western Coastal Plains between Sahyadris and Arabian Sea.

subject: Geography
text:
Also known as Thar or Great Indian desert, which covers Western Rajasthan and the adjoining part of Pakistan. Desert is called Marusthali.

  • The Eastern part of the Marusthali is rocky, while its Western part is covered by shifting sand dunes locally called dhrian.
  • The Eastern part of Thar desert upto Aravalli range is semi-arid plain, which is known as Rajasthan Bagar. It is drained by a number of seasonal streams creating fertile tracts locally known as Rohi.

details.summary: Description of the Thar (Rajasthan) Desert, its divisions and features.

subject: Geography
text:
These islands group lies close to the Malabar coast of Kerala. This group of 25 islands is composed of small coral islands.

  • The islands North of 11° N latitude are known as Amindivi islands and those South of it are Cannanore islands.

details.summary: Description of the Lakshadweep island group.

subject: Geography
text:
Andaman and Nicobar archipelago has been formed by the extension of the tertiary mountain chains of Arakan yoma. These islands lie close to equator and experience equatorial climate and have thick forest cover.

  • Some of the islands are fringed with coral reefs.
  • The entire group of islands is divided into two broad categories–The Andamans in the North and the Nicobars in the South. The Great Andaman group of islands in the North is separated by the Ten Degree Channel from the Nicobar group in the South.

details.summary: Description of the Andaman and Nicobar island group.

subject: Geography
text:
The Himalayan river system is divided into three major river system, which are as follow

  • The Indus, also known as Sindhu, is the Western most of Himalayan rivers in India. It is one of the largest river basins of the world covering an area of 1165000 sq km (in India it is 321289 sq km) and a total length of 2880 km (in India 1114 km).
  • It originates from a glacier near Bokhar Chu in the Tibetan region near Mansarovar lake. In Tibet, it is known as Singi Khamban or Lion’s mouth.
  • In Jammu and Kashmir, its Himalayan tributaries are Zanskar, Dras, Gartang, Shyok, Shingar, Nubra, Gilgit etc. Its most important tributaries, which join Indus at various places, are Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas and Sutlej.

details.summary: Details of the Indus River System within the Himalayan rivers.

subject: Geography
text:
The Ganga system is the second major drainage system of India. It rises in the Gangotri glacier near Gaumukh (3900 m) in the Uttarakhand. Here, it is known as the Bhagirathi. At Devprayag, the Bhagirathi, meets the Alaknanda, hereafter, it is known as the Ganga.

  • The Alaknanda has its source in the Satopanth glacier above Badrinath. The Alaknanda consists of the Dhauli and the Vishnu Ganga, which meet at Joshimath or Vishnu Prayag. The other tributaries of Alaknanda such as the Pindar joins it at Karna Prayag, while Mandakini or Kali Ganga meets it at Rudra Prayag.
  • The left bank tributaries of Ganga are Ramganga, Gomti, Kali or Sharda, Gandak, Kosi and Mahanadi. The right bank tributaries of Ganga are Yamuna and Son. Yamuna joins the Ganga at Allahabad.
  • Kosi is called as ‘Sorrow of Bihar’ while Damodar is called as ‘Sorrow of Bengal’ as these cause floods in these regions. Hooghly is a distributory of Ganga flowing through Kolkata.

details.summary: Details of the Ganga River System within the Himalayan rivers.

subject: Geography
text: It is one of the largest river of the world. It is known as Tsangpo in Tibet, Dihang or Siang in Arunachal Pradesh, Brahmaputra in Assam and Jamuna in Bangladesh.

details.summary: Description of the Brahmaputra River System.

subject: Geography
text:
Brahmaputra and Ganga River Systems

  • Brahmaputra forms the largest number of riverine islands.
  • Majuli is the largest riverine island in the world.
  • The combined stream of Ganga and Brahmaputra forms the biggest delta in the world, the Sunderbans, covering an area of 58752 sq km. Its major part is in Bangladesh.
  • Brahmaputra is volume-wise the largest river of India, whereas lengthwise Ganga is the longest in India.
  • Tributaries of the Brahmaputra are Manar, Subanshri, Dibang, and Lohit.

details.summary: Facts regarding the Brahmaputra and Ganga rivers, including island formation, delta size, and tributaries.

subject: Geography
text:
The Peninsular River System

  • The Peninsular drainage system is older than the Himalayan one.
  • A large number of the Peninsular rivers are seasonal, as their flow is dependent on rainfall.
  • Most of the major rivers of the Peninsula such as Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna, and Cauvery flow Eastwards and drain into the Bay of Bengal. These rivers make deltas at their mouths.
  • Narmada and Tapi are the only long rivers, which flow Westward and make estuaries rather than making a delta because of their swift flow and steep slopes.
  • The drainage basins of the Peninsular rivers are comparatively smaller in size.

details.summary: Characteristics of the Peninsular river system, including flow direction, delta/estuary formation, and seasonal nature.

subject: Geography
text:
Lakes

A lake is an area of variable size that is filled with water and surrounded by land. Lakes form due to receding glaciers, plate tectonics, volcanism, meandering rivers, landslides, and human damming. Man-made lakes are referred to as reservoirs.

  • Wular lake (Jammu and Kashmir) is the largest fresh water lake in India. Tulbul Navigation Project is located on this.
  • Sambhar, Didwana, Lunkaransar, Panchpadra are some of the important saline lakes of Rajasthan.
  • Ukai reservoir (Gujarat) is a man-made lake on river Tapi. Ranapratap Sagar and Jawahar Sagar (Rajasthan) and Gandhi Sagar (Madhya Pradesh) are located on river Chambal. Govind Sagar (Himachal Pradesh) is a huge reservoir.
  • Nagarjuna Sagar (Andhra-Telangana) on river Krishna, Nizam Sagar (Telangana) on Manjra and Tungabhadra (Karnataka) on Tungabhadra are man-made lakes.
  • Govind Ballabh Pant Sagar (Chhattisgarh-Uttar Pradesh) has been constructed on Rihand. Stanley reservoir is located in Tamil Nadu on Kaveri.
  • Loktak lake (Manipur) is the largest fresh water lake in North-Eastern India. Keibul Lamjao is a floating national park located inside the lake.
  • Chilika lake (Odisha) is the largest lagoon in India. Kolleru lake (Andhra Pradesh) is a lake located around delta region. Pulicat lake (Andhra Pradesh) is a lagoon.
  • Vembanad is located in Kerala. Lonar lake is a crater lake located in Buldhana, Maharashtra.

details.summary: Definition of lakes, causes of formation, and specific facts about major Indian lakes including fresh water, saline, man-made, and lagoon types.

subject: Geography
text:
The Climate of India

  • India has tropical monsoon type of climate. It is greatly influenced by the presence of Himalayas in the North as they block the cold masses from Central Asia. It is because of Himalayas that the monsoons shed their water in India.
  • The Tropic of Cancer (23.5°N) divide India into two almost equal climatic zones, namely; the Northern zone (sub-tropical) and the Southern zone (tropical).

details.summary: Overview of India's tropical monsoon climate, the role of the Himalayas, and the division by the Tropic of Cancer.

subject: Geography
text:
The warm temperature or the sub‑tropical climate of the Northern zone gives it cold winter seasons and hot summer seasons. The Southern tropical climate zone is warmer than the North and does not have a clear cut winter season.

The Southern zone has the midday Sun almost vertically overhead at least twice every year and the Northern zone does not have the mid‑day Sun vertically overhead during any part of the year.

There are various factors which influence the climate of India. Location and latitude play an important role in affecting the climate of India. The Tropic of Cancer divides India into tropical and sub‑tropical climatic regions. The Indian Ocean influences the climate of the peninsular.

The Himalayan range protects India from bitterly cold and dry winds from Central Asia and moreover acts as a barrier in bringing monsoonal rainfall. Heating of the interior part during summer attracts monsoon winds and causes monsoon rainfall. In winter Western disturbances cause snowfall in mountains and rainfall in plains.

details.summary: Overview of climatic zones and influencing factors in India.

subject: Geography
text:
Indian climate is characterised by distinct seasonality. The Indian Meteorological Department (IMD) has recognised the following four distinct seasons:

  • The cold season or winter season.
  • The hot weather season or summer season.
  • The South‑West monsoon season or rainy season.
  • The season of the retreating monsoon or cool season.

details.summary: Four distinct seasons recognized by IMD.

subject: Geography
text:
India is a land of great variety of natural vegetation. The Himalayas are marked with temperate vegetation; Western Ghats and Andaman and Nicobar islands have tropical rain forests; deltaic regions have tropical forests and mangroves; desert and semi‑desert areas are known for variety of bushes and thorny vegetation.

Indian vegetation can be divided into the following groups:

  • Tropical Forests – divided into Moist Forest and Dry Forest.
  • Moist Forest – classified as Tropical Wet Evergreen Forests and Tropical Semi‑Evergreen Forests.
  • Tropical Wet Evergreen Forests – found where annual rainfall exceeds 250 cm; annual temperature about 25°‑27°C; average annual humidity exceeds 77%; dry season is distinctly short; includes areas such as the western side of the Western Ghats, a strip running from North‑East to South‑West across Arunachal Pradesh, upper Assam, Nagaland, Andaman and Nicobar Islands; species include white cedar, mesua, jamun, hopea, mahogany, ebony, etc.
  • Tropical Semi‑Evergreen Forests – found where annual rainfall is 200‑250 cm; mean annual temperature 24°‑27°C; relative humidity about 75%; includes areas such as the western coast, Assam lower slopes of the Eastern Himalayas, Odisha and Andamans; species include aini, semul, kadam, rosewood, kusum, etc.
  • Tropical Moist Deciduous Forests – found where rainfall is 100‑200 cm per annum; mean annual temperature about 27°C; average relative humidity 60‑70%; includes areas along the Western Ghats, a strip along the Shiwalik range including Terai and Bhabar from 77°E to 88°E, hills of Eastern Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Chhotanagpur and part of Odisha and West Bengal; species include teak, sal, laurel, white chuglam, badam, mahua and bamboo, etc.
  • Littoral and Swamp Forests – occur in and around deltas, estuaries and creeks; species include sundari, rhizophora, srwpines, sonnoratic, etc.; can survive in fresh as well as brackish water.
  • Dry Forest – classified as Tropical Dry Evergreen Forests and Tropical Dry Deciduous Forests.
  • Tropical Dry Evergreen Forests – found along the coasts of Tamil Nadu; short stature; annual rainfall about 100 cm; mean annual temperature about 28°C; mean humidity about 15%; species include khirni, jamun, tamarind, neem, etc.
  • Tropical Dry Deciduous Forests – similar to moist deciduous forests; shed leaves in dry season; can grow in areas with rainfall 100‑150 cm per annum; species include teak, axlewood, tendu, palas, bel, etc.
  • Tropical Thorn Forests – generally occur in areas of low rainfall and high temperature; species include Khair, Neem, Babul, Cacti, Palas, etc.

details.summary: Classification of Indian vegetation into tropical forests, dry forests, and thorn forests.

subject: Geography
text:
CDS Pathfinder: The areas are North-Western parts of the country including Rajasthan, South-Western Punjab, Western Haryana, Kutch etc.

Sub-tropical Forest

Sub-tropical forest are of three types

  • Sub-tropical Broad-leaved Hill Forests
    • These forests occur in the Eastern Himalayas to the East of 88°E longitude at altitudes varying from 1000 to 2000 m.
    • The mean annual rainfall is 75 cm to 125 cm, average annual temperature is 18°-21°C. They form luxurious forests of evergreen species.
    • Species of trees—Oaks, Chestnuts, Sals and Pines (on lower and higher margin respectively) etc.
    • They also occur in the Nilgiri and Palni Hills at 1070-1525 m above sea level. These forests are generally called shales.
  • Sub-tropical Moist Pine Forests
    • They are found at the height of 1000 to 2000 m above sea level in the Western Himalayas between 73°E and 88°E longitudes.
    • Chir is the most dominant tree.
  • Sub-tropical Dry Evergreen Forests
    • Found in the Bhabar, the Shivaliks and the Western Himalayas upto about 1000 m above sea-level.
    • Rainfall is between 50 to 100 cm.
    • Olive, Acacia, Modesta and Pistacia are the important species of trees.

details.summary: Overview of sub-tropical forest types in India including broad-leaved hill forests, moist pine forests, and dry evergreen forests with their characteristics and species.

subject: Geography
text:
Temperate Forest

Temperate forest is further divided into 3 types

  • Montane Wet Temperate Forests
    • The forests grow at a height of 1800 to 3000 m above sea level.
    • The mean annual rainfall is 150 cm to 300 cm, the mean annual temperature is about 11°C-14°C and the average relative humidity is over 80%.
    • Species of trees—deodar, chilauni, Indian chestnut, birch, blue pine etc.
    • They are found in the higher hills of Tamil Nadu and Kerala, in the Eastern Himalayan region to the East of 88° E longitude.
  • Himalayan Moist Temperate Forests
    • These forests are mainly composed of coniferous species such as pines, cedars, silver, firs, spruce etc are most important trees.
    • These forests occur in the temperate zone of the Himalayas between 1500 and 3300 m. Rainfall varies from 150 cm to 250 cm.
  • Himalayan Dry Temperate Forests
    • These are coniferous forests with xerophytic shrubs. Deodar, chilgoza, oak, olive etc are the main trees.
    • Such forests are found in the inner dry ranges of the Himalayas.

details.summary: Description of temperate forest types in India: montane wet, Himalayan moist, and Himalayan dry forests with altitude, rainfall, temperature, and tree species.

subject: Geography
text:
MANGROVES

Mangroves are very specialised forest ecosystem of tropical and sub-tropical regions of the world bordering sheltered sea-coasts. They occur all along the Indian coastline in the sheltered estuaries, tidal creeks, backwaters, salt marshes and mudflats.

Mangroves are dominated by salt tolerant halophytic plants of diverse structure and are invaluable marine nurseries for a large variety of fish and other marine fauna. They support a large variety of birds, amphibians and many other local arboreal, benthic and water creatures.

Mangroves have a dense network of aerial roots, which help to aerate the root system and anchor the tree. Sundari is widespread in sunderbans, screw pines, canes and palms are common in deltas, cracks are often lined with Nipa.

details.summary: Characteristics of mangrove ecosystems along Indian coastlines, their structure, species, and ecological importance.

subject: Geography
text:
SOIL

  • Soil is formed when rocks are broken down by the action of wind, water and climate. This process is called weathering.
  • Soil forms different layers of particles of different sizes called Horizons. Each layer is different from the other in thickness texture, colour and chemical composition.

Major Soils of India

On the basis of genesis, colour, composition and location, the soils of India have been classified into the following types

  • Alluvial Soil
    • They cover the largest area in India (40%) and is the most important soil from agricultural point of view. Alluvial soil is widespread in the Northern plains and the river valleys.
    • Through a narrow corridor in Rajasthan, they extend into the plains of Gujarat.
    • Geologically, the alluvium is divided into new alluvium which is known as Khadar and old alluvium, as Bhangar. The newer alluvium is sandy and light coloured, whereas, older alluvium is more clayey, dark coloured and contains lime concretions.
    • The conglomerate deposits in piedmont area are generally known as Bhangar. This soil is suitable for rice, wheat, sugarcane, oil seeds and jute cultivation.
  • Black Soil/Regur Soil
    • The principal region of black soil is the Deccan plateau and its periphery. This is formed from Deccan basalt trap rocks and occur in areas under the monsoon climate, mostly of semi-arid and sub-humid types.
    • This soil is characterised by dark grey to black colour, high swelling and shrinkage, plasticity, deep cracks during summer and poor status of organic matter, nitrogen and phosphorus while this is rich in lime, iron, magnesia and alumina.
    • Impeded drainage and low permeability are the major problems. Cotton is mostly grown on this soil.

details.summary: Soil formation, horizons, and major soil types in India: alluvial and black soil with their properties and agricultural significance.

subject: Geography
text:
Red and Yellow Soils

  • These soils are derived from granite, gneiss and other metamorphic rocks. These soils are formed under well drained condition. These soils are high textured and contain low soluble salts.
  • They are slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, well drained with moderate permeability. They are also poor in nitrogen, phosphorus, lime, humus etc.
  • Red soils cover a large part of Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh and Odisha.

details.summary: Red and Yellow Soils are derived from granite, gneiss and other metamorphic rocks, formed under well drained conditions, high textured, low soluble salts, slightly acidic to slightly alkaline, moderate permeability, poor in nitrogen, phosphorus, lime, humus, and found in Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh and Odisha.

subject: Geography
text:
Laterite Soil

  • Laterite soil is peculiar to India and some of the tropical countries where there is high temperature and heavy rainfall with alternating wet and dry periods. During rainfall silica is leached downwards and iron and aluminum oxide remains in the top layers.
  • In hilly areas they are more acidic than that of low areas. They are less fertile and poor in humus, nitrogen, phosphate and calcium.
  • Lateritic soils are found in Odisha, West Bengal, in some parts of Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Jharkhand and Maharashtra.

details.summary: Laterite soil is peculiar to India and some tropical countries with high temperature and heavy rainfall with alternating wet and dry periods; silica leached downwards, iron and aluminum oxide remain; more acidic in hilly areas; less fertile, poor in humus, nitrogen, phosphate, calcium; found in Odisha, West Bengal, parts of Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Jharkhand and Maharashtra.

subject: Geography
text:
Desert Soil

  • In the North-Western part of India, desert soil occurs over the major parts of Rajasthan, South of Haryana and Punjab and Northern part of Gujarat. The soil in the plains are mostly derived from alluvium and pale brown to brown to yellow brown and fine sandy to loamy fine sand and is structureless.
  • The clay contents low and presence of alkaline Earth carbonates is an important feature. By increasing the water holding capacity, the productivity of the soil can be increased, which involves addition of organic matter and clay.

details.summary: Desert soil occurs in North-Western India over major parts of Rajasthan, South of Haryana and Punjab and Northern Gujarat; derived from alluvium, pale brown to brown to yellow brown, fine sandy to loamy fine sand, structureless; low clay content, presence of alkaline Earth carbonates important; productivity can be increased by adding organic matter and clay to increase water holding capacity.

subject: Geography
text:
Swampy/Peaty Soil

  • Peaty soil originate in areas of heavy rainfall, but inadequate drainage facility.
  • This soil is usually found at the foot hills and extend in strips of varying widths at the foot of Himalayas in Jammu and Kashmir, Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and West Bengal.

details.summary: Peaty soil originates in areas of heavy rainfall with inadequate drainage; found at foot hills and in strips of varying widths at the foot of Himalayas in Jammu and Kashmir, Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and West Bengal.

subject: Geography
text:
Saline Soil

  • Saline soil is formed due to accumulation of soluble salts which consists of chlorides and sulphates of calcium and magnesium.
  • In India, areas around 7 million hectares are salt affected distributed in different states.

details.summary: Saline soil formed due to accumulation of soluble salts (chlorides and sulphates of calcium and magnesium); in India about 7 million hectares are salt affected, distributed across different states.

subject: Geography
text:
Forest Soil

  • As the name suggests, forest soil is formed in the forest areas, where sufficient rainfall is available.
  • The soil vary in structure and texture depending on the mountain environment where these are formed.

details.summary: Forest soil forms in forest areas with sufficient rainfall; its structure and texture vary depending on the mountain environment.

subject: Geography
text:
Soil Erosion and Degradation

  • The destruction of the soil cover is described as soil erosion, while decrease in its fertility is soil degradation. Wind and water are powerful agents of soil erosion because of their ability to remove soil and transport it.
  • Wind erosion is significant in arid and semi-arid regions. In regions with heavy rainfall and steep slopes, erosion by running water is more significant.

details.summary: Soil erosion is destruction of soil cover; soil degradation is decrease in fertility; wind and water are powerful agents; wind erosion significant in arid and semi-arid regions; water erosion more significant in heavy rainfall and steep slope regions.

subject: Geography
text:
AGRICULTURE IN INDIA

India is a vast country endowed with a great variety of natural environments and thus provides conditions for a large number of crops to be grown in various parts.

details.summary: India is a vast country with great variety of natural environments, providing conditions for a large number of crops to be grown in various parts.

subject: Geography
text:
Types of Farming

Various geographical, physical and socio-economic factors are responsible for giving birth to different types of farming in different parts of the country.

details.summary: Various geographical, physical and socio-economic factors lead to different types of farming in different parts of the country.

subject: Geography
text:
Subsistence Farming

  • Farmers cultivate small and scattered holdings with the help of draught animal and family members.
  • The tools and techniques used are primarily primitive and simple and main focus is on food crops.
  • The farmers and his family members consume the entire farm production.

details.summary: Subsistence farming involves small scattered holdings cultivated with draught animal and family members; primitive simple tools; focus on food crops; entire production consumed by farmer's family.

subject: Geography
text:
Plantation Farming

  • It involves growing and processing of a single cash crop purely meant for sale.
  • It is capital intensive and the other necessary things needed are vast estate, managerial ability, technical know how, fertilizer, good transport facilities, processing factory etc.
  • This type of agriculture is mainly practiced in Assam, sub-Himalayan West Bengal and in Nilgiri, Anaimalai and Cardamom hills in South.

details.summary: Plantation farming involves growing and processing a single cash crop for sale; capital intensive; requires vast estate, managerial ability, technical know how, fertilizer, good transport, processing factory; mainly practiced in Assam, sub-Himalayan West Bengal and Nilgiri, Anaimalai and Cardamom hills in South.

subject: Geography
text:
Shifting Agriculture

  • It is practised by the tribals in the forest areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Nagaland, Manipur, Tripura, Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh, Odisha, Madhya Pradesh and Andhra Pradesh.
  • In this type of agriculture, a piece of forest land is cleared mainly by tribal people with felling and burning of trees and crops are grown.
  • Dry paddy, buck wheat, maize, small millets, tobacco and sugarcane are the main crops grown under this type of agriculture.
  • This is a very primitive method of cultivation which results in large scale deforestation and soil erosion especially on the foothill sides.

details.summary: Shifting agriculture practised by tribals in forest areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Nagaland, Manipur, Tripura, Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh, Odisha, Madhya Pradesh and Andhra Pradesh; forest land cleared by felling and burning; main crops: dry paddy, buck wheat, maize, small millets, tobacco, sugarcane; primitive method causing large scale deforestation and soil erosion especially on foothill sides.

subject: Environment
text: Organic farming is a new trend of farming in which all input used for farming are natural, no chemicals are used. Green manures and compost are used. Sikkim is the first organic state of India.

details.summary: Organic farming uses natural inputs and compost, with Sikkim as the first organic state in India.

subject: Environment
text:
Three types of cropping seasons are found in India:

  • Kharif – Requires much water, long hot weather for growth, grown in June with the arrival of South‑East monsoon. Examples: rice, jowar, maize, cotton, groundnut, jute, tobacco, bajra, sugarcane, pulses, etc.
  • Rabi – Grown in winter, requires cool climate during growth and warm climate during germination of seeds and maturation. Sowing is done in November and harvested in April–May. Examples: wheat, gram, mustard, rapeseed, etc.
  • Zaid – A brief cropping season practised in irrigated areas, sown in February–March, harvested in June. Examples: urad, moong, watermelons.

details.summary: Kharif, Rabi, and Zaid are the three cropping seasons in India with distinct climatic requirements.

subject: Environment
text:
Indian crops are divided into the following categories:

  • Food Crops – Rice, wheat, maize, millets, jowar, bajra, ragi, pulses, gram, tur.
  • Cash Crops – Cotton, jute, sugarcane, tobacco, oilseeds, groundnut, linseed, sesamum, castor seed, rapeseed, mustard.
  • Plantation Crops – Tea, coffee, spices, cardamom, chillies, ginger, turmeric, coconut, rubber.
  • Horticulture Fruits – Apple, peach, pear, apricot, almond, strawberry, mango, banana, citrus, food and vegetables.

details.summary: Classification of major crops into food, cash, plantation, and horticulture categories.

subject: Environment
text:
Human beings interact with nature through technology and create institutions to accelerate economic development. A resource is a source or supply from which benefit is produced, an economic or productive factor required to accomplish an activity or undertake an enterprise and achieve desired outcomes.

Human Resources – The set of individuals who make up the workforce of an organisation or economy. Human capital is sometimes used synonymously with human resources.

Natural Resources – Naturally occurring substances that are considered valuable in their relatively unmodified (natural) form. A natural resource’s value rests in the amount of the material available and the demand for it, determined by its usefulness to production.

Classification of Natural Resources – Natural resources are mostly classified into renewable and non‑renewable resources. Renewable resources can renew themselves if not over‑harvested and used sustainably. The rate of sustainable use of a renewable resource is determined by its replacement rate and the amount of standing stock of that particular resource.

details.summary: Overview of human and natural resources, including classification of natural resources into renewable and non‑renewable.

subject: Geography
text:
Non-Renewable Resources

  • It is a natural resource which are present in a fixed quantity and it cannot be used again once it gets exhausted.

Mineral Resources

  • A mineral is an aggregate of two or more than two elements. A mineral has a definite chemical composition, atomic structure and is formed by inorganic processes.
  • In economic geography, the term mineral is used for any naturally occurring material that is mined and is of economic value.
  • Minerals generally occur in the Earth’s crust in the form of ore.
  • The availability and per capita consumption of minerals is taken as an important indicator to assess the economic development of a country.

details.summary: Definition of non-renewable resources and minerals, their composition, and economic significance.

subject: Geography
text:
The Mineral Regions of India

  • The North-Eastern Peninsular Belt: It comprises of Chota Nagpur plateau, Odisha plateau and West Bengal. It is the richest mineral belt of India. Coal and Iron are very abundant in the region.
  • Central Belt: It comprises of Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh and Maharashtra. It contains deposits of manganese, bauxite, limestone, marble, coal, gems, mica, iron etc.
  • The Southern Belt: It comprises Karnataka plateau but extends upto Tamil Nadu upland. It is rich in ferrous minerals and bauxite but lacks in coal deposits.
  • The South-Western Belt: It includes Southern Karnataka, Kerala and Goa. It has deposits of iron-ore, garnet and China clay, Monazite sand etc.
  • The North-Western Belt: It extends along the Aravalis in Rajasthan and in adjoining part of Gujarat. It is rich in non-ferrous minerals (copper, lead, zinc), uranium, mica, precious stones, aquamarine and emerald etc.

details.summary: Description of the five major mineral belts in India: North-Eastern Peninsular, Central, Southern, South-Western, and North-Western.

subject: Geography
text:
Metallic Mineral Mines

  • Iron: Kemmangundi, Sandur and Hospet (Karnataka); Barbil-Koira (Odisha), Bailadila and Dalli-Rajhara (Chhattisgarh), North Goa.
  • Manganese: Found in Karnataka, Odisha, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra.
  • Chromite: Found in Odisha, Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh.
  • Copper: Malanjkhand Belt (Balaghat, Madhya Pradesh), Khetri-Singhana Belt (Jhunjhun), Singhbhum (Jharkhand).
  • Bauxite: Found in Odisha, Gujarat, Jharkhand, Maharashtra, Chhattisgarh.
  • Gold: Kolar and Hutti (Karnataka), Ramgiri in Anantapur (Andhra Pradesh).

Non-Metallic Mineral Mines

  • Limestone: Found in Andhra Pradesh, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Chhattisgarh.
  • Dolomite: About 90% of the dolomite is found in Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Gujarat, Karnataka, West Bengal.
  • Asbestos: Rajasthan, Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka.
  • Gypsum: Found in Rajasthan, Jammu and Kashmir.
  • Graphite: Occurs in Kalahandi, Bolangir (Odisha) and Bhagalpur (Bihar).

subject: Geography
text:
Energy Resources in India

  • India is a fast growing country and therefore, the demand for the energy is also continuously growing. India has exploited almost all the sources of energy such as hydroelectricity, thermal energy, nuclear energy, solar energy, wind energy etc.
  • The natural resources for electricity generation in India are unevenly dispersed and concentrated in a few pockets.
  • Hydro resources are located in the Himalayan foothills and in the North-Eastern Region (NER).
  • Coal reserves are concentrated in Jharkhand, Odisha, West Bengal, Chhattisgarh, parts of Madhya Pradesh, whereas lignite is located in Tamil Nadu and Gujarat.
  • North Eastern region, Sikkim and Bhutan have vast untapped hydro potential estimated to be about 35000 MW in NER, about 8000 MW in Sikkim and about 15000 MW in Bhutan.

details.summary: Overview of energy demand, distribution of hydro and coal resources, and untapped hydro potential in NER, Sikkim, and Bhutan.

subject: Geography
text:
Conventional Sources of Energy

  • The conventional sources of energy are generally non-renewable sources of energy, which are being used since a long time. Conventional sources of energy are coal, petroleum and natural gas.

Thermal Energy

  • Thermal electricity is produced with the help of coal, petroleum and natural gas.
  • About 65% of the total electricity produced is thermal in character.
  • Thermal electricity has special significance in those areas, where geographical conditions are not very favourable for generation of hydroelectricity.
  • It accounts for more than half of the installed capacity in 14 states.

Hydroelectricity

  • The hydroelectric power generation in India made a humble start at the end of the 19th century, with the commissioning of electricity supply in Darjeeling during 1897, followed by a hydropower station at Sivasamudram in Karnataka during 1902.

Atomic Energy

  • Nuclear power is fourth largest source of electricity in India after, thermal, hydroelectricity and conventional source of power.

details.summary: Details on conventional energy sources including thermal energy statistics, history of hydroelectricity in India, and the ranking of nuclear power.

subject: Science & Technology
text:
Non-Conventional Energy Sources

  • Solar energy
  • Wind energy
  • Biomass energy
  • Fuel cell
  • Electric vehicles
  • Tidal energy
  • Hydrogen energy
  • Geothermal energy

The renewable energy programme in India began with the establishment of the Department of Non-Conventional Energy Sources in 1982. The Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency was set up in 1987. In 1992, DNES was converted into the Ministry of Non-Conventional Energy Sources, which was renamed in 2006 as the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE). The ministry has since undertaken various programmes on new technologies.

details.summary: Overview of non-conventional energy sources and the evolution of India's renewable energy policy.

subject: Economics
text:
Economic Activities

Human activities that generate income are broadly grouped into five categories:

  • Primary Activities – Directly dependent on the environment; include hunting, gathering, pastoral activities, fishing, forestry, agriculture, mining, and quarrying.
  • Secondary Activities – Add value to natural resources by transforming raw materials into valuable products.
  • Tertiary Activities – Provide services that require special skills, such as health, education, law, and governance.
  • Quaternary Activities – Centered around research and development, involving specialized knowledge and technical skills.
  • Quinary Activities – Focus on the creation, rearrangement, and interpretation of new and existing technologies.

details.summary: Classification of economic activities from primary to quinary.

subject: Geography
text:
INDUSTRIES

The industries sector is regarded as the growth engine for economic development of a nation. As India is an emerging economy, in the post reform era 22% of the employment generation has been attributed to industrial sector.

Cotton Textile Industry

The first modern cotton textile mill was established in Bombay in 1854 by local parsi entrepreneurs with the name of Bombay spinning and weaving company. Mumbai is called cottonopolis of India and Ahmedabad is called Manchester of India. Coimbatore is called Manchester of South India and Kanpur is called Manchester of Uttar Pradesh.

Distribution

  • Maharashtra (Mumbai, Sholapur, Pune, Kolhapur, Satara, Wardha, Aurangabad and Amravati)
  • Gujarat (Ahmedabad, Vadodara, Rajkot, Surat, Bhavnagar, Porbandar, Maurvi and Viramgam)
  • Tamil Nadu (Chennai, Tirunelveli, Madurai, Tuticorin, Salem, Virudhnagar and Pollachi)
  • Karnataka (Bengaluru, Belgaum, Mangaluru, Chitradurga, Gulbaraga and Mysore)
  • Uttar Pradesh (Kanpur, Etawah, Modinagar, Moradabad, Bareilly, Agra, Meerut and Varanasi)
  • Madhya Pradesh (Indore, Gwalior, Ujjain and Bhopal)
  • Rajasthan (Kota, Jaipur, Sri Ganganagar, Bhilwara and Udaipur)

Woollen Textile Industry

The first woollen textiles mill was set-up in 1876 at Kanpur. Jammu and Kashmir is a large producer of handloom woollen goods.

Distribution

  • Punjab (Dhariwal, Amritsar, Ludhiana, Ferozpur)
  • Maharashtra (Mumbai)
  • Uttar Pradesh (Kanpur, Mirzapur, Agra and Tanakpur)

Jute Textile Industry

First modern jute mill was set-up in 1855 at Rishra near Kolkata. India is the largest producer of raw jute and jute good production, whereas it is second largest exporter of jute goods after Bangladesh.

Distribution

  • West Bengal
  • Bihar
  • Uttar Pradesh
  • Andhra Pradesh
  • Assam
  • Odisha
  • Tripura
  • Chhattisgarh

Silk Textile Industry

India is the second largest producer of natural silk, after China and is the only country producing all four varieties or natural silk viz Mulberry, Tasar, Eri and Muga of which golden yellow Muga silk is unique in India.

Distribution

  • Karnataka (leading producer)
  • West Bengal
  • Bihar

Rubber Industry

The first factory of synthetic rubber was set-up at Bareilly.

Distribution

  • Bareilly (Uttar Pradesh)
  • Baroda (Gujarat) Synthetic rubber units
  • Mumbai
  • Ahmedabad
  • Amritsar-Reclaimed rubber units

Tea Industry

Tea cultivation in India was first started in the mid-19th century in Darjeeling, Assam and Nilgiris. Nearly 98% of the tea production comes from Assam, West Bengal, Tamil Nadu and Kerala, while the rest of it comes from Karnataka, Terai region of Uttarakhand, Himachal Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur and Tripura.

Sugar Industry

Uttar Pradesh is the leading producer of sugar.

Distribution

  • Uttar Pradesh (Gorakhpur, Deoria, Basti, Gonda, Meerut, Saharanpur, Muzaffarnagar, Bijnor and Moradabad)
  • Bihar (Darbhanga, Saran, Champaran and Muzaffarpur)
  • Punjab (Phagwara and Dhuri)
  • Haryana (Ambala, Rohtak and Panipat)
  • Maharashtra (Nashik, Pune, Satara, Sangli, Kolhapur and Solapur)
  • Karnataka (Munirabad, Shimoga and Mandya)

Paper Industry

The first paper mill in the country was set-up at Serampore (Bengal) in 1832, which failed. In 1870, a fresh venture was started at Ballygunge near Kolkata. Raw material Bamboo (70%), Salai wood (12%), Sabai (9%), Bagasses (4%) and Waste paper and Rags (5%).

  • Hindustan Paper Corp
  • Vellore
  • Mysore Paper mill
  • Bhadravati
  • Maharashtra (Mumbai, Pune, Ballarpur and Kamptee produce paper and vikhroli)
  • Andhra Pradesh (Rajahmundry and Sirpur)
  • Madhya Pradesh (Indore, Bhopal and Shandol)
  • Karnataka

subject: Transport
text: India has the fifth largest railway network in the world after the USA, Russia, China and Canada. The Indian railway operates in three different gauges: Broad, Meter and Narrow. It is the largest public sector undertaking of the country and the world’s largest railway network under single management. The first Indian railway line in India was operated for public traffic in 1853 between Mumbai and Thane over a distance of 34 km. The first electric train in India was ‘Deccan Queen’, introduced in 1929 between Bombay and Poona. The headquarters of Indian railway is in New Delhi. The fastest train in India is the Gatimaan Express, whose maximum speed is 160 km/hr. Indian railways has the second biggest electrified system in the world after Russia. The total route covered is approximately 63000 km. Vivek Express has the longest train route in India connecting Dibrugarh and Kanyakumari. It is 8th longest in the world. The second longest train route is of ‘Himsagar Express’ from Jammu Tavi to Kanyakumari covering 3726 km and passes through ten states. The oldest steam engine ‘Fairy Queen’ still runs on rail. Uttar Pradesh has largest railway network in India. Mumbai CST is busiest railway junction of India. Railway track electrification was introduced in early 1920s. The first two sections from Victoria Terminus to Kurla and from Victoria Terminus to Bandra were electrified. About 26% of the rail lines have been electrified. Anil Kakodkar Committee was constituted for Rail Safety in 2011.

details.summary: Indian Railways is the world’s largest railway network under single management, with a vast history and extensive electrification.

text:
Roadways

In 1943, Nagpur plan classified the roads into four categories:

  • National highway
  • State highway
  • District roads
  • Village roads

Indian road network is the 2nd largest in the world.

India has a road network of over 4.8 million km.

National highways are constructed and maintained by Central Public Works Department (CPWD).

Expressway

  • Expressway is a highway especially planned for high speed traffic, limited point of access or exit.
  • Expressways are the highest class of roads in the Indian roads network. Indian roads has approx 942 km expressway.
  • The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways is already in the process of preparing a draft for creation of a National Expressway Authority of India (NEAI) on the line NHAI.

Some Important Information Regarding the National Highways

  • NH44 is the longest NH of India, running from Srinagar to Kanyakumari.
  • NH5 and NH17 run along the Eastern and the Western coast respectively.
  • NH15 represents the border road in Rajasthan desert.
  • NH47A is the shortest highway in the Indian highway network.
  • Maximum length of highway is present in State of Uttar Pradesh.

National Highway Development Programme (NHDP)

  • The Golden Quadrilateral project involves connectivity of:
    • Delhi to Kolkata (NH2)
    • Delhi to Mumbai (NH8, NH76 and NH79)
    • Mumbai to Chennai (NH4, NH7 and NH46)
    • Chennai to Kolkata (NH5, NH6 and NH60)

  • North‑South and East‑West corridors:
    • NS corridor connects Srinagar to Kanyakumari.
    • EW corridor connects Porbandar (Gujarat) to Silchar (Assam).

Airways (for context)

  • 1935 – ‘Tata Airlines’ started operation between Mumbai and Thiruvananthapuram; 1937 – Mumbai to Delhi.
  • 1953 – Private airlines nationalised; Indian Airlines and Air India formed.
  • 1995 – International Airports Authority of India and National Airports Authority merged to form Airports Authority of India, which manages the Civil Aviation Training College at Allahabad and National Institute of Aviation Management and Research at Delhi.

text:
General Facts about Ports

  • The waterways authority in India divides Indian ports into three categories: major, minor, and intermediate.
  • India has about 200 ports, with 13 major and the rest intermediate and minor.
  • Project Sagarmala has been conceived for development.

Ports of Eastern Coast

  • Kolkata: Oldest port, India’s riverine port having two dock system.
  • Paradip: It handles iron ore and some amounts of coal and dry cargo.
  • Chennai: All weather port having deep drafted berth, oil jetties, iron ore terminals, etc.
  • Visakhapatnam: Seaport and well known for its outstanding performance. It serves the Bhilai and Rourkela steel plant.
  • Tuticorin: Artificial deep sea harbour, all weather port offer direct weekly container service to USA.
  • Ennore: First corporatised major port in India.

Ports of Western Coast

  • Mumbai: It handles maximum traffic, natural harbour mostly petroleum and dry cargo.
  • Kandla: Tidal port and important traffic handled are crude oil, petroleum, edible oil, foodgrains.
  • Marmagao: It handles iron ore. It has a naval base.
  • New Mangaluru: It is an all weather port.
  • Cochin: Major natural port in Willingdon Island.
  • Jawaharlal Nehru: It is called as Nhava Sheva.

Important Facts

  • Largest container port of India is Jawaharlal Nehru port in Mumbai.
  • The largest natural port is in Visakhapatnam.
  • Kandla in Gujarat is a tidal port. It has been made into a free trade zone.
  • New Mangaluru port is also called the ‘Gateway of Karnataka’.
  • Mumbai port is the busiest port of India.
  • Mundra port is largest private port of India.
  • The Union Cabinet has given its in-principle approval for setting up a major port of Enayam near Colachel in Tamil Nadu. On completion the port will become country’s 13th major port.

subject: Geography
text:
Population

  • Population geography is closely related to demography. It is concerned with the study of demographic processes and their consequences in and environmental context.
  • Population density is the degree of compaction in population the closeness of persons living on a given surface, the spatial balance of their social and economic assets.
  • Population density shows the population pressure on land resource.
  • There are various ways to measure population density such as crude or arithmetic density, nutritional or physiological density, agricultural density, economic density etc.
  • Among them arithmetic density is mostly used.

details.summary: Definition of population geography, population density, and methods of measuring population density.

subject: Geography
text:
Population distribution and density are influenced by a variety of factors:

  • Physical factors: land forms, vegetation, soils, and water supply
  • Climatic factors: temperature, rainfall, etc.
  • Availability of natural resources
  • Means of transport and communication

Population growth refers to the change in population and can be measured in absolute numbers and in percentage. The basic components of population growth are fertility, mortality, and migration.

Migration is the permanent, seasonal, or temporary shift of residence for a substantial duration.

Population composition refers to measurable characteristics that differentiate one group from another, such as age‑sex composition, literacy, rural‑urban composition, and occupation.

India is one of the most populous countries in the world, with a 2011 census population of 121.01 crore. Uttar Pradesh is the most populous state (19.95 crore), followed by Maharashtra, Bihar, West Bengal, and Andhra Pradesh. Sikkim has the least proportion of the population.

India’s average population density is 382 persons per sq km. Arunachal Pradesh has the lowest density (17), while Bihar has the highest (1102). Among Union Territories, Delhi has the highest density (11297) and Andaman & Nicobar the lowest (46).

Growth of population in India has gone through four phases:

  1. Period of stagnant growth rate (before 1921)
  2. Period of steady growth (1921‑1951)
  3. Period of rapid growth (1951‑1981)
  4. Period of declining growth rate (after 1981)

During 2001‑2011, the declining growth rate was 17.64%. Kerala registered the lowest growth rate (4.86%) whereas Daman and Diu had the highest (53.54%).

Rural‑urban composition: 68.84% of the population lives in rural areas and 31.16% in urban areas. Goa is the most urbanised state (62.17% urban), followed by Tamil Nadu (48.45%), Kerala (47.72%), and Maharashtra (45.23%). Himachal Pradesh is predominantly rural.

Sex ratio: number of females per thousand males. According to the 2011 census, India’s sex ratio is 943.

Literacy: overall literacy rate is 74.04%. Rural literacy is 68.9% and urban literacy is 84.9%. Female literacy is 79.92% in urban areas and 58.75% in rural areas.

Tribes of India: India hosts a large number of indigenous peoples (Adivasis) who are largely dependent on hunting, agriculture, and fishing. Major tribal groups include Gonds, Santhals, Khasis, Angamis, Bhils, Bhutias, and Great Andamanese.
